Mr. Bur don reported from the Committee, who mere Report <mG appointed to take into Consideration an Act, made in the Thirteenth Year of the Reign of His present Ma- Aiu! jesty, intituled, "An Act to explain, amend, and reduce into One Act of Parliament, the Statutes now " in being, for the Amendment and Preservation of the " Public Highways within that Part of Great Britain ‘‘.called England, and for other Purposes;" and also, an Act, made in the Thirty-fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for the more " effectually repaving of such Parts of the Highways " of this Kingdom as are to be repaired by Two Pa- rilhesand also, another Act, made in the Thirty-fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for varying some of the Provisions " in an Act of the Thirteenth Year of His present Majesty's Reign, respecting the Public Highways within " that Part of Great Britain called England, which relate to the Performance of Statute Dutyand also, an Act, made in the Thirteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act to explain,

" amend, and reduce into One Act of Parliament, the " General Laws now in being for regulating the Turnpike Roads in that Part of Great Britain called " England, and for other Purposes and to report their Observations, together with their Opinion thereupon, to the House; That the Committee had considered the said Acts accordingly, and had come to several Resolutions thereupon, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Resolutions of the Committee were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That it would tend to the more effectual Execution of the Laws for the Preservation of the Highways, if Commissioners were appointed, in certain Cafes, with the same Powers and Authorities as the Justices of the Peace now exercise at their Special Highway Sessions, and were to hold Meetings within their respective Limits or Divisions.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That it should be competent for the Justices of the Peace, of any Limit or Division, assembled at their Special SelEons of Highways, to apply to the Justices of the County, at their next General Quarter Sessions, or any Adjournment thereof, by any Writing under their Hands, to appoint Commissioners of Highways, not being Turnpikes, within their Limit or Division; and that the Justices, at their General Quarter or Adjourned Sessions, should appoint Commissioners, provided One Month previous Notice shall have been given, by the Clerk of the said Justices, in (bme Newspaper, usually circulated within such County, of such intended Application, and in case it shall appear to the Justices, at their laid General Quarter or Adjourned Sessions, that the major Part of the Justices, of the Limit or Division so applying, do concur in the said Application.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That such Commissioners should conlift of the Justices of the Peace a^ing for such Limit or Division, together with such Persons as may be appbinted by the General Quarter Sessions, and that they should be required to have a proper Qualification.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee *

That the Special Highway Sessions of the Justices, and the

40 Geo. III. ai° M. 323

the Meetings of the Commissioners, where Commissioners shall be appointed, should be holden by Adjournments, not exceeding the Space of Three Calendar Months.

Resolved', That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Clerk of the Justices, at their Special Highway Sessions, should aft as Clerk to the Commissioners, where Commissioners may be appointed to meet; and that the Proceedings of the Justices or Commissioners, in their respective Limits or Divisions, should be returned to {he Clerk of the Peace annually, at the Michaelmas General Quarter SeiEons.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Justices of the Peace, at their Special Highway Sessions, or the said Commissioners, should have Power to appoint, at their Discretion, a superintending Surveyor or Surveyors, with a Salary, for the Whole, or for any Part of their Limit or Division, proportioning his or their Salary among the Parishes, Townships, or Places, to which he or they shall be appointed within the said Limit or Division, so as that the said Salary, together with any Salary which may be allowed to any Parish or Township Surveyor, if any such Surveyor shall be appointed with a Salary, do not in the Whole exceed One-eighth Part of a Rate of Six Pence in the Pound, as limited by the Act of 13 III. Cap. 78. Sec. t.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in Parishes where Two or more Surveyors shall have been appointed, and pach has Charge of the Roads of a feporate District, the whole Parish should be responsible for the Whole of the Roads, unless the several Districts should have separate Overseers, and provide (Separately for the Maintenance of their Poor.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is expedient that all Assessments which, by the Act of 13 Geo. III. Cap. 78. the Justices at their Special Highway Sessions are empowered to charge upon the Parishes, Townships, or Places, within their Limit or Division, should be charged by the General Quarter Sessions, or feme Adjournment thereof, upon the usual Application of the Surveyor or Surveyors of such Pa-Tilhes, Townships, or Places, or of the Surveyor, with a Salary appointed, by the Justices or Commissioners, to the said Justices at their Special Sessions, or to the said Commissioners at their Meetings, and upon their Certificate to the General Quarter or Adjourned Sessions, of the same being necessary.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Laws now in Force are insufficient for the Removal of Obstructionss by Snow or otherwise.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Justices of the Peace, at their Special Sessions, or the said Commissioners, should have Power to direct the Highways to bfc opened within their respective Limits or Divisions, in Cafes of Obstructions by Snow, in 0 a summary Manner, and to order Payment of such Sums as may be expended for that Purpose out of any Compositions. Forfeitures, or Rates of the Parish, Township, or Place, inhere such Obstructions may occur, provided that no such Order should be made, unless the Highway so to be opened be an Highway leading from Market Town to Market Town, and that the Expences of clearing away the said Obstructions should in no same amount to more than a Sum equal in the Whole to an Assessment of Six Pencefii the Pound upon such Parish", Township, or Place, which Assessment the Justices or Commissioners may, by Application to the next General Quarter Sessions, be empowered to levy, or may take out of the Composition, paid in lieu of the Statute Labour within such Parish, Township, or Place, according to the Circumstances of the Cafe.

Rcjclved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in case of any wilful or negligent Obstruction in ary Road which may require immediate Removal, the Surveyor should have Power to remove the fame, at the VOL. 55.

Expence of the Person causing such Obstruction, without giving previous Notice for such Removal.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Justices of the Peace, at their Special Highway Sessions, or the said Commissioners, should have Power (on the Application of the Inhabitants of any Parish, Township, or Place, within their Limit or Division, or the major Part of them, convened' at their usual Place of Meeting, proper Notice thereof having been given) to apply to the General Quarter Sessions for an Assessment, not exceeding Annually the Rate which the Quarter Sessions are now authorized to im-

?>(e, to be laid upon the said Parish, Township, or lace, for a limited Number of Years, and that the said Justices of the Peace, at their Special Highway Sessions, or the said Commissioners, should have Power to borrow Money upon the Assessment so laid for the Repair of the Highways within such Parish, Township, or Place, and to appoint the Person or Persons to whom, any Money so borrowed shall be entrusted, which Money so to be borrowed, the Justices, or Commissioners aforesaid, should cause to be paid off, by Instalments, out of the said Assessment.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Laws now in being are insufficient, with respect to such Highways as are repaired Ratione Tenure?.

Resolved, That it Is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Justices of the Peace, at their Special Highway Sessions, or the said Commissioners, should have Power to agree with such Persons as are liable to the Repair of the Highways Ratione for a certain

Number of Years, as to the Duty to be performed, and the Sums to be paid, for the Purpose of repairing such Highways.

Resolved, That it is tlje Opinion of this Committee, That, in case the Persons liable to the Repair of Roads Ratione Tenura shall refuse or neglect to enter into an

Agreement with the Justices of the Peace, at their Special Highway Sessions, or with the Commissioners, at their Meeting of Highways, it should be lawful for the said Justices or Commissioners to present the fame, with their Proceedings thereon, to the General Quarter Sessions of the Peace, giving, at the lead. Ten Days previous Notice thereof to the Persons so refusing or ne-glefting; and, in case the said Persons shall appear to traverse the said Presentment, then the same should be tried, at the General Quarter Sessions, by a Jury of the Country, as to the Fast of the proposed Agreement being reasonable, and such as ought to have been ac- , cepted, upon whose Verdict the Justices, at Quarter Sessions, should ground their Order for the Statute Work, or Composition in lieu of the Repair Ratione Tenura, which Order should be final and conclusive, provided that, in case the Verdict of such Jury shall be in Favour of such Person so presented, he should be allowed his reasonable Costs and Charges out of the County Rates, or in case the said Persons shall not appear, or shall submitto the Determination of the Justices, then the said Agreement should be thenceforth valid and conclusive, and the Surveyor or Surveyors, appointed by the said Justices or Commissioners, should continue thenceforth, until the End of the Term for which such Agreement purports to be made to require, and call out the Labour and Composition of such Persons so repairing the Highways Ratione , under

the same Provisions and Penalties as are in Force relative to the Statute Labour and Composition of Parishes, Townships, or Places, by the existing Laws.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is expedient that the same Powers, which the Surveyor or Surveyors are now authorized to exercise for procuring Materials to repair the Highways, should be extended for the procuring of Materials to repair Highways Ratione Tenura, and that, in certain Cafes, upon

the

Wendlcbury Inclosure Bill, passed.

the Confines of Counties, Ridings, Limits, or Divisions, the Powers of procuring Materials ought to be extended and enlarged.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Provisions relative to Removal of Obstructions, and also those respecting the Repair of Highways Ra-tione Tennr.-e, ought to be extended to the Turnpike Roads, with a Power to the Commissioners of Turnpikes to apportion the Expence of removing such Obstructions between the Trust and the Parish, Township, or Place, where they have occurred.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Rate of Composition for Statute Duty, as fixed by the Laws now in being, ought to be advanced in some Proportion to the advanced Value of Labour.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Justices of the Peace, at their General Quarter Sessions, should have Power to order any Expences incurred by the Justices or Commissioners, under this or the General Highway Ad, by the Presentment of Roads, or other Proceedings relative to the Repair of Highways, to be paid out of the General County Rates.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Restrictions of the General Highway Ad, as to the Number of Horsesand other Beasts of Draught, to be used in Waggons and Carts upon the Highways, are insufficient.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Carriage of Timber Trees upon the Turnpike Roads, during the Winter Months, ought to be fub-jeded to additional Tolls.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That further Provisions are necessary for preventing the improper Construction of Wheels, and the Allowance of an additional Number of Horlesand other Beasts of Draught, in consequence of the Use of such Wheels upon the Turnpike Roads.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of thi6 Committee, That the Act of 34 Geo. III. Cap. 74. should be repealed, for the Purpose of reviving the Provisions of the Act of 13 Geo. III. Cap. 78. respecting Statute Labour, but that the Provisions contained in the said Act of 34 Geo. III. Cap. 74. respecting Labourers, and also, respecting the Exemption of certain Poor Persons from Payment of the Rates to which they are liable for the Repair of the Highways, should be re-enacted.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is necessary to remove certain Doubts which have arisen as to the Penalties levied at Weighing Engines for Overweight, and the Exemptions which have been claimed thereupon.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Restrictionsvvhichexist in certain Turnpike Acts, with respect.to the Erection of Gates, ought not to extend to the Erection of Weighing Engines in such Places as the Trustees shall think necessary upon the said Turnpike Roads.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into further Consideration upon Wednesday Morning next.

Ordered, That such a Number of Copies of the said Report be printed, as shall be sufficient for the Use of the Members of the House.

MR. Tyner reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the several Persons, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and other Trustees for executing Two several Acts, passed in the Thirtieth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, and in the Fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing and widening the Roads leading from Spalding High through Littleivcrth, and by , and over

Deeping Stone Bridge, in the County of Lincoln, to Ma-:ey Outgang, in the County of Northampton, adjoining to the High Road there, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Turnpike Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the lame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Acts were read: And,

Mr. Wildbcre Wilkinson, being examined, said, That

the Trustees have proceeded to put the said Acts in Execution, and for that Purpose have borrowed several considerable Sums of Money on the Credit of the Tolls authorized to be taken on the said Roads, which Money together with the Tolls, have been duly applied according to the Directions of the said Acts; but that the said Money so borrowed cannot be repaid, nor can the said Roads be properly amended, and kept in Repair, unless the Term of the said Acts, which is near expiring, be continued, and several of the Powers and Provisions thereof altered and amended, and some further Tolls granted.

Petition in favour of Kent Gaol Bill.

3 $6 20 Martii. 1800.

Peace acting for the Western Division of the County of Kent, to purchase a convenient Piece of Ground for building a Gaol for the said County, and for empowering the said Justices to apply Part of the County Stock of the said Division towards the lame, and for other Purposes therein mentioned; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners are urged by Sense of that Duty which they, as Magistratej, owe to the County of Kent at large, to represent that, by the Provisions of the said one Part of the said County, called The

Division, hath been burthened, solely and exclusively, not only with the Charges and Expences of purchasing the Ground upon which the County Gaol at Maidstone now (lands, and of building the said Gaol, but hath been, from the Time of the passing of the said Act, and is now also, burthened with, and liable to, the Charges and Expences of repairing the said Gaol, and of making such Additions thereto as have been, or may be, found necessary, in order to accommodate the great Numbers of Prisoners confined therein,' by reason of the same being a Gaol for the whole County of Kent> and not exclusively a Gaol for any One Part or Division of the said County; and that, for a Series of Years pad, sanctioned by no Law but Custom, the said County of Kent hath been divided into an Eallern and Western Division, and the Eallern Division hath contributed towards the Maintenance of such Prisoners only as were sent to the Felons Part of the said Gaol from such Division; and the Wellern Division hath, at the Charge of the Inhabitants of such Division, supported the Prisoners sent from the said Wellern Division to the said Part tof the said Gaol, and that such Custom is partial, unjust, and oppressive, inasmuch as, from the Contiguity of the said Wellern Division to the Me-, tropolis, the Prisoners committed from that Division far exceed in Number the Prisoners from the Eallern Division, and the consequent Expence therefore imposed on the Inhabitants of the Western Division exceeds; in an unreasonable Proportion, the Expence of the Eallern Division; and that, independent of the Repair of the said Gaol being borne exclusively by the Inhabitants of the said Western Division, they support also, at their foie Charge, Two Bridewells, situate in the said Western Division; viz. Oneat Maidstone aforesaid, and Oneat Dartford; and that all Debtors in the

Cullodyof the Sheriff of the said County are confined in the said Gaol at Ma, and that the Expence charged to the County for their Maintenance, whether they be font from the Eallern or Western Division of the said County, is borne solely by the Inhabitants of the said Western Division; and that the said Gaol is the only Prison of the said Sheriff, and the Keeper of it is the only Gaoler from whom the said Sheriff takes a Security; and that as the Justices, as well of the Eall-cmasof the Western Division of the said County, are appointed by One and the same Commission, and the Police of the County is general, the Petitioners conceive that the Expence incident to the due Administration of it ought to attach on the Inhabitants of the whole County at large; and that it is unjust and inequitable that,' from any Circumstance of Locality, One District of a County, in a Matter which affects the ln-terest of the Whole, should, for the Furtherance of general Justice, be partially burthened: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may pass into a Law, in order that the whole County of Kent may contribute in Discharge of an Expence incurred for the Service of the whole County, and not exclusively for the Service of any particular Part of it.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

the said Division, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was also presented to the House, and read; likewise taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth. That the said Application is made with the evident Intent to obtain the Authority of Parliament for extending the Burthen of the Maintenance and Repair of the said Gaol, to which, by the said Act, the Western Division was alone subjected, over the whole County; and that the Petitioners perceive the Ground of the proposed Alteration to be, that the said Gaol is used as a Prison, or Place of Confinement, by the whole County at large, but the Petitioners represent that the same is not the only Common Gaol for the said County, for that there is, and hath been from Time immemorial, another Gaol situate at Saint Dunstan's, near Canterbury, within the Eallern Division of the said County, which is a Common Gaol for the said County, to which it hath been the uniform and immemorial Practice to commit all Prisoners charged with Offences done within the said Eallern Division, and that the Gaol at Maidstone is never used 'as a Place of Confinement for such Prisoners, except during the Affixes for the County, which are held there, and that the whole Expences of such Prisoners, not only during their Confinement in the said Gaol at Saint Dunfan's, but on their Removal to Maidfone in order to take their Trials at the Assizes, and during the whole Time of their Confinement in that Gaol, as also the Expences of the Re-building, Maintenance, and Repair, of the said Gaol, at Saint Dunfan's, have immemorially been, and now

are, exclusively borne by the said Eallern Division; 'and that it appears, by the said Act of the Ninth Year of his said late Majesty, that the said Gaol at Maidfone was deemed a County Gaol for the Wellern Division only, and so conscious were the Inhabitants of that Division, that the Burthen of the Re-building, Repair, and Maintenance thereof, ought in Justice to be borne by them, that the High Sheriff, Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen, and Freeholders, acting for, and residing in, the said Western Division, on whole Petition the said Act was obtained, made it Part of the Prayer of their Petition, that the Justices might be empowered to apply the then County Stock of the said Western Division, and to raise within the said Division such Sums as should be necessary for the Purposes of the said Act; and that to charge the Inhabitants of the said Eallern Division with a Portion of the Expence of the Maintenance and Repairs of the Gaol at in Addition

to the whole Charges of the Maintenance and Repair of the Gaol at Saint Dunfan's, which they exclusively bear, would be contrary to the Principles of Equity and Justice; and that it is not less just now, than it was at the passing of the said Act, that each Division should exclusively maintain its own Gaol, and there is not, therefore, the Shadow of aGround for the present singular Attempt (after an Acquiescence of upwards of Sixty Yea^) to question the Justice, and do away an essential Part of the Terms on which the said Act was palfed: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, Agents, and Witnesses, against the said Bill, and that the same may not be passed into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel,

Agents, and Witnesses, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

The House was moved, That the Order, made upon Seccn(, Ktad-Wedtiefday lad, for reading the said Bill a Second Time. inc of Kent Tomorrow, might be read. scire "

And the said Order being read accordingly;

Ordered, That the said Order be discharged.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, a Member present informed Your Committee, That there was an ancient Bridge over the River Thames at Datchet, in the County of Bucks, which being in a very decayed State, at length became impassable, and, in consequence thereof, such Parts which remained were, in the Month of June 1795, pulled down, whereby great Inconvenience has arisen to the Public, as there has been no convenient Passage over the Thames, in that Part of the Country, ever since; and that the Petitioners are informed it is intended to erect' a new Bridge over the Thames, in a Situation more convenient and useful for the Public; viz. from a Place called Neville's Bridge, in the Parish of New Windsor, to the opposite Shore, near a Place called Southky, in the Parish of Datchet aforesaid, which is at fbme Difiance from the Scite of the former Bridge; and that the said new Bridge will form a Communication between the Towns, Parishes, and Places above mentioned, and divers other Parts of the Kingdom: — And, the Member further said. That it would be a great Benefit and Convenience to the Petitioners, and others, Inhabitants of the said Towns, Parishes, and Places, by making a shorter Communication between the Metropolis and the said Town of Nezv Windsor, and be of Public Utility, if a Road were made from the said Town of New Windsor over the said intended Bridge, and from thence to or near Datchet Common Gate, on the Road from Datchet to Siamveil, in the County of Middlesex, and if the

Road from thence to the Hand Pod at Foyle, were amended, widened, and kept in Repair, and if a new Road were made from the said Hand Post to or near the Sixteenth Mile Stone on the Road from Colnbrook to London, or some other convenient Spot on the said last mentioned Road.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereto subscribed, being Proprietors of Shares in the Huddersfield Canal Navigation, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That by an Act, passed in the Thirty-fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal from and out of the Canal of Sir John Baronet,

at or near the Town of Huddersfield, in the West Riding of the County of York, to join and communicate with the Canal Navigation from Manchester to or near A/hton-undtr-Lyne and Oldham, at or near the Town of 'under-Lyne aforesaid, in the County Palatine of Lan^afier, certain Persons were incorporated for the Purpose of making and completing the said Canal Navigation, and the Sum of ,£.184,000, hath been expended in making the said Canal Navigation, but a very considerable Por- Vol. 55.

339

tion of the said Clnal yet remains to be completed; anti that by the Bill now depending for enabling the Hr.rider field Canal Company to finish and complete the Huddersfield Canal, and for amending the Act, passed in the Thirty-fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for making and maintaining the said Hu Idersfield- Canal, it is proposed to insert a Clause or Clauses for compelling every original Subscriber to the said Undertaking, and every Person possessing a Share or Shares therein, to lubscribe a rateable Proportion towards the making and finishing the said Canal, and, in case of Neglect or Default, then that the Person or Persons so neglecting or refusing shall forfeit his or their original Subscription; and that any such compuifory Clause or Clauses, if passed into a Law, would be extremely injurious and of-preffive, and more particularly so to those Proprietors who, from the Pressure of the Times, and a Want of pecuniary Rclources, are not enabled to advance or subscribe any more Money to the said Concern than they have already subscribed; and that any Clause or Clauses directing a Forfeiture of the original Share or Shares of any Subicriber or Holder, would also be very oppressive, and indeed ruinous, to many of the original Subscribers, who subscribed their Money upon the Faith and Credit of F.ftimates and Calculations furnished by those concerned for the Company of Proprietors, and upon which every Reliance was placed: And therefore praying, That they may be beard, by themselves, or their Counsel, against such compuifory and forfeiting Clauses, and that the Petitioners may have such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the Order of the Day, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for appointing Commissioners to put in Execution an Act, of this Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act for continuing and granting to His Majesty " a Duty on Pensions, Offices, and Personal Estates, in " England, Wales, and the Town of Berwick upon " Tweed, and certain Duties on Sugar, Malt, Tobacco, " and Snuff, for the Service of the Year One thousand " Eight hundred j" together with those named in Two former Acts for appointing Commissioners of the Land Tax, be now read.

The House resolved itself into the said Committee.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Bragge took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Bragge reported from the Committee, That they had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be received Tomorrow Morning.

Mr. Rose presented to the House, according to Order, a Bill to explain and amend an Act, made in the Thirty-sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for the better Regulation of Mills And the same was received; and read the First Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second Time.

Ordered, That the said Bill be read a Second Time Tomorrow Morning.

A Petition of the unfortunate Debtors, confined in His Majesty's Gaol the Castle of Lancaster, was presented to the House, and read; Complaining of their Distress, and praying Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

The other Order of the Day being read;

Ordered, That the Bill (now ingrafted) for indemnifying Persons serving in Volunteer Corps, who have omitted to take out Certificates for wearing Hair Powder,- and to amend so much of an Act, made in the Thirty-fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for granting to His Majesty a Duty " on Certificates issued for using Hair Powder;" as relates to the exempting Persons serving in Volunteer Corps from the said Duty, be read the Third Time Tomorrow Morning.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

A Member present informed Your Committee, That the said Road is of great Public Utility, tends to the Improvement of the Estates in the Neighbourhood thereof, both in England and Scotland, and to the In-, crease of the Trade and Commerce of the Town of Newcafll'e upon Tyne, in the county of , Northumberland, and the County of Roxburgh, and forms a Part of the Line of that Road, which is by many Miles the nearest Road between the City of Lon and the City of Edinburgh; and that, by reason of many heavy Carriages passing and repalling upon the fame, in all Sealons of the Year, the said Road constantly requires Reparation, and the Materials used for a great Part thereof are of such a soft Nature that it is impossible to keep the said Road in Repair, or pay and keep down the Interest of the Money borrowed, unless the said Act be revived and continued, and the Powers thereof enlarged, altered, and amended.

A Petition of the Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Commissioners for executing an Act, passed in the Thirty-sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for dividing several Commonable Lands in the Parish of Barrington, in the County of Cambridge, was presented to the House, and read} Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes of the House, that a Petition of Richard Esquire,

hath been presented. Hating several Grievances, which he pretends to have suffered by the Misconduct of the Petitioners, in carrying the said Act into Execution, and praying the House to take his same into Consideration, and to grant him such Relief as the Hardship of it shall appear to require; and that the said Petition contains many Misrepresentations of the Condufl and Proceedings of the Petitioners, as Commissioners, in carrying the said Act into Execution, and divers Statements, highly injurious to their Character, and which the Petitioners, with great Deference, assert, will, upon Examination, appear to be wholly void of Foundation; and that the Petitioqers have, in all Respects, to the belt of their Judgment, conformed to the Directions of the said Act, and the Oath which they have taken, to act impartially, and they are ready and desirous to meet any Enquiry which the House may think fit to direct into their Conduct or Proceedings as such Commissioners; and that, in or about the Month of June 1799, the said Richard Bendyfhe commenced an Action, in His Majesty's Court of Common Pleas, against the said Commissioners, which is (till depending, but the said Richard Bendyfhe hath not yet thought tit to declare, or to proceed further in his said Action: And therefore praying, if the House shall think fit to order any Enquiry upon the Petition of the said Richard Bendyfhe, That they may be at Liberty to be heard, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, at the same Time, in order to disprove the Allegations contained in his said Petition, or that they may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Then a Petition of the Governor and Company of Petition pre-Merchants of England trading into the Levant Seas, femeJ' being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer (by His Majesty's Command) acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read;

Setting forth. That the Trade between this Kingdom and Turkey has, for a long Series of Years, been carried on by a Society of Merchants incorporated by Charters, and regulated by Acts of Parliament; and that, in order to carry on this Trade with Safety, and protect His Majesty's Subjects in the Turkish Dominions, it has been found necessary that an Ambassador or Public Minister should be font from England to reside at Constantinople, and that Consuls, Vice Conluls, and other Officers and Servants, Ihbuld be established in other Parts of Turkey where British Subjects reside, and where the English Merchants carry on Trade; the whole Expence of which has been borne by the Turkey Company, which, together with other Expences incident to carrying on this Trade, have of late Years amounted to about £. 8,000, per Annum; and the Petitioners feel it incumbent on them to represent, that the House which has always been appropriated for the Reception of His Majesty's Ambafia dor at The Porte is falling to Decay, and it will be necessary to cause a new one to be built, in case it should be thought expedient to provide a permanent residence for a Public Officer of so much Consequence, a Measure which muff: be left to the Wisdom of Parliament, and, if adopted, will necessarily be attended with considerable

JExpyice i

ance of Parliament: And therefore praying the House to take these Premises into Consideration, and grant them such Relief as may be thought necessary and proper.

that, for the general Benefit of the Proprietors of Horles and other valuable Cattle, they have Pleasure in Bating, that Seventy-two Pupils have passed Examination at the said College, many of whom are now settled in different Towns of the Kingdom, and are practising the Knowledge they have acquired to the great Advantage of the Public; and it is with peculiar Satisfaction the Petitioners are enabled to Bate, that the Importance of the InBitution haring been taken into Consideration by His Royal Highness the Commander in Chief, the Propriety of appointing Persons educated at the College to be Veterinary Surgeons in the several Regiments of Cavalry has been determined on, in pursuance of a Report from a Board of General Officers, to whom the Subject had been referred; and that, in consequence of such Decision, Thirty-four Pupils, whose Education has been completed, are engaged in the Service of the Army, and Twenty-eight other Pupils are now pursuing their Studies at the College, several of them intending to fill similar Situations as loon as they shall be deemed duly qualified, each of them being subject to the same rigorous Examination of the Medical Committee, and to be certified in the same Manner as has 'hitherto been practised in respect of the other Pupils of the College: — And, the Petitioners further Bate, That, desirous of rendering to the utmoB of their Power their InBitution advantageous to the Public Service, the Colonels of the different Cavalry Regiments have been invited to fend each a Farrier to the College, in order to his being taught the Strudture, Economy, and different Diseases of the Horse's Foot, and inffrudted in a Mode of shoeing, tending very materially to its Preservation, and that many Army Farriers have been consequently admitted into the College for In-Bruction in that particular Part of Veterinary Knowledge; and that the College continues under the Di-redtion of the Professor Mr. Co/emau, a Gentleman of Talents and Skill, and who, by many useful and important Discoveries in the Science, has, in the Opinion of the Petitioners, fully juffified the Expectations formed of irs Improvement from his Exertions j and that the Petitioners have already Bated to the House the Difficulties which have occurred in the Execution of their Plan, and particularly from the embarassed State of their Finances; and, though the Aid so liberally granted by Parliament has in a great Degree alleviated their Difficulties, it has yet proved inadequate to remove them entirely, n >twithstanding the Petitioners have, with the utmoB Frugality, reduced their Annual Expenditure much within the EBimate of the Committee of the House to whom their Petition was referred, and within those Limits to which they are Bill of Opinion it would be p:oper to extend it, in order that the Public may derive the full Benefit of such an Establishment, the Petitioners have again with Regret to Bate that (under the heavy

Pressure of Debt, of which, an Account is before the House) without further Aid from Parliament it will be impossible to bring to Perfection an Establishment which, from the Advantages accruing from the more skilful Care of so important a Branch of Public Property as the Horses of the Army, is become more than ever an Ob-jedt of National Importance; and that the Petitioners were unable to obtain His Majesty's Recommendation, before the lateB Day appointed by the House for receiving Private Petitions had elapsed: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to exhibit a Petition for the Purpose above-mentioned, or that they may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered', That, in Consideration of the particular Lear given, Circumstances set forth in the said Petition, Leave be given to present a Petition, as desired by the said Noblemen, Gentlemen, and others.

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for more effectually repairing, widening, and improving the Road from the Village of Magor to the Bridge-foot in the Town of Chepstow, in the County of Monmouth, and several other Roads in the Counties of Monmouth, Gloucester, Hereford, and Brecon, to continue in Force for Twenty-one Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the Appointment and Regulation of Pilots for the conducing of Ships and Vessels into and out of the Port of Kingson upon Hull; and for ascertaining the Salvage for Anchors, Cables, and other Ships Materials, found in the River Humber; and for the better ascertaining the Tonnage of Ballad Lighters employed at the said Port; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for separating the Commons or Waste Grounds of the Manor of East Horseley, in the County of Surrey, which lie in the several Parishes of East Horseley, and Ockham, within the said Manor, and for settling the Rights of Common thereon; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for more effectually repairing the Road from Ale-mouth, through Alnwick and to Hexham, and a

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainted the House, That he had a Meflhge from His Majesty to this House, signed by His Majesty; and he presented the same to the House; and it was read by Mr. Speaker (all the Members of the House being uncovered); and is as followeth; viz.

GEORGE R.

It is with the most sincere Satisfaction that His Majesty finds Himself enabled to communicate to this House the joint Address of His Lords and Commons of Ireland, laying before His Majesty certain Resolutions, which contain the Terms proposed by them for an entire Union between the Two Kingdoms. His Majesty is persuaded that this House will participate in the Pleasure with which His Majesty observes the Conformity of Sentiment manifested in the Proceedings of His Two Parliaments, after long and careful Deliberation on this most important Subject; and He earnestly recommends to this House, to take all such further Steps as may belt tend to the speedy and complete Execution of a Work so happily begun, and so interesting to the Security and Happiness of His Majesty's Subjects, and to the general Strength and Prosperity of the British Empire.

R.

Rank and Precedency next and immediately after the Lords Spiritual of the same Rank and Degree of Britain, and shall enjoy all Privileges as fully as the Spiritual Lords of England do now, or as any other Spiritual Lords of England may hereafter, enjoy the fame, the Right and Privilege of fitting in the House of Lords, and the Privileges depending thereon, and particularly the Right of fitting on the Trial of Peers excepted; and that the Persons holding any Temporal Peerages of Ireland, existing at the Time of the Union, shall, from and after the Union, have Rank and Precedency next and immediately after all the Persons holding Peerages of the like Orders and Degrees in Great Britain, subsisting at the Time of the Union; and that all Peerages of land, created after the Union, shall have Rank and Precedency with the Peerages of the United Kingdom so created, according to the Dates of their Creations; and that all Peerages, both of Great Britain and Ireland, now subsisting or hereafter to be created, shall, in all other Respects, from the Date of Union, be considered as Peerages of the United Kingdom; and that the Peers of Ireland shall, as Peers of the United Kingdom, be sued and tried as Peers, except as aforesaid, and shall enjoy all Privileges of Peers as fully as the Peers of Great Britain, the Right and Privilege of fitting in the House of Lords, and the Privileges depending thereon, and the Right of fitting on the Trial of Peers, only excepted.

Resolved, That, for the same Purpose, it would be fit to propose, as the Fifth Article of Union, That the Churches of that Part of Great Britain called England, and of Ireland, shall be united into One Church, and that when His Majesty shall summon a Convocation, the Archbishops, Bishops, and Clergy of the several Provinces in Ireland, shall be respectively summoned to and fit in the Convocation of the United Church, in the like Manner, and subject to the same Regulations as to Election and Qualification, as are at present by Law established with respect to the like Orders of the Church of England-, and that the Doctrine, Worship, Discipline, and Government, of the said United Church, shall be preserved as now by Law established for the Church of England, saving to the Church of Ireland all the Rights, Privileges, and Jurisdictions, now thereunto belonging; and t hat |fie Doctrine, Worship, Dif-cipline, and Government, of the Church' of Scotland, shall likewise be preserved as now by Law. and by the Ad: of Union, established for the Church of;

and that the Continuance and Preservation for ever of the said United Church, as the established Church of that Part of the said United Kingdom called England and Ireland, shall be deemed and taken to be an essential and fundamental Article and Condition of the Union.

Resolved, That, for the same Purpose, it would be fit to propose, as the Sixth Article of Union, That His Majesty's Subjects of Great Britain and Ireland shall, from and after the First Day of January One thousand Eight hundred and One, be entitled to the same Privileges, and be on the same Footing as to Encouragements and Bounties on the like Articles, being the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture, of either Kingdom respectively, and generally in respect of Trade and Navigation in all Ports and Places in the United Kingdom and its Dependencies: And that in all Treaties made by His Majesty, His Heirs and Successors, with any Foreign Power, His Majesty's Subjects of Ireland shall have the same Privileges, and be on the same Footing, as His Majesty's Subjects of Great Britain: That, from the First Day of January One thousand Eight hundred and One, all Prohibitions and Bounties on the Export of Articles, the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture, of either Country to the other, shall cease and determine, and that the said Articles shall thenceforth be exported from one Country to the other without Duty or Bounty on such Export: That all Articles, the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture, of either Kingdom, (not herein after enumerated as subject to specific Duties) shall from

To the KING'S Most Excellent MAJESTY.

t

The humble Address of the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, in Parliament assembled.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We You,r Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, in Parliament assembled, beg Leave to acquaint Your Majesty. That we have taken into our most serious and deliberate Consideration, the great and important Subject of a Legislative Union between Great Britain and Ireland, which was laid before us in his Excellency the Lord Lieutenant's Message to both , Houses of Parliament on the Fifth Day of February last, accompanied by the Resolutions of the Two Houses of the Parliament of Great Britain, proposing that great Measure, and the earnest and solemn Recommendation of Your Majesty.

Deeply impressed with the Necessity of rendering the Connexion of Great Britain and this Kingdom indiffo-luble, and truly sensible of the repeated Efforts which have been made by Foreign and Domestic Enemies, to Ibake that Connection and to eff'ed their entire Separation, we fully approve and cordially embrace the Principle of incorporating Great Britain and Ireland into One Kingdom, under Your Majesty's auspicious Government, by a complete and entire Union of their Legifla-tures.

We do consider the Resolutions of the Two Houses of the British Parliament, as wifely calculated to form the Balls of such a Settlement: We have adopted them as our Guide in the Measures we have pursued, and we now feel it our Duty to lay before Your Majesty, the Resolutions to which we have agreed; which Resolutions, we humbly submit to Your Majesty may form the Articles of Union between Great Britain and Ireland, and which, if they shall be approved by the Two Houses of the Parliament of Great Britain, we are ready to confirm and ratify, in order that the same may be established for ever by the mutual Consent of both Parliaments.

We doubt not that Your Majesty, and Your Parliament of Great Britain, will consider these Resolutions as the most unequivocal Testimony of our zealous Loyalty to Your Majesty's sacred Person, Family, and Government, and as an unalterable Pledge of our Attachment to the British Empire: We offer them in the full Conviction, that by incorporating the Legislatures, and by consolidating the Resources of the Two Kingdoms, we shall increase the Power and Stability of that Empire; and that, by uniting ourselves with Your Majesty's Subjects of Great Britain, under One Parliament, and under One Government, we shall most effectually provide for the Improvement of our Commerce, the Security of our Religion, and the Preservation of our Liberties.

JOHN GAYER, Pari.

G. F. HILL, Cler. Dom. Com.

The House proceeded to take into Consideration the Amendments made by the Lords to the Bill, intituled, An Act for extending, from the Twenty-fifth Day of March One thousand Eight hundred, until the Twenty-fifth Day.of March One thousand Eight hundred and One, the Period of Preference granted, and continued by several Acts, to Bodies Corporate, and Persons, for the Redemption of Land Tax, and for enlarging several of the Powers contained in the said Acts.

And the said Amendments were read; and are as fol-loweth; viz.

Pr. 4. 1. a 1. Leave out " Grant" and insert

" Mortgage or Rent Charge."

Pr. 5. 1. 1. After " concerning" insert " any."

1. 2. Leave out " Grants" and insert " Mortgage or Rent Charge."

And it appearing to the House, that the Words,

" Mortgage or Rent Charge" had been inserted in the ' V-o 1,. 55.

Second Clause in the Bill, by the Committee of this House, to whom the said Bill was committed, but not in the Two next Clauses, where the Sense required that the same Alteration should have been made; and that the Amendments made by the Lords were 4rfiy for the Purpose of supplying this Omission, conformably to tire manifest Intention of this House;

The said Amendments were severally read a Second Time; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That Mr. Bragge do carry the Bill to the Lords; and acquaint them, that this House hath agreed to the Amendments made by their Lordships.

Ordered, That a Special Entry be made in the Journal of this House of the Reasons for agreeing to the Amendments made by their Lordships to the said Bill.

A Petition of the Mayor and Commonalty of the City of New Saturn, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners obfefve, by the Votes, that a Petition of the Right honourable Jacob Earl of Radnor, Recorder of the said City, hath been presented to the House, Praying for Leave to bring in a Bill forgiving to the exempt Jurisdiction of the City and Close of New Sarum a Power of confining, in the Common Gaol for the County of situate in Fish-

erton Anger, adjoining to the said City, Felons, Debtors, and other Prisoners, from the said Jurisdiction, pursuanl to an Agreement made with the Magistrates of the said County; and that an Act wfts passed in the Twenty-fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for removing and re-building the Council Chamber, Guildhall, and Gaol of the said City, and for ascertaining the Tolls of the Market, and regulating the Chairmen within the said City, and the Mayor and Commonalty of the said City were thereby authorized to build and maintain, within the said City, or the Suburbs or Precincts thereof, a Gaol for the said City, and the Close thereof, and to take upon themselves the Custody and safe Keeping of such Persons as should be confined therein; and it was by the said Act provided, that, until such new Gaol should be erected, all the Debtors, Felons, and other Persons, within the said City, and the Close thereof, who then were, or should be, liable, or ought to be, committed to the said Common Gaol of the said City, should, as Occasion should require, be committed by the Justices of the Peace for the said City, or Close thereof, to, and should be confined in, the Common Gaol of the County of Wilts; and that the old Gaol belonging to the said

City was, under the Authority of the said Act, taken down, and a new one was intended to be erected; but it hath not been done, it being conceived that such Debtors, Felons, and other Persons, would be more safely and conveniently confined in the said County Gaol, the same being very large and secure, and immediately adjoining to the said City, than they would be in a new Gaol, to be erected within the said City, of the Suburbs or Precincts thereof, as directed by the said Act, and as stated in the said Petition already presented to the House; and it Is therefore expedient that, instead of erecting a new Gaol, pursuant to the Directions of the said Act, the Agreement entered into by the Petitioners with the Magistrates for the said County, for the Purpose above mentioned, should be ratified and carried into Effect, and it is necessary that some of the Powers and Provisions of the said Act should be explained, amended, and enlarged; and that, Doubts having arisen respecting the Office of Clerk of the said City, and the Rights, Privileges, and Appurtenances thereunto belonging, vested in and by the said Act in the Mayor and Commonalty of the said City, an Agreement had been entered into with the Right Reverend Father in God John Lord Bishop of Sarum, to whom the Gift or Grant of the said Office belonged, before the passing of the said Act, for an Explanation of so much thereof as relates to the Grant of such Office, and the Rights and Privi-

Wimbledon, in the County of , was referred j That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Turnpike Bills, had not been complied with, so far as the same require Notices to be inserted in the Newspapers, and affixed on the Sessions House Door , but it appeared to the Committee, that the Trustees of One of the adjoining Roads had some Time ago determined to take the Roads mentioned in the Petition under their Care, and which they have declined on Account of their very bad Condition, besides being unwilling to apply to Parlia-

Vol. 55.

ment for that Purpose only, and which was not known to the Petitioners until the Time limited for giving such Notices had expired; that- the Roads intended to be repaired comprize most of the pres'ent Public Highways in the said Parishes, which are in a very ruinous Condition, and One of them has been lately indicted, and there is great Reason to apprehend that more of them will be indicted, unless Power is given to repair them in the present Session of Parliament; that the Composition Money raised on the said Parishes is not sufficient so defray One-third Part of the Expence of maintaining the Roads; and that it is not intended that Power should be given to open and make any new Roads, except in One Place, to the Extent of Two-thirds of a Furlong j and that, the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; arid is as followeth; viz.

Inhabitants of the said Borough, and of the Street of Cafilegate, within the Liberties thereof, was referred j That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Paving Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them.

Aprilis. . 1800.

to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. William Foreman, being examined, said, That the said Borough of Berwick upon Tweed is very large, and has of late Years very much increased in Population, and in its Number of Buildings, and that the Streets of the said Borough, and the Quays or Wharfs belonging thereto, and that Part of the Bridge over the River Tweed which is within the Liberties of the said Borough, are at present very ill lighted, and the Footpaths of the said Streets are in bad Repair, and ill paved, and are subject: to many Obstructions, Nuisances, and Annoyances; and that it would be of great Benefit, Safety, and Convenience to the Inhabitants of the said Borough, and to all Persons resorting thereto, if the said Streets, Quays, or Wharfs and Bridge aforesaid, were well lighted, and the Footpaths were flagged or paved; and if all Obstructions, Nuisances, and Annoyances, in the said Borough, and on the Quays and Bridge, were prevented for the future.

Report from Sir John Sinclair reported from the Sclex Committee, rWtt«OTm appointed to consider of the most effectual Means of WasteLand . facilitating, under the Authority of Parliament, the Inclosure and improvement of the Waste, Uninclosed, and Unproductive Lands, Commons, Common Arable Fields, Common Meadows, and Common of Pasture, in this Kingdom, and to report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House; and who were empowered to report from Time to Time; That the Committee had considered the Matter to them referred, and had directed him to make a Report thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it. in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read j and is as followeth; viz.

Your Committee, in considering the Subject referred to them, have principally had in View the Impediments to Inclosures under the Authority of Parliament, arising from the Expences incurred in such Procedure; and have consequently endeavoured to trace the Nature and Amount or those Expences, as far as the various and complicated Circumstances attending them would admit, through the several Stages of the TransaXion; the Result of which they shall, in the First Place, proceed to lay before the House.

Your Committee find that a Meeting is frequently convened, by Public Advertisement, for the Purpose of tonlidering the Propriety of applying to Parliament for an intended Inclosure; at which it sometimes happens, that Persons not interested in the Business attend; and that the Expences of such Meetings, usually held at some Inn, as well as that of the Advertisements, are ofitn charged in the Solicitor's Bill.

A Petition to Parliament is then prepared; the Expence attending which rarely exceeds the Sum of Two - Guineas.

Notices of the intended Application are then, in pursuance of the Standing Orders of this House, to be affixed to the Church Door of each Parish in which the Lands to be inclosed are situated, for Three Sundays in the Months of Av.gujl or September; the Expence of which naturally varies, according to the Number cf Parishes, and the Distance of the Churches from the Residence of the Solicitor or Agent concerned; it being ufiaal for only One Person, if possible, to be employed for this Purpose, in consequence of the Necessity of his attending afterwards in Town, to prove the FaX before the Committee on the Petition. The Charge in general appears to be from One to Three Guineas for each Parish.

The Draft of the Bill itself is either copied by the Solicitor in the Country from some former AX, as far as Circumstances will admit, or prepared originally by the Parliamentary Solicitor; in both which Cafes, it is obvious, that a Number of similar Clauses, either required by the Orders of the House, or authorized by general J?raXice, are constantly inserted. The Proportion of -f-

these general Clauses to the Provisions of a local and peculiar Nature, cannot be precisely ascertained; but Your Committee have Reason to suppose that they may, in feme Instances, amount to Two-thirds, and, in others, not to more than Two-fifths of the Whole: The Expence of preparing and copying this Draft, being charged by the Sheet, must depend upon the Length of it, which must in all Cases be increased by these general Clauses.

The PraXice of the Legiflapire, requiring Proof of the Content of a certain Number of the Parties interested, by their actually signing the Bill, it is necessary to employ a proper Person, and sometimes more than One, to procure this, and afterwards to attend in London to prove it before the Committees of both Houses. As it is occasionally necessary to travel to a considerable Distance, and into different Parts of the Kingdom, for this Purpose, the Expence attending it, is in such Cases considerable, and in One Instance it appears to have amounted to between Seventy and Eighty Pounds, to procure the Consent of One Individual. It is also stated to Your Committee, That the great Number of Consents supposed to be necessary, according to the present Practice of Parliament, whether Three-fourths, according to the Ideas of some, or Four-fifths according to those of others (for there is no fixed Rule) is a great Bar to Inclosure. Your Committee are thence led to submit it to the Wisdom of the House, whether it may not be expedient in future, to allow the Proof of a less Number of Consents, provided they amount to a decided Preponderance, to be sufficient for obtaining a Bill.

The Bill having beeh brought in, read a First and Second Time, and committed, it is necessary to bring Witnesses to Town, to prove that the Orders of the House have been complied with in the foregoing Particulars, and to verify the Allegations in the Preamble. All this is attended with different Degrees of Expence, according to the Number of Persons employed, the Distance of their Residence from the Metropolis, and the accidental Delays which may retard the Progress of the Bill to the House of Peers; when the same Persons must again attend to be sworn at the Bar of the House, and afterwards examined before the Committee. In Cafes where the Bill meets with Opposition, this must necessarily be considerable; and in all it is sufficient to deserve Attention.

The subsequent Progress of the Bill through Parliament, is subject to the Payment of the several Fees, particularly specified in the Table annexed to this Report; (Appendix, N 9.) The Amount of these, it is evident, must vary according to the Size of the Bill, the Number of Interests affeXed by it, and the Opposition it may happen to meet with. The Length of the Bill chiefly operates as an Increase to the Expence in this Stage of the Proceeding, by the additional Charge of Ingrafting, and Printing. The only other incidental Expence, not yet noticed in this Part of the TransaXion, is that of a Town or Parliamentary Solicitor; usually some Person whose Experience in such Business, and Acquaintance with the Forms of Parliament, render his Assistance particularly desirable; and that of a Country Solicitor, whose local Knowledge, and immediate Connexion with the Parties interested, in many Cafes, make his Attendance also material. The Charge of the former, for his whole Services, is usually Twenty Guineas; but in controverted or any complicated Cafes, considerably more; that of the latter is subject to necessary Variations, according to the Length of Attendance and other Circumstances, but must in most Cafes be considerable.

When the Bill has received the SanXion of the Le-giflature, the usual Mode of carrying it into Essex through the Intervention of Commissioners, gives Rife to Charges and Expences of a different Nature. The Ne^ ceffity of peculiar Qualifications, as well as a Reputa- *

The next general Object that has Occurred to Your Committee is the Charges of the Solicitor, whether ailing as such, in the necessary Conduit of the Bill through Parliament, or, after it has passed, in the additional Capacity of Clerk to the Commissioners. Should the Alterations before suggested, as to the Mode of Proof before the Two Houses, be adopted, Your Committee are led to hope that these Charges would necef-(arily be considerably reduced; and that in many Cafes, where the Measure met with no Opposition, the Attendance of the Solicitor, or any other Person from the Country, might be dispensed with. But while the drifting Charges, whatever they may be, are undefined in their Nature, and subjeil to no Controul but through the Medium of an expensive Litigation, Abuses will in many Instances exiflr. Your Committee fee no Remedy for these, unless it should be found practicable to ascertain the Nature of such Charges with some Degree of Precision, and then to subject them to Taxation, in the same Manner as Coils in the Courts below, either by lbme Officer of those Courts, or by Officers of the Two Houses of Parliament, or others specially appointed for that Purpose. The particular Duty and Charges of the Clerk to the Commissioners might, as appears to Your Committee, be prescribed by the general or particular Act, and, like that of the Commissioners and Surveyor, controuled by the Sand ion of an Oath of Office.

With respect to the Commissioners themselves, upon whose Ability and Integrity so much depend, it might not, perhaps, be expedient to subject them to similar Controul, left Men of Respectability should be deterred from engaging in so laborious and useful an Employment } but the Abuses above noticed might perhaps be remedied, by defining in some Degree the Number of Hours which ought actually and bondfide to be devoted to each Meeting, and requiring that it - should not be occupied by Attention to any other Business; and also, by regulating, according to the Place of Residence of each Commissioner, the Charges to be allowed for travelling Expences. With a View to ascertain how far the former of these Regulations had been complied with, it might be desirable that the Clerk should be required to keep a Register of all the Days and Times employed in the Business of the Inclosure; which, as well as the Books of Account, should be open to the Inspection of all Persons concerned.

On a full Consideration of the Subject of Parliamentary Fees, properly so called, which has occupied much of the Attention of Your Committee, they fee no Ground to recommend to the House any general Regulations on that Head. As a suitable Recompence for the Time, Attention, and Abilities of the several Persons to whom they are payable, they find no Reason to object to their usual Amount j and from a Companion of it to that of the other Expences necessarily incidental to this Procedure, they are not inclined to think it can in general operate as a Discouragement to this Mode of Improvement. In particular Instances, however, which are not unfrequent, of small Wastes and Commons, it is obvious that the whole Expence of conducting an Inclosure, under the Authority of Parliament, must always bear so large a Proportion to the Value of the Land to be divided, as to preclude the Possibility of Improvement in that Mode. It seems to Your Committee worthy the Consideration of the House, how far it might be advisable, in certain Cafes of such a Description, to be ascertained either by the Number of Acres, or Value of the Land, (in addition to the general Regulations above suggested) to remove such Part of the Impediment as is more immediately under its Controul, by providing that such Bills should only be considered, in the Payment of Fees, as Single Bills,

and be entitled to any other Indulgence which Parliament in its Wisdom should fee fit. Your Committee ground this Recommendation, on the Supposition that such Portions of Land could by no Possibility be brought into Cultivation in the ordinary Mode, and that therefore the Reduction proposed, is not so much to be considered' as a Diminution of probable and accustomed Perquisites to the Officers of the Two Houses, as the Means of making that productive of Emolument to a certain Amount, which would otherwise never be at all available to that Effect.

On the Whole, Your Committee have thought they should best fulfil the Intentions of the House, in referring to them to consider of the most effectual Means of facilitating, under the Authority of Parliament, the Inclosure and Improvement of the Waste and other Unproductive Lands of the Kingdom, by confining the Regulations they might fugged, to such Points as appeared to them simple and of easy Attainment; by which the Expence attending Inclosure, under the present System, would be considerably diminished, and the Plan would in other Respects be improved. And if the Suggestions they have ventured to recommend, should have the good Fortune of meeting with the Approbation of Parliament, they'flatter themselves, that such Expences, instead of being great and undefined, would be so moderate, and in general so capable of being estimated, that, in so far as regards large Inclosures, the principal Objections to the present System would be done away, and a great Encouragement would be given to Improvement.

For the further Information of the House, upon the several Matters before suggested. Your Committee have thought proper to annex to their Report, by way of Appendix, the Evidence taken by them, in so far as respects the particular Points above alluded to.

APPENDIX. (No. 1.)

"Thomas Harrison, Esq; of Wolverton, near Stoney Stratford, in the County of Bucks;

Examined.

Have you been concerned in many Bills of Inclosure?

In several. I think as many as Twenty; probably more.

As Solicitor, Commissioner, or both?

Sometimes as Solicitor; as Commissioner frequently, and often as Agent for the Parties interested.

What is the first Step, when an Inclosure is proposed in any District?

Generally to convene a Meeting of the Proprietors, either individually, or by Advertisement in some Provincial Newspaper in the Neighbourhood.

When a Public Meeting is held, at whose Expence is such Meeting?

The Meeting is held at an Inn, and each Person generally pays his own Expence. The Solicitor is paid for his Attendance and Expence in the general Account. It sometimes happens that the whole Expence of such Meeting is charged to the general Account also: which ought to be checked as much as possible, as. many Persons attend those Meetings, and even bring their Friends there, when they know they are to be at no Expence. It would be a good Plan, when any Public Meeting is called, toinfert in the Notice, that each Person was to pay his own Expence.

What is the next Step?

To prepare a Petition for Leave to bring in a Bill, and to get it signed by some of the Proprietors. The Expence of preparing and presenting the Petition is not more than Two Guineas.

Have

40 Geo. III. in° dprilis. . 385

Have you seen many Meetings called?

Sometimes several are necessary; and it is better than employing Solicitors to go about to get Signatures.

What are the Expences attending the fixing of the Notices on the Church Doors?

The Expence is insignificint in common Inclosures; about a Guinea: But in larger Inclosures, it must depend upon the Number of Parishes, and the Distance at which the Solicitor resides from each.

Is it not often attended with great Expence, proving Notices before both Houses?

Yes, when it requires Persons to come from a Distance: For Instance; in an Inclosure of Mapowdery last Session, it was necessary for me to bring a Witness from thence, to prove the Notices. This cost about Seven Guineas, though the greatest Economy was used, and the Person received nothing for his Trouble, being Bailiff of the Estate.

What is the next Step?

The next Step is preparing the Bill; which is generally done by a Country Attorney. The Charge of this is various; as, in Addition to the Charge per Folio, the Solicitor charges for his Trouble, and for making Enquiries regarding the Particulars of the Property proposed to be inclosed. Perhaps this Charge may be from Six to Seven Guineas.

Is it not your Opinion, that the Size of Inclosure Bills might be greatly diminished, and the Expence consequently reduced, were a General Law palfed, containing the usual Clauses in all Bills of Inclosure, to which all Private Acts might refer, for the Powers of the Commissioners, and the Forms of their Proceedings?

No doubt of it. I think to a considerable Extent. The Expence of drawing up, copying, printing, and ingrafting the Bill, would be thereby materially reduced.

If such a Law were passed, and the Bill accordingly shortened, would it not Amplify the Business so much, that it would be easier to procure Consents to such Bills?

The Expence being thereby diminished, would be an Inducement to the Parties interested to agree to the Inclosure, as will any other Mode by which the Charges can be reduced.

Is it not necessary to procure the written C°nfeqt of the Parties interested?

The usual Mode is, that every Proprietor should bd applied to for his Consent, and that the Answer received should be proved before both Houses of Parliament; and the Expence of procuring Individual (Consents is often very great.

Would it not materially diminish the Expence of

Proving Consents before the Two Houses, if, instead of 'arole Evidence, Affidavits before One or more Magistrates, that the Bill was subscribed by the Party, was considered as sufficient, in particular where the Party is redding at a great Distance from the Property to be in-cioled?

In such Cases it might save a very considerable Expence.

What is generally supposed to be the Proportion of Consents required?

I have always thought Three-fourths might {land a good Chance of succeeding, even in Cafes of Oppo-fition.

Would it not promote Inclosures, if Two-thirds In Value were sufficient to procure an Act of Inclosure?

I think it would.

Would not such a Rule diminish the Risk of any Opposition to the Act?

Vol. 55.

It certainly would tend to promote Inclosure.

Is there any Mode by which, in your Opinion, the Charges of the Solicitor could be diminished?

The only Mode which occurs to me, is to oblige the Commissionei s to do without a Cleric, which is often attended with a great Expence — Two Guineas a Day.

Who is generally appointed Clerk?

The Solicitor.

Does he derive any Advantage besides his Daily Allowance?

Yes, for all his special Business; such as, for giving Notices, writing Letters, &c.

Can you inform the Committee of any particular In-' stance where the Expence of the Solicitor is considerable?

I can hardly state any Instance where the Expence has not been considerable. In One same I remember an Attorney's Bill came to Seven Hundred Pounds, though the Act had no Opposition. This did not include the Expence of the Commissioners; it included the Expences of both Houses, and the Charges of a legal Nature.

What occurs to you regarding the bell Mode of diminishing the Expence of the Commissioners?

The Expence of the Commissioners is very great. In One Instance which lately came within my Knowledget the Bill of the Commissioners came to Four Guineas per Day, besides their Expences. The Act directed only Two Guineas; but they dated they worked double Days, and therefore were entitled to double Fees,

Would it not be a useful Regulation, that the same Commissioners should not aft but in One Inclosure on the same Day?

It certainly would; and would accelerate the Business of Inclosure, if Commissioners were prohibited being concerned in more than Three Inclosures, at the utmost, at the same Time. The Delays and Neglects of the Commissioners in completing the Business entrusted to them, is more injurious to the Parties interested, than the Sum allowed them; and indeed bears no Proportion.

- Are there no Means of checking the Expence of the Commissioners-? «,

I know of none; and when Appeals are made to the Magistrates, they find it difficult to give Redress; which might render some new Proviso in Inclosure Bills necessary.

Would it be of any Advantage to limit the Time at which the Award shall be completed?

- I think it would.

If in case the Award is not signed within a given Time, should not the Commissioners give a satisfactory Reason, to the next Quarter Sessions, for not having fodone, at the Requisition of any Three Proprietors?

Yes.

Might not the Expence of Surveys be diminished ? -

Yes; in many Instances where old Surveys are properly authenticated. In some Instances I have offered such Surveys, and they have been universally rc-jested.

Do you think the Expence of the Award could bp diminished?

I do not fee any particular Expence could be saved, In some Instances the Act is recited, which might be avoided, and several other tedious Recitals.

What is the First Step generally taken by Parties wish-ing an Inclosure?

Generally by calling a Public Meeting, to consider the Propriety and Terms of the Inclosure; and in many Cafes there is a Variety of such Meetings.

Have you not heard that the Expence of those Pub-, lie Meetings is sometimes charged to the Expence of the Inclosure?

I have heard so.

What is the general Expence of Notices previous to an Application; those Notices required by the Rules of the House?

About a Guinea and a Half for each Parish, where a Country Solicitor is employed, which afterwards‘mud be attended with a considerable Expence, by the Attendance of the Parties to p$pve such Notices.
