Mod certainly; as it would save the Expence of Witnesses attending Parliament, to prove such Consent, or that they diffenred or were neuter; and it would be a dill greater Saving, if the Hand-writing of the Party to any Letter, approving or disapproving of the Bill, was admitted.

What is the usual Charge of drawing and copying Bills of Inclosure?

Two Shillings per Folio of Seventy-two Words, for drawing; and Eight-pence per Folio, copying.

How many Copies are generally made?

From Two to Six.

Would it not be a great Saving, in drawing up, copying, and subsequent Proceedings on Bills of Inclosure, if many general Clauses usually inserted in Inclosure Bills, were enacted by a General Law?

Yes; it would be a Saving of nearly One-half, and sometimes more.

Would it not be greatly in Favour of Inclosures, if io great a Quantum of Confcnts as is now usually obtained, and thought necessary, were not required?

Yes; I think if only Two-thirds in Value were required, it would increase the Number of Inclosures; and I know many in my own Practice, which would have taken place if such a Rule were adopted; and if proper Commissioners were appointed, it would be impossible for the Rights and interests of the Parties to be affected thereby.

Would it not be a great Saving, in passing Bills of Inclosure, if the Attendance of the Country Solicitor and Evidence were not necessary pending the Bill in Parliament?

Most certainly it might; and in Cafes where no Opposition were made, their Attendance would not be necessary.

Do you not think in general, that Explanations might be had, of the local Circumstances of the Districts proposed to be inclosed, by Correspondence, as well as by the personal Attendance of the Country Solicitor?

Certainly.

Is not the Expence of a Town Solicitor much less than that of a Country Solicitor?

Certainly; as they only charge for the actual Days which they attend on the Business in Parliament, and Country Solicitors are obliged to remain in Town during the Passing of the Act through both Houses, or the greatest Part of that Time; and I believe there have been many Instances where such Attendance has been from Six to Ten Weeks.

What is the usual Rate of Fees on a double Bill of Inclosure?

I believe from £. 170 to £. 200, including Clerks Fees and Ingrossment.

Is the Payment of this Quantum of Fees any Ob-ftacle to great Inclosures?

Certainly not.

Might it not be an Encouragement to small Inclosures, if some Means were suggested, by which the Payment of Fees was diminished, or done away, in so far as respected them?

Certainly.

Is there any other Expence attending the Passing of Bills of Inclosure, the Prevention of which might promote Inclosures?

If Bills were passed with greater Expedition, a very considerable Expence would be saved; by which Means, Inclosures would be much promoted: For Example, if the Chairman of the Committee of the House of Lords were empowered, by an Act, to swear Witnesses, instead of their being sworn at the Bar of the House.

Do any Means occur to you, by which the Expence of Commissioners might be diminished?

By confining the Number of Commissioners to as few as possible.

How many Commissioners are usually appointed?

Three.

(No. 3.)

George Maxwell, Esq; of F near Stilton, in the County of Huntingdon;

Examined.

Have you had much Experience, as a Commissioner, or otherwise,. in Bills of Inclosure?

Yes; from the Year 1773 or 1774. Have acted as a Commissioner in upwards of a Hundred Bills of Inclosure, and have solicited Three or Four Bills my-l'elf.

Would it diminish the Expence of Inclosures, and promote them, if the usual Clauses in such Bills were consolidated into One General Law?

Yes; very much lessen the Expence in drawing, copying, printing, and ingrossing; and in the Award, as it is the Practice of moll Solicitors, so far as my Knowledge reaches, to recite all those General Clauses in the Award.

Are not the Charges of Country Solicitors extremely various?

Yes; some charge double what others do, through all the Progress of the Business: As for Instance, in procuring Consents; in ipublishing Notices of Meetings; making Copies of Notices, and all the Proceedings of the Commissioners; for the Solicitor is generally appointed Clerk.: Some are satisfied with the same Allowance as the Commissioners; and others charge over and above that for whatever they do. The Charge also varies in drawing the Bill and the Award of the Commissioners; Vol. 55,

likewise in ingrofiing and inrolling the Award, and in obtaining Consents of the exchanging Parties.

Is it understood that there is at present any Check on the Charges of the Solicitor?

None.

Would it not be a material Service in carrying on Inclosure Bills, if the Charges of such Solicitor were ordered to be taxed before some Court?

Yes, in all Cases; and this should be a general Taxation, in order to preclude the Invidioufness of leaving it to Commissioners to obtain a Taxation, or not. There are many Solicitors who act with great Honour and Moderation, while others aim to make all the Profit they can.

Do you thinkaClerk isneceflary to the Commissioners?

Yes; in order to prove their Proceedings in case of Litigation *

Have you known any Instance where the Bill of the Solicitor has been refused by the Commissioners, but afterwards paid?

Yes, I have; in consequence of an Action having been brought against the consenting Proprietors, who authorized the Commissioners to pay the Bill rather than enter into a Litigation.

Do you know any Instance where it will be attended with Difficulty to obtain the Number of Consents generally supposed to be necessary?

I do; in the same of the intended Inclosure of the Commons of Spalding, Pinchbeck, and other Parishes in JJncolnshire. These Commons consist of about

16,000 Acres, and they are intercommonable to about Fourteen Parishes. The small Proprietors are very numerous; and to obtain the Consents of Four-fifths, will be very expensive and difficult.

Do you think that Two Commissioners would be sufficient in common Inclosures?

I do; with the Power of calling a Third, that might be nominated by the Proprietors in the Bill, in case of Variance.

Have you ever acted as Commissioner when a fixed Sum was allowed for the whole Business?

Yes; each Commissioner was allowed One Hundred Guineas. The Parish was about 3,000 Acres.

How did that Plan answer?

It was not at all satisfactory to me. In the first Place, I resided Fifty Miles from the Parish, One of the other Commissioners resided within Half a Mile of the Parish, and the Third within Ten or Eleven Miles; yet the whole Weight of the Business fell upon myself. And another Objection to a fixed Allowance is, that in case of Litigation against the Commissioners, the whole Allowance may be expended in such Litigation; for extra Attendances might be required, for which the Commissioners would get no Allowance.

Would there be any Objection to the Proceedings of the Commissioners being open at all Times to the Proprietors and their known Agents ? '

I think the Accounts of the Money received and expended should at all Times be open, and the Register of their Attendance; with a View that the Proprietors may fee that the Commissioners are entitled to the Charges they make for their Attendance: But with respect to the Minutes of their Proceedings, it might be dangerous, and lead to great Delay.

Why occasion Delay?

Because any litigious Proprietor might in every Stage of the Business appeal to the Quarter Sessions against any Part of their Proceedings; and upon Notice of such Appeal, the Commissioners could proceed no farther until the Appeal was decided: and thereby the Execution of the Act would be delayed.

Why do you recommend that the Register of the Attendance of Commissioners should at all Times be open?

Because I have known many Instances of Commissioners, who seldom or never attended at all, charging more than other Commissioners who attended the whole Execution of the Ad. Upon this Head, I wish to fugged the Propriety of a Standing Order, that no Commissioner should be allowed to charge for a greater Number of Travelling Days than are necessary for his going to and from his own Residence. I have known Instances, where a Man resided within Five Miles of the Parish where the-Inclosure was, who has charged for travelling from the Distance of One or Two Hundred Miles.

Is there no Check at present on such Abuses in the Conduct of the Commissioners?

The Commissioners have no Jurisdiction over the Charges of each other j and if an Appeal is made against the Charges, no Enquiries are ever inflicted by the Justices, as to the separate Charges of each Commissioner; and though one may have charged no more than he is entitled to, and another may have charged Three or Four Times as much as he is entitled to, they are all equally involved in the Decision; which could not happen if a Register was kept of the Attendance of each Commissioner.

Is an Appeal to the Quarter Sessions the only existing Mode of controuling the Conduct of Commissioners?

It is the only Mode in general pointed out by the Ad, and I never heard of an yother being practised.

Whether it would be advisable, and would controul the Conduct of the Commissioners, if there was a Committee of Referees appointed, of Persons not interested in the Inclosure, who might have the Power of removing Commissioners, and appointing others. Complaint only to be made by, suppose Three-fifths, of the Proprietors in Number and Value?

I think it would be a useful Controul.

Have you examined the Standing Orders of the House, regarding the Commissioners paying in the Money into the Hands of a Banker?

Yes I have, and approve much of the Principle of the Order; but think it wants some Qualifications; for the Commissioners should be declared not responsible for the Money whilst in the Banker's Hands so appointed; nor should any Commissioner be responsible for any Money drawn for, unless he signs the Order; and I also think that such Order should be entered in the Account, and signed only at a Public Meeting of the Commissioners.

Have you ever acted where Quality Men were nominated in the Ad?

I have.

Have you found them of Use in assisting the Business of the Inclosure ? .

It certainly lessens the Business of the Commissioners; but that saves nothing, as their Pay is generally the same; and I. think it is impossible for any Commissioners to allot Land, with the same Justice, that has been valued by other Persons, as they would be enabled to do if they valued it themselves.

Do you think the Surveyor should be appointed by the Ad ?;

No; I think he should not, but should be appointed by the Commissioners. The Surveyor, if he is appointed by the Ad, is appointed by the Proprietors, and considers himself as their Servant, and not the Servant of the Commissioners, and often discloses Matters 9

privately to fomi of the Proprietors, which ought not to be known: For Instance, he knows the Value set upon every Part of the Land, and has it in his Power to in-struft any Proprietor to petition for particular Spots to be allotted; which he would not do if he were not'recommended by the Proprietors.

How is the Surveyor usually paid?

By the Acre for measuring and mapping, and by the Day for Attendance on the Commissioners.

How much per Acre, and how much per Day?

They have One Shilling and Six Pence per Acre for measuring and mapping, and making all the Calculations for the Commissioners, flaking out the Allotments, and describing in Writing the Abuttals and Boundaries of the Allotments, in order to their being inserted in the Award; and they have a Guinea and a Half per Day for Attendance on the Commissioners. They are also paid for the reduced Plan; for which some charge Two Pence per Acre, and others from Five to Fifteen Guineas, which is less than Two Pence per Acre.

Would it not lessen the Expence of an Inclosure very much, if the Office of Surveyor were disposed of, under fair Competition, to the lowest given Sum, for executing the whole Business, by advertising for Proposals to such Effect, and taking Care that the contracting Party be competent to the Undertaking?

I doubt whether that Plan would answer, as it would be so difficult for the Commissioners to know the Qualifications of the Competitors; as to which there should not be the smallest Doubt, as it is always a very important Trust which is committed to him.

Is there any Check on the Conduct of the Surveyor, as to the Whole of his Proceedings?

He is generally sworn to make a true and perfect Survey; and in other Cafes, after he has made the Whole of the Calculation, and prepared every Thing for the Award — The latter Mode I consider the bell. I think in all Cases it would be proper for the Commissioners to stipulate with the Surveyor, as to the Terms under which he is to act and be paid; and that it is necessary to enter into an express Contraft for that Purpose.

Should there not be a Difference in the planning, &c. of a Common Field from a Common?

If it is a Common only, the Charge should not exceed One Shilling per Acre, there being no Difficulty on Account of Fences, &c.

Do you think that One Surveyor is, generally speaking, sufficient?

Yes, certainly. I am of Opinion, that it is unnecessary to have a general and a particular Surveyor for the same Inclosure; and that instead of being a Check, they are only a Clog to the Business; it occasions also an additional F.xpence, for though the Price per Acre is the fame, yet when they attend the Commissioners, they arc both paid the usual Allowance for Attendance.

Do you think that a Surveyor ought, in case of the Death or Secession of a Commissioner, to be appointed a. Commissioner?

I think not, unless under very peculiar Circumstances.

Is not the making of Roads attended with much Expence to the Inclosure?

Yes.

Do you approve of the general Principle of forming and making the Roads at the Expence of the Inclosure?

I do; but think that in the Detail it is attended with much more Expence than is necessary. The Commissioners should have no more to do therewith, than

Did you draw up the Inclosure Bill for the Parish of Hanworth and the adjoining Parishes?

I did.

How are the making and keeping up of Fences regulated in Acts of Inclosure?

The Public Fences are done under the express Directions of the Commissioners, and paid out of the Inclosure Fund. The Boundary Fences are apportioned amongst the different Proprietors. The interior ones are done by the Proprietor.

How might the Expence of the Award be diminiffied?

By leaving out all the reciting Part, and referring, by a few general Words, to the Act. Many Solicitors at present contend for the Necessity of inserting the principal Clauses of the Ad, and all the Proceedings of the Commissioners, which swell the Size and increase the Expence coniidcrably. I was a Commissioner under the Act for inclosing Eaton, in the County of Bedford, the Award of which has been signed only within this Fortnight. This Award amounts to Sixty-ieven Skins, without any Recital; and if it had been done in the old Way, would have amounted to double that Number of Skins.

What is the usual Expence of drawing, ingrossing, and inrolling the Award?

The Expence varies. Some Solicitors charge Ten Shillings per Skin for drawing, the same for ingrossing, and the same for inrolling.' Others charge double for each; there being at present no settled Rule, nor any Means for taxing such Charges.

Is the present Mode of appealing to the Quarter Sessions in all Cales sufficient?

I think it is very insufficient; and in particular the Accounts and Proceedings of the Commissioners are not Efficiently protected, as there is no Appeal from the De-cilion of the Justices to any other Court. With respect to the Accounts, the Proprietors themselves should be enabled to settle them by Public Notice, to be given by the Commissioners, of a Meeting of the Proprietors, in consequence of a Public Notice, and the same to be determined by a Majority in Value there present.

Can you state to the Committee the Nature of the Charges usually made for soliciting and obtaining such an Act of Parliament?

Yes. I did, in the Course of the last Year, publish a Pamphlet, intituled ". The Solicitor's in " liament, concerning Estate B, and Bills of

annexed to which is a Bill of Cods for soliciting an Inclosure Ad. The Charges dated in that Bill are those usually made by Solicitors for the like Budness. In drawing up that Bill, I had before me several Bills of the Sort, furnished me by other Solicitors, redding in different Parts of the Country, as well as in Town. I was particularly anxious in drawing out that Statement of Charges, to be rather under than to exceed the usual Amount. That Bill of Cods I meant to be a Model for Charges in similar Cafes; but is not a correct Copy of any particular Bill. The Charges, it is evident, mud vary according to Circumstances. I beg Leave to add, that in that Bill, no Allowance is made for the Charge of a Country Solicitor's Attendance in Town, during the Progress of the Bill, which fe most Cafes is customary.

Have you found any Difficulty in procuring Consents, and proving the same before the Two Houses?

Yes y both in regard to Proprietors living at a Didance, and redding Abroad. In the former Calc I have found it necessary to go to Bath and Durham, to procure the Contents of Proprietors. The Journey to Durham cod

31. 6s. 6 d.though I went by the Mail. In regard to obtaining the Consent of the Proprietor Abroad, I prepared a Power of Attorney to his Steward in the Country, who redded near the Parish to be inclosed, to authorize him to sign his Consent to the Bill. The Execution of which Letter of Attorney was proved by an Affidavit sworn before the Consul at Oporto; and the Consent thus given, was admitted by both Houses of Parliament. The whole Expence of obtaining this Con-lent amounted only to £. 1. 13 8

John Dorington, Esq;

Examined.

By what Names are the Bills of Inclosure which pass the Two Houses of Parliament usually known?

They are called Single Bills, Double Bills, Three Single Bills, Two Double Bills, Five Single Bills, Three Double Bills, and Four Double Bills.

What is the Dednition of each Sort?

Single Fees are taken on Bills which concern an Individual only. Double Fees are charged where a Number or a Body of People are interested. Three Single Fees are charged where a Number or Body of People are interested, and an Individual, whole Interests are distinct. Two Double Fees are charged where there are Two Bodies of People concerned whole Interests are distinct: and so of the rest, whether Five Single, Three Double, or Four Double.

How is it ascertained whether any particular Bill ought to pay as a Single Bill, or as a Double Bill, &c.?

The Clerk of the Fees forms his Opinion of the Fees that each Bill ought to pay, from the Preamble and Providons of the Bill. If, from Want of local Knowledge, he at any Time mistakes the Providons of the Bill, it is rectified by Explanation from the Solicitor of the Bill; but where he has thought that the Distin&ioa . of Interests has justided the Charge, he has conceived it his Duty to perdft in it, and the Parties have either paid the Fees, or applied, by Means of some Member, to the Speaker for his Opinion. The Clerk of the Fees does not, at present, recoiled any Instance where, on such an Appeal, his Demand has been thought to be improper.

Can you state to the Committee the Fees payable on the different Sorts of Inclosure Bills in the Two Houses?

It is impossible to be exact, as the Fees of Ingrossment must vary according to the Size of the Bill; but I have drawn up, for the Information of the Committee, the following Table, collected from Accounts of Fees actually paid on Bills of the different Sorts which have, passed the Two Houses.

A Petition of the Manufacturers and others, concerned in the Woollen Trade, of the County of Gloucester, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, by One of the Articles of the proposed Union between Great Britain and Ireland, the Petitioners observe, with extreme Concern, that Wool, the Growth of this Country, may be imported into the Sifter King-'dom; and that the Petitioners beg Leave - to impress upon the House the very great Importance and Value of the Woollen Trade, and to remind the House of the especial Care which the Legislature has taken, from Time to Time, to preserve to this Country the exclu-five Consumption of its own Wool; and that the Petitioners do humbly represent, that the Wool, the Growth

of this Country, is not more than equal to the Demands of the Manufacturers, as is sufficiently demonstrated by the very increased Prices which Wools have of late Years borne; and that the Petitioners feel a most serious Alarm at the Consequences that mult result from allowing Wool to be sent out of the Kingdom under any Circumstances, as such a Measure must inevitably facilitate the illicit Exportation of it to Foreign Countries; and that the Petitioners on these Grounds are deeply im-prelfed with the Conviction that such a Meafare, if passed into a Law, would materially affect the Manufacturing and Landed Interests of the Country, and would operate as a moll serious Check on the Industry and Labour of the lower dalles, at present so extensively employed in the various Branches of the Woollen Manufacture: And therefore praying, That the Exportation of Wool to Ireland may not be permitted by any Law to be passed by the House.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the £onsideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of His Majesty's most Gracious Message of the 2d Day of this Instant April, communicating to this House the Resolutions of the Lords and Commons of respecting an Union

between the Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland, with their Address to His Majesty thereupon.

Mr. Wilberforce reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Noblemen, and the humble Petition of the several other Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Guardians of the charitable Institution, commonly called The Asylum, or House of Refuge for the Reception of Orphan Girls, the Settlements of whose Parents cannot be found, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the Reverend William Agutter, Chaplain and Secretary to The Asylum, being examined, said, That the Institution was entered into by several Noblemen, Gentlemen, and others, in the Year 1758, and that the same hath been from that Time carried on, in an House and Premises, situate in the Parish of Saint Mary, Lambeth, in the County of Surrey; that the Charity hath been supported by the Voluntary Subscriptions and Donations, and a great Number of Orphan Girls have been received into and maintained and educated thereby, and, at proper Ages, apprenticed therefrom; and that such Orphan Girls have not only been Iheltered and protested from Vice and Want, but carefully instructed in the Principles of Religion, and in Reading, Writing, Needlework, and Household Business, and trained to Habits of Industry and Regularity, whereby the Public have been, and continue to be, provided with a Supply of diligent and sober Female Domestic Servants: — And, being further examined, he said, That Experience hath shewn that this Charity hath been hitherto of considerable Use and Advantage to the Public, and that it is apprehended, if countenanced and supported by the Laws of the Realm, and established upon a permanent Foundation, and veiled with Powers for better enabling the Subscribers thereto to carry into Execution their charitable and useful Designs, the Charity would be of much more ex-

Vol. 55.

tensive Use, and of still greater Benefit and Advantage to the Public.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for establishing and well governing the charitable Institution, commonly called The Asylum, or House of Refuge for the Reception of Orphan Girls, the Settlements of whose Parents cannot be found; and for incorporating the Subscribers thereto, and for the better empowering and enabling them to carry on their charitable and useful Designs: And that Mr. Wilberforce, the Lord Hawkefbwry, and Mr. Ryder, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Merchants, Manufactureers, and Wool Dealers, of the City of Norwich, and County of the same City, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners find, by One of the Articles of the Union of Great Britain with Ireland, that the Wool of Great Britain is proposed to be exported to Ireland; and that to permit the Exportation of Wool from this Kingdom to Ireland will be injurious to the Trade and Manufactures of the City and County of Norwich; and that, as the many prohibitory Laws have hitherto proved inefficient to the Purpose of preventing the illicit Trade, the Petitioners are of Opinion, that the exporting British Wool to Ireland will materially iqcrease the Evil: And therefore praying, That the Exportation of Wool to Ireland may not, by any Law to be passed by the House, be permitted.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of His Majesty's most Gracious Message of the 2d Day of this lnstant April, communicating to this House the Resolutions of the Lords and Commons of Ireland respecting an Union between the Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland, with their Address to His Majesty thereupon.

TRANSLATION of a Treaty between His Majesty and the Elector Palatine of Bavaria signed at Munich, March 16th, 1800.

Be it known, unto all those whom it may concern, That his Serene Highness the Elector Palatine of Bavaria, finding himself, in Capacity of Member of the Empire, and in consequence of his Attachment to its Constitution, engaged in the War which the Germanick Body has been compelled to declare against France, as well for the Defence and Support of its Constitution as for the Integrity of its Territory, and fully convinced of the Necessity of employing for this salutary Purpose, not only the Forces which the Laws of the Empire require from each of its Members under the Title of Contingent, but to develope still greater Means in order the sooner to obtain an honourable and permanent Peace, which the seizing on the Part of France, of a considerable Portion of the Dominions and Revenues of his Serene Electoral Highness, renders him incapable of doing, without Assistance, to the Extent that he could wish, has applied to His Brita Majesty, (who, in Consequence of the hostile Aggression of France, finds Himlelf also at War with the same Enemy) requesting His Majesty to assist his Serene Electoral Highness to carry these Measures into Execution, by adopting such Arrangements as might be judged proper. His Majesty, on His Side, participating in the Sentiments of his Serene Electoral Highness in this Respect, and desirous of giving him a Proof of His Friendship and of His Desire of promoting, as far as depends upon Himl'clf, the justand salutary Object which his Serene Electoral Highness has in View, has in Consequence sent to Munich, William Wickham, Esquire, His Minister Plenipotentiary and Commissary named for this Purpose, in order to settle more particularly all Points relative to this important Object; and his Serene Highness the Elector Palatine of Bavaria has named, on his Part, for the same Purpose, the Baron Maximilien Joseph de , his

Chamberlain, acting Privy Councillor, Minister of State and of Conferences, having the Department for Foreign Affairs, Honorary Great Cross of the Order of St. John of Jerusalem, who, after the Exchange of their respective full Powers, have agreed upon the following Articles;

Article I.

His Serene Highness the Elector Palatine of Bavaria shall place at the Disposition. of His Majesty the King of Great Britain,a Body of Twelve Thousand Men Infantry and Cavalry, it being always well understood that the Proportion of Cavalry shall not exceed One-eleventh Part of the whole Corps, to lerve in whatever Part of Europe His Majesty shall require, during the Term of One whole Year, to be dated from the Day on which the Corps fully compleat shall be reviewed by the Commissary of His Britannick Majesty.

This whole Corps, as well as the General appointed by his Serene Electoral Highness to command it, shall be

under

4 2 23° Ap. 1800.

\inder the Orders of such Commander in Chief of the Allied Armies as it shall please His Majesty

to point out for that Purpose: they shall obey him according to the Laws of War and Military Discipline in every Thing which concerns the Progress of the War and the Combination of Operations, it being well understood, however, that in every Thing which only relates to their Discipline and to their Interior and particular Organization, the Palatine Bavarian Troops furnished by Virtue of this Treaty shall remain under the immediate Command of their own Officers, and under the Orders of their Bavarian General} they shall always be employed together, without ever being separated, unless Military Considerations should require it; they shall be treated in all Points, as well in whatever concerns Military Service, as in every other Respect, upon the Footing of perfect Equality with the Troops of the Power with whose Army they shall act.

Moreover, the said Corps shall be absolutely independant of, and in addition, to, the Troops his Serene Eledoral Highness is required to furnish as his Contingent to the Army of the Empire.

Article II.

This Corps, exercised, disciplined, armed, equipped, and supplied with every Military Equipage, with Field Artillery in the Proportion of Two Pieces per Battalion, and the necessary Ammunition, shall be ready to march, and shall march in the following Manner:

The First Half shall be mustered either at or Augjburgh, or at such other Town in as shall be pointed out by the under signed Plenipotentiaries, on the First Day of April, and shall be there passed in Review by the Commissary of His Britannick Majesty, appointed for this Purpose:

The Second Half shall be mustered at One of the above mentioned Places on the Twenty-fifth of the same Month of April, or sooner if it can be done, and shall in like Manner be there passed in Review.

Article III.

In order to defray the Expences of the Levy and Equipment of this Corps, and to facilitate to his Serene Electoral Highness the Means of completing and enabling it speedily to join the Troops destined to ad against the Common Enemy, His Britannick Majesty engages to pay to his Serene Eledofal Highness the Sum of Four-score Banco Crowns for each Horseman, mounted, armed, equipped and exercised, and Thirty Banco Crowns for each Foot Soldier, likewise armed, equipped, and exercised. — The Crown Banco to be valued at 4 9 i

Sterling. One Half of this Levy Money shall be paid on the very Day on which the First Division shall be passed in Review, and approved by the Commissary of His Britannick Majesty; the other Half on the Day when the Second Division shall be passed in Review, and approved in the same Manner.

Article IV.

The Pay of these Troops, as well as their Subsistence upon the War Establishment, as practised in the Bavaria an Palatine Army, shall take place from the Day of the Signature of the present Treaty; but no actual Payment shall be made before the First Review shall have taken place. This Payment shall continue to be made by His Britannick Majesty as well for the Pay of the Troops as for all other Allowances whatever, and without Exception, as long as the Corps shall be at His Disposal.

In order to prevent all Disputes which might arise upon the Subject, the High Contracting Parties shall agree, through their respective Commissaries named for this Purpose, upon a fixed Sum, according to which these different Articles shall be computed and paid during the Continuance of the present Treaty.

His Britannick Majesty consents to make an extraordinary Allowance to this Corps (in addition to the Current Expences) of One Month's Pay, and Emoluments

towards defraying the Expences of its Return, whenever it shall be sent back into the Dominions of his Serene Eledoral Highness.

Article V.

As long as this Treaty is in Force, all Palatine Bavarian Deserters shall be faithfully given up whenever they shall be discove-ed in Places dependant upon His Britannick Majesty, or in any Corps levied by His Orders.

Article VI.

His Serene Eledoral Highness engages to keep this Corps always complete, and to fend every Three Months, and even oftener, if the Situation of Affairs should absolutely require it, the Recruits necessary for that Purpose, equipped and exercised.

Article VII.

It shall be at the Option of His Britannick Majesty's Commissary to review the Whole, or Part, of this Corps Once a Year, or oftener; nevertheless, that there may not be any Risk of deranging the Operations of the Campaign, it must not be more frequently for each Corps than Once in Two Months. The Commissaries and Officers, as well Generals as Commanders of Regiments, and every Officer, or other Person, charged with conducting the Recruits to the Corps, shall each be obliged to furnish to His Britannick Majesty's Commis-fary the Returns either of the Whole of the Subsidiary Corps, or of the different Regiments, or of the Recruits, whenever the said Commissary shall judge proper to demand it.

Article VIII.

His Serene Highness the Elector having, at the express Desire of His Majesty, by virtue of the Sixth Article, entirely renounced all the Advantages resulting from vacant Pay, which in all similar Treaties has been regarded as the principal Fund for supplying the Expences of recruiting, and having, by the Seventh Article, furnished every possible Facility to His Britannick Majesty's Commissary to verify the exact State of the Corps at all Times, and the Number and Condition of Recruits which may be sent to it. His Britannick Majesty being fully sensible of the Advantage of this Arrangement, both for keeping the Corps complete, and for the effectice Services which it will be by that Means enabled to render, not only at the Beginning, but during the whole Continuance of the Campaign, engages to pay to his Serene Highness, for the Expences of recruiting, a Sum calculated at the Rate of Thirty Crowns Banco for each Recruit, disciplined, armed, and accoutred, who shall be provided in the Place of the Men who die or are discharged from the Service during the Time these Troops are employed by His Majesty.

The Deserters are expressly excepted from this Article, and his Serene Highness the Elector shall be at the whole Expence of replacing the m.

Article IX.

The Artillery and other Effects and Implements of War loft against the Enemy, shall be replaced at the Expence of His Britannick Majesty, at a fixed Price to be agreed upon by the Commissaries of the High Con-trading Parties.

Article X.

His Britannick Majesty promises to attend to the Safety of the Dominionsand Possessions of his Serene Eledoral Highness, and to direct the Military Operations as far as depends upon Him, and as the Circumstances of the War, and the Interests of the Common Cause will permit, in such Manner as that the BavaPalatine Countries actually occupied by his Serene Eledoral Highness, or by the Allied Armies, shall be llieltered and Ipared as much as possible; but if, notwithstanding the Precautons which will be taken with this View, any Part of the

above

40 Geo. IIL 230 — 240 Apr His. 413

above mentioned States of his Serene Electoral Highness were to be attacked by the Enemy in Rel'entment for the present Treaty, His Majesty will take, in

Concert with His Allies, those Measures which shall be judged the most suitable for procuring to his Serene Electoral Highness an Indemnity proportioned to the Losses which such an Invasion should have occasioned to any of these Provinces.

Article Xt. '

In order to give to his Serene Electoral' Highness a iftill stronger Proof of His Friendship, as well as of the lively and sincere Interest which He takes in the Preler-vation and Prosperity of his House, His Britannick Majesty will observe the same Conduct with regard to the other Possessions of his Serene Electoral Highness, as the same shall be re-conquered and delivered from the Hands of the Enemy, and will moreover employ Him-self in the most effectual Manner, in Concert with His Allies, to obtain, at a General Peace, the complete Restitution of the Dominions which the Electoral House possessed at the Commencement of the present War, such as they flood at that Period.

Article XII.

The Corps stipulated for in the present Treaty may be increased to 20,000 Men, in Consequence of an Augmentation of the Expences of Levy and Equipment, as well as of Pay and other Emoluments, calculated upon the Basis of the present Treaty, according to such Augmentation of the Number as may be agreed upon between the High Contracting Parties.

Article XIII.

The Clauses and Stipulations of the present Treaty shall be communicated wholly and without any Reserve to his Imperial and Royal Majesty the Emperor of the Romans, and to his Imperial and most Eminent Majesty the Emperor of all the; they shall be at Liberty

to accede to it, in as far as the Nature of the different Articles and Stipulations will permit, as well as to such Modifications or Additions as the High Contracting Par. ties may hereafter add thereto *

Article XIV.

The Ratifications of the present Treaty shall be exchanged in the Space of Four Weeks, or sooner, if possible. In Witness whereof the undersigned have signed the present Treaty, and have affixed thereunto the Seal of their Arms.

Done at Munich, the Sixteenth Day of March One thousand Eight hundred.

(Signed) William (L. S.)

A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are there-underwritten, Inhabitants of the Borough of rencester, in the County of G, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners fee, with great Concern, the Intention of introducing a Clause into the Bill for uniting the Two Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland, whereby Wool will be permitted to be exported from this to the Sifter Kingdom; and that this Measure will prove extremely detrimental to the Woollen Manufactory of this Kingdom at large, and to the County of in particular; and that the Adoption of any Measures which may tend in the least Degree to check the Employment of the Poor at this particular Time, might be attended with the most dangerous Consequences: And therefore praying. That the above Measure may not pass into a Law.

A Petition of the Clothiers and Land Owners of wick, in the County of Gloucester, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, with Regret, that, in the Arrangement for an Union with Ireland, it is proposed that the Acts of Parliament which prohibit the Exportation of Wool, the Growth of this Kingdom, should be repealed; and that the Pari fir of PainJ'wick is calculated to contain nearly 6,000 Inhabitants, and, at a moderate Computation, Three-fourths of them are employed in the different Branches of the Manufacture of Woollen Cloth; and that the Petitioners have, in the Course of the last Three

40 Apri

A. 1800.

Years, expended large Sums in erecting Machinery and suitable Buildings, which, it is apprehended, would in a great Measure be rendered useless, and the Inhabitants be thrown out of Employ, whereby they would have to depend upon the Landed Interest for Support, should the Exportation of British Wool be permitted, as the present Growth is not sufficient to supply the Manufacturers of this Kingdom: And therefore praying. That theexisting Laws, , which prohibit the Exportation of Wool, may not be repealed.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of His Majesty's most Gracious Message of the 2d Day of this Instant April, communicating to this House the Resolutions of the Lords and Commons of Ireland respecting an Union between the Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland, with their Address to His Majesty thereupon.

His present Majesty, for dividing several Commonable Lands in the Parish of Barrington, in the County of Cambridge, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, on the 5th Day of March last, a Petition of Richard Bendyjhe, of Barrington, in the County of Cambridge, Esquire, was presented to the House, stating, that the Petitioners had been guilty of great Partiality and MisconduCV in carrying the said Act into Execution, and containing many Assertions highly reflecting upon their Character, and praying, that the House would take his same into Consideration, and'grant him such Relief' as the Hardship of it should seem to require; and that the Petitioners, conscious that the Charges contained in the Petition of the said Richard Bendyjhe were wholly void of Foundation, did, on the 28th Day of March last, present their Petition to the House, stating, - among other Things, that they were ready and desirous to meet any Enquiry which the House might think fit to direct into their Conduct or Proceedings as such Commissioners; and praying. That, if the House should think fit to direct any Enquiry upon the Petition of the said Richard Bendyfhe, they might be at Liberty to be heard, at the same Time, in order to disprove the Allegations contained in his laid Petition; and that, ever since the said 28th Day of March last, the Petitioners have been ready to meet any Enquiry into their Conduct, and they and their Witnesses are now attending in Town for that Purpose, at a considerable Expence, but the Petitioners have lately been informed, that the said Richard Bendyjhe intends to decline proceeding further upon his said Petition; and that the Petitioners therefore, anxious to vindicate their Character from the Accusations most unjustly made against them by the said Richard Bendyjhe, and to confute the Calumny thus injurioully charged upon them in the House, do most humbly pray, That the House will be pleased to order that the Allegations contained in the Aid Petition of the said Richard Bendyjhe may be immediately enquired into, or that they may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem just.

A Petition of the Merchants and Woollen Manufacturers of Tiverton, in the County of Devon, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have been informed, that, among the Articles of the intended Union with , one is de-

signed to repeal the Laws against the Exportation of Wool from this Kingdom, as far as relates to Ireland, which they apprehend will be attended with injurious Consequences to the Woollen Manufacturers of this Country, and of Tiverton in particular, by draining the Wool, scarcely enough for common Annual Supply, from that Vicinity, so well situated for Exportation, and, by its Tendency, to advance the Price of their staple Commodity, which is already much too high for the present Demands of Trade, and open a Path of illicit Exportation to other Countries, productive of the most pernicious Effects, not only to the Manufacturer, but also to the Land Owner, Farmer, and every Species of Property in this Kingdom; and therefore imploring the Protection of the House against such Article of Union.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committeeof the whole House, to whomit is referred to consider further of His Majesty's most Gracious' Message of the 2d Day of this Instant April, com-nfunicating to this House the Resolutions of the Lords and Commons of Ireland respecting an Union between the Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland, with their Ad-drels to His Majesty thereupon.

A Petition of the Merchants, Manufacturers, Land Petition from and Mill Owners, and others, interested in the Prospe- Kenad again rity of the Woollen Manufactures of the Burgh of the Export -Kirkby in Kendal, in the County of and tio" Wo0 '

its Vicinity, was presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That the Petitioners are friendly to the Union of Great Britain with Ireland, as firmly believing that that Measure will add to the general Strength and Prosperity of the Empire; and that the illicit Exportation of Wool from Great Britain to Foreign Countries (notwithstanding the manyexisting Laws prohibiting and guarding against such Exportation) was certainly carried on so long as those Countries were capable of carrying on their Woollen Manufactories; and that the Petitioners, knowing the great Advantage which the

Woollen Manufactories of Foreign Countries reap from a Mixture of the Wool of Great Britain with the Wool which is the Growth of those Countries, are fearful that the great Temptations usually held out by such Foreigners, as an Encouragement to such illicit Trade, will have the Effect of producing an Exportation of Wool to a great Degree, when it may not only be practicable, but ealy; and that the Petitioners find, by One of the Articles of the Union ot Great Britain with Ireland, that the Wool of Great Britain is proposed to be exported to land; and that the Petitioners are satisfied, that, under the Pretence of conveying such Wool to Ireland, the Exportation of that Article to Foreign Countries will take place to a great Extent (when Peace arrives) without any Possibility of its Prevention, to the incalculable Loss of the Petitioners: And therefore praying. That the Exportation of Wool to Ireland may not, by any Law to be passed by the House, be permitted.

A Petition of the Merchants, Clothiers, and others. Petition from concerned in the Wool and Woollen Trade, redding in Totnes, in the County of Devon, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe, with inexpressible Concern, that, in the Arrangement of the Union with our Sifter Kingdom, (he proposes that the existing Laws, prohibiting the Exportation of British Wool, should be repealed, lo fir as relates

to herself, whilst on her Part lhe claims the Continuance of the protesting Duties for her Woollen Manufactures; and that the Growth of Wool in Great Britain is not sufficient to supply the Manufacturers with a Quantity equal to the present Demand for Home Consumption and Foreign Markets, and therefore, if any Part is permitted to be taken away, the Petitioners mull fuller very material Injury; and that the Petitioners are most ferioully alarmed, in case British Wool should be permitted to be exported, that, under Pretence of carrying it to Ireland, great Quantities would be conveyed to Foreign Countries, without the Possibility of its being prevented, particularly in Times of Peace, whereby the British Merchant and Manufacturer would suffer, without the new Members of the Empire being benefited, and other Countries would be supplied with the Means for supplanting the Petitioners in Foreign Markets: And therefore praying, That, in the Arrangement of the Union between the Two Kingdoms about to take place. Great Britain may not be put to the Rilk of being deprived of an Article which has been the great Source of Wealth and Happiness to its Inhabitants.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole Floufe, to whom it is referred to conficler further of His Majesty's ir.oft Graciou *

Mr. Bragge, according to Order, reported from the Commitee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of'exempting Burr Stones taken from a Quarry near Conway in North Wales, to be used as Mill Stones only, from the Duty imposed by an Act, made in the Thirty-fourth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for granting to His Majesty " certain Duties of Customs on Slate, Stone, and Marble;" and who were instructed to consider of so much of an Act, made in the Thirty-eighth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for the " better Protection of the Trade of this Kingdom; " and for granting new and additional Duties of Customs on Goods imported and exported, and on the " Tonnage of certain Ships entering Outwards or Inwards to or from Foreign Parts, until the Signing the " Preliminary Articles of Peace," as charges a Duty on Oil or Blubber imported into this Kingdom from the Greenland Fisheries and Davis's Streights, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is expedient that Burr Stones, taken from a Quarry near Conway, in North Wales, to be used as Mill Stones only, should be exempted from the Duty imposed by the said Act.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is expedient to permit Blubber, imported into this Kingdom from the Greenland Fisheries and Davis's Streights, to be boiled into Oil, and that such Oil should be admitted to Entry and pay Duty accordingly.

The said Resolutions being feve rally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Sd. which, by the Account above inserted, appears to be now due to the Public, with such farther Interest as may accrue thereon till the same shall be paid, together with the Particulars and Amount of

" Whole of their Engagements, which were chiefly " Bills drawn from Grenada and accepted, to a greater Amount (at a previous Period of Ease and Facility " in Trade) at from 90J to 30" , which could not afterwards be put off beyond those Periods of Payment " without absolute Bankruptcy: But there were also " many other Engagements for Goods of the Manufacture of Great Britain shipped to the' West; " for Floating Money lodged by Correspondents; for " Monies borrowed on Discounts from Bankers; and " even for more permanent Loans, which the Calamities of " the Times had obliged the Lenders to withdraw from " them. That to these different Sorts of Demands " were to be added the considerable, Sums which they " had applied to the Settlement of their own Estates, " and those of their Correspondents, which had suffered " to so great an Amount during the Period of War and " Insurrection. That, as no particular separate Appropriation of the different Funds could be made Out " with any Precision, so to state the Appropriation of " the Whole would require a Copy of their Books during " the Period enquired after, which would occupy Two " or Three Thousand Pages in Folio. That it was " presumed it would sufficiently appear in what Manner it had happened that the Partnership had not " been able to set apart any of the Funds which had " accrued to the House during the Time specified, towards the Liquidation of the Debt to Government,

" by referring to a List of Balances due to them in Report on 1 " Grenada alone, during the Eight last Years. That '"cl!' " the Loans had been made to them by Government " to enable them to support the Advances which the " Insurrection and other unfortunate Events had increased to such an enormous Extent. That, from a " Continuation of those Causes, and the incautious " Acceptances before mentioned in Time of Eale and " Peace, for which Remittances had either totally " failed, or had been received in no Sort of Proportion,

" the Grenada Debts had continued of such a Magnitude as to prevent any Payment to Government,

" without occasioning, by refuiing to answer unavoidable Demands, an immediate Failure, to the great Injury, not only of the Partnership, but also of their " Sureties, their Creditors, and the Public at large."

N° 1. Under Title Funds, is taken from a List certified upon Oath by Mr. William; who states himself to have acted as Confidential Clerk to Messrs. A. Hvujloun and Co. for many Years, and to be well acquainted with their Books and Affairs- It will be ob-served that the Deduction from the Gross Sum owing to the House for bad Debts is nearly about One-fifth of the Whole; but it appears that such Deduction was not taken upon a General Average, but by a Consideration of each particular Debt, no Abatement being made from many, and from others'various Proportions being subtracted. Your Committee cannot judge of the Propriety of those Allowances: Mr. Bell certifies that they appear to him to be reasonable and sufficient. He also states that the Books of the House are fairly and regularly kept. It may be proper, however, to observe here, that by the Act of 37 Geo. III. C. 27, (Sect. 13, 14, 15, and 16) which first permitted the Commissioners to accept of Securities on Plantations in Grenada and St. Vincent's, (and they had not by that Act any Power given them to take such Security on Estates in any other of the West India Islands)that Power was confined by several Restrictions, One of which was, that Mortgages granted to them on such Estates should not be deemed sufficient Security for any Sum exceeding the fair Average Value of the Produce of the Premises in Two Years. The Value of the West India Estates, in the Third Class of Property now under Consideration, must have been calculated on Ten Years Purchase at least. The most valuable of those Estates is indeed in Stt Chrifiophet's, where Plantations are said to be generally valued considerably higher than in the Islands of Grenada and St. Vincent.

A "Petition of the Clothiers residing in the City of New Sarum, was prefen ted to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observing, in the Arrangement of Union proposed by our Sifter Kingdom, (he requires that the existing Laws, for the Prohibition of British Wool, shall be repealed, so far as relates to

herself, notwithstanding (he, at the same Time, appears to claim the Continuance of protesting Duties to her Woollen Manufactures, the Petitioners therefore are greatly alarmed at the Importance of this Proposition; and that the Petitioners are of Opinion, the Growth of Wool in Great Britain is not, at present, more than sufficient to supply the Manufacturers to execute their Commissions for Home.and Foreign Markets, and, if any Part thereof is suffered to be taken away, the Petitioners must feel a material Injury; and that the Petitioners fee with Concern, in cal'e British Wool is permitted to be exported to Ireland, it may, under false Pretences, be conveyed to Foreign Countries, and that no Vigilance can prevent it in Times of Peace, consequently this Country would then not only experience a Loss in Proportion as the Sifter Country derives an Advantage, but other Nations will be able to obtain a Preference in Foreign Markets: And therefore praying, That they may not, in the Arrangement of Union between the Two Kingdoms, be deprived of an Article which has ever been known to be a great Source of Support to the numerous Poor of the said City and Neighbourhood, and of general Wealth and Happiness to the Inhabitants of Great Britain.

A Petition of the Manufacturers, and others, concerned in the Wool and Woollen Trade, residing in, or near to, the Town of Banbury, in the County of Oxford, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners notice, with inexprefiible Anxiety, amongst the Resolutions passed by the Parliament of Ireland, for an Union with this Kingdom, a Proposition or Declaration, " That, from and after the i ft Day of " January 1801, all Prohibitions and Bounties on the " Exports of Articles the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture, of either Country to the other, shall cease " and determine j" and that, fully convinced that the Growth of Wool in this Kingdom is far inadequate to its present Consumption, and that it has Occasion for the Assistance of a Foreign Supply, they strongly dread, that, should the Proposition or Resolution above alluded to be carried into Effect, the Manufacturers of this Kingdom would be highly prejudiced, if not the Manufacture ruined; and that the Petitioners firmly apprehend, and they trust not without just Grounds, that under Pretext of exporting Wool to the Sifter Kingdom, this Staple Commodity will easily ani# readily find its Way into Foreign Kingdoms, not only to the great Detriment of the British Manufacturers, but to the enabling our Rivals to supplant them in Foreign Markets: And therefore praying. A Petition of the Merchants, Manufacturers, Land and Mill Owners, and others, interested in the Prospe-rity of the Woollen Manufactures of the Town and Parish of Haslingden, in the County of Lancaster, was

presented to the House, and read: Setting forth, That the Petitioners are friendly to the Union of Great Britain with Ireland, as firmly believing that that Measure will add to the general Strength and Prosperity of the Empire: That the Petitioners find, by One of the Articles of the Union of Great Britain with Ireland, that the Wool of Great Britain is proposed to be exported to Ireland, and the Petitioners, sensible that the Woollen Manufactories have always been the Staple Trade of this Kingdom, having been the Foundation of the Industry, the Domestic Happiness, the Wealth, and National Dignity, of this Country, and, as it has likewise been the Policy of our Forefathers to preserve our native Wool at Home, the Petitioners conceive, that allowing the Exportation of it, under any Circumstances, would be both impolitic and dangerous, as it mult ultimately tend to the Destruction of our Manufactories, and to the inevitable Ruin of the industrious Poor now employed in them; and that, impressed with the strongest Conviction that the Wool grown in Great Britain will not be more than sufficient to supply the Consumption of its present Manufactories, and which are daily increasing, the Petitioners pray. That the Exportation of Wool to Ireland may not, for the cogent Reasons already given, be suffered to pass into a Law. .

A Petition of the Merchants, Manufacturers, Land and Mill Owners, and others interested in the Prosperity of the Woollen Manufactures of the Town and Neighbourhood of Bury, in the County of Lancaster, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners consider the Union of Great Britain with Ireland as a desirable Object, being firmly of Opinion that that Measure will be attended with many great Advantages to both Countries; and that it is an undoubted FaCb, that Wool was exported from Great Britain to Foreign Countries in a Clandestine Manner, so long as those Countries were capable of carrying on their Woollen Manufactories, notwithstanding the many Laws which have from Time to Time been passed to prohibit and guard against such illicit Exportation; and that the Petitioners, conscious that Foreign Countries derive a very great Advantage in their Woollen Manufactories from a Mixture of Wool of their own Growth with that of Great Britain, are apprehendve that the great Temptations which such Foreigners usually hold out to encourage such illicit Trade will have a Tendency to produce an Exportation of Wool to a great Extent, when the Opportunities for that Purpose are increased j and that the Petitioners observe, in One of the Articles of the Union of Great Britain with Ireland, that it is proposed to allow the Exportation of the Wool of Great Britain to Ireland; and that the Petitioners are firmly persuaded that, at the Termination of the War, the Exportation of British Wool to Foreign Countries will be carried on, with the greatest Facility, to a great Extent, under Pretence of conveying such Wool to Ireland, and which will be attended with the most ruinous Consequences to the Petitioners: And therefore praying, That there may be no Law passed permitting the Exportation of Wool to Ireland.

A Petition of the Yarn Makers, Wool Dealers, and Manufacturers of Worsted and Woollen Goods in the County of Suffolk, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the.{binning of Wool furnishes the principal Employment of the Wives and Children of the Labouring Poor in the said County; and that the Wool spun in the said County, when manufactured into Worsted Stuffs, is increased Ten-fold of its original Value, and that principally by what is paid for Labour; and that our own Manufactories are fully capable of working up all the Wool grown in these Kingdoms; and that the Petitioners understand, that, by an Article in the proposed Union of Ireland with Great Britain, the Laws, prohibiting the Exportation of Wool, are to be repealed, so far as they relate to Ireland; and the Petitioners conceive, that such a Measure would be highly injurious to the Woollen Manufactures of these Kingdoms, inasmuch as the allowed Exportation of Wool to Ireland would facilitate the illicit Exportation of it to Foreign Countries beyond all Possibility of Prevention; and that, by diminishing the Supply of Wool wanted by the Manufacturers of these Kingdoms, the Employment of the Poor would be lessened, and the Community deprived of the Advantage of increasing its Wealth by the Produce of Labour: And therefore praying, That the Exportation of British Wool to Ireland, may not, on any Account, be permitted.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of His Majesty's most Gracious Message of the 2d Day of this Instant April, communicating to this House the Resolutions of the Lords and Commons of Ireland respecting an Union between the Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland, with their Address to His Majesty thereupon.

A Petition of the Woollen Manufacturers, and others, concerned in the Woollen Trade, in the Town of Wive life ombe, in the County of Somerset, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners, favourable as they are to an Union with Ireland, observe, with inexpressible Concern, that the Laws now existing, prohibiting the Exportation of British Wool to that Country, should be repealed, whilst, on her Part, Ike claims the Duties for protecting her Woollen Manufactures; and that the Petitioners conceive the Wool grown in Great Britain is scarcely sufficient to supply the Demands of the Manufacturers, and therefore if Wool, in its Raw State, is allowed to be exported, the Petitioners and their Labourers must suffer a very great Injury; and that the Petitioners are alarmed that, in case British Wool is allowed to be exported, under Pretence of carrying it to Ireland, large Quantities will find its Way into Foreign Countries, by which the British Merchant and Manufacturer will be materially injured, as it will be the Means of the Petitioners being rivalled in a Foreign Market: And therefore praying, That the pro-poled Permission of exporting British Wool to Ireland may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of His Majesty's most Gracious Message of the 2d Day of this Instant April, communicating to this House the Resolutions of the Lords and Commons of Ireland respecting an Union between the Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland, with their Address to His Majesty thereupon.

A Petition of the Merchants, Manufacturers, Land and Mill Owners, and others, of the Forest of Rojfendale, and Places adjacent, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, interested in the Prosperity of the Woollen Manufactures of this Country, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are friendly to the Union of Great Britain with Ireland, so far as they conceive it will tend to increase the general Strength and Prosperity of the Empire; and that the Petitioners find, by One of the Articles of the Union of Great Britain with Ireland, that the Wool of Britain is proposed to be exported to Ireland-, and that the Petitioners have Reason to believe the present Annual Growth of Wool in this Kingdom is scarcely sufficient for the Supply and Consumption of the different Manufactures, and the Exportation of that Article from Great Britain would deprive the Weavers, and others employed in the Manufactory, of Employment, and oblige them to emigrate to Foreign Countries; and that the Petitioners are persuaded that, under the Pretence of conveying Wool to Ireland, the Exportation of that Article to Foreign Countries would take Effect to a great Extent, without any Possibility of its Prevention, to the incalculable Loss of the Petitioners: And therefore praying, That the Exportation of Wool from Great Britain may not Be permitted by any Law to be passed by the House.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to

SI R Henry Paulet St. John Mildmay reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Rector, Churchwardens, and Inhabitants, of the Parish of Chelmsford, in the County of whose Names are

thereunto subscribed; and also, the Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Inhabitants of the Town of Chelmsford, in the County of Essex, were severally referred; That the Committee had examined the Matters of the said Petitions, and had directed him to report the fame, as they appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition, Mr. John Johnson, a Surveyor, being examined, said. That the Parish Church of Chelmsford is a very ancient, (lately, and spacious Pile of Building, and is become much decayed, and that great Part thereof, with the Roof and Side Walls, have lately fallen down, and remain in a ruinous State, inso much that it is deemed indispensably necessary such Parts as have fallen down should be re-built, and that the other Parts of the Building should undergo an immediate, thorough, and Tubftantial Repair: Then,

Mr. Thomas Archer, being examined, said, That a proper Survey has been taken of the necessary Want of Reparation to the said Church, and an Estimate made thereof by an able and experienced Architect, whereby it appears that the Sum necessary to effectuate such Repairs is too large to be raised by the present Inhabitants without the Aid of Parliament; and that the said Church is not in a State fit for the Performance of Divine Worship.

To prove the Allegations of the second-mentioned Petition, Mr. Thomas Archer, being further examined, said. That, on Account of the Accident, by which the greater Part of the said Church was lately destroyed, it became necessary to take down the Organ which formerly flood therein, and that it is fit the same should be again placed in the said Church, and that some permanent Provision should be made for paying a Salary to an Organist, the Expence whereof hath heretofore been defrayed by Voluntary Contributions, the Amount whereof hath been precarious :-rAnd, the Witness further said, That the Town of Chelmsford is large and populous, and the Church Yard being situate in the Centre of the Town is subject to various Nuisances, Annoyances, and Misdemeanors; particularly, such as permitting Hogs to go therein, breaking and destroying the GraveStones, and injuring the Trees by hanging Lines thereto; which Nuisances, Annoyances, and Misdemeanors, it is the Wifti of the Inhabitants, should be prevented for the future.

Koval Assent A Message by Sir Francis Molyneux, Gentleman Ulher to Bill . of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty's Commission, for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House, in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House, at the Delire of the Lords authorized by virtue of His Majesty's Commission afore-mentioned, had been at the House of Peers, where a Commission under the Great Seal was read, giving, declaring, and notifying the Royal Assent to the several Public Bills therein mentioned; and also empowering His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, His Royal Highness the Duke of York, His Royal Highness the Duke of Clarence, His Royal Highness the Duke of Kent, His Royal Highness the Duke of Cumberland, His Royal Highness the Duke of Gloucester, the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, and several other Lords, to declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills: And that the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, the Earl Spencer, and Lord Grenville, named also in the said Commission, did accordingly declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills: Which Bills are as followeth; viz.

An Act to enable the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury to issue Exchequer Bills, to a limited Amount, on the Credit of such Aids or Supplies as have been, or shall be, granted by Parliament, for the Service of the Year One thousand Eight hundred; and to enable the Governor and Company of the Bank of England to advance Cash or Bullion to be remitted Abroad, on Account of Foreign Subsidiesor Services Abroad:

An Act for granting a Bounty on the Importation of Oats until the First Day of One thousand

Eight hundred i

An Act to enable Courts of Equity to compel a Transfer of Stock in Suits, without making the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, or the United Company of Merchants of England trading to the East Indies, or the Governor and Company of Merchants of Great Britain trading to the South Seas, or other Parts of America, Party thereto:

An Act to permit the Importation of Goods and Commodities from Countries in America, belonging to any Foreign European Sovereign or State, in Neutral Ships, until the Twenty-ninth Day of September One thousand Eight hundred and One:

An Act for dividing, allotting, inclosing, draining, and preserving, the Open Fields, Commons, Fens, and Waste Grounds, within the Parish of in the County of Norfolk:

An Act for continuing for Twenty-one Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, the Term, and altering and enlarging the Powers, of Two Acts, passed for widening and repairing the High Road leading from Heron Syke, which divides the Counties of Lancaster and Westmorland, to the Town of Kirkby in Kendal, and from the said Town of Kirkby in Kendal, through the Town of Shop, to Emont Bridge, in the said County of Westmorland.

A Petition of the Bakers resident in the City and Petition of Suburbs of Winchester, and Places adjoining, in the wSn'hefter, County of Southampton, was presented to the House, and &c. read; Taking Notice of the Bill for better regulating the Price and Assize of Bread; and Setting forth, That the said Bill is, in its Tendency, oppressive to the Petitioners, and others in the same Business, and, if carried into a Law, will so clog and hinder them in the Management of their Business, and so strip them of every Profit in the fame, as to oblige them to seek other Occupations for Subsistence; and that, by the said Bill, it is intended 7

that the Price of Bread should be set at Twenty-one Peck Loaves to the Sack, allowing the Baker from Six to Fourteen Shillings per Sack for Baking, which will be the utter Ruin of the' Petitioners, as such Bill does not make a sufficient Allowance to pay the Expences of manufacturing the Flour into Bread, and it will be impoffi-ble to make Twenty-one Peck Loaves to the Sack, and the Expences in manufacturing a Sack of Flour into Bread are at least Six Shillings; and that the Petitioners have been very much aggrieved for several Years past in Consequence of a Discretionary Power being vested in the Magistrate in setting the Assize of Bread; and that, for the Reasons above assigned, and in Consequence of the very advanced Prices of every Article in Life, and the great Increase of Wages, the Petitioners conceive they ought always to be allowed Ten Shillings at least; per Sack for manufacturing (with the additional Duty on Salt) and, if the House should fix the Profit at less than Ten Shillings per Sack, it will be totally importable for the Petitioners to subsist: And therefore praying the House to take their same into Consideration, and that the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed.

An ingrossed Bill for amending the several Acts passed for making, extending, finishing, and completing the Canal Navigation from Manchester to or Hear under Lyne and Oldham, and the several Cuts and other Works authorized to be made and done by the Company of Proprietors of the said Canal Navigation, and for granting to the said Company further And other Powers, was read the Third Time;

An ingrossed Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, by Way of Ryder, for inverting Motley paid for the Purchase of Land belonging to Persons under any Disability, where it exceeds Two Hundred bounds.

And the said Clause was Thrice read; and, upon the Quezon put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill, by Way of Ryder.

Another ingrossed Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, by Way of Ryder, for the like Purpose, where the Purchase Money is between Twenty Pounds and Two Hundred Pounds.

And the said Clause was Thrice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to By the House, to be made Part of the Bill, by Way of Ryder.

Another ingrossed Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, by Way of Ryder for the like Purpose, where the Purchase Money is less than Twenty Pounds.

And the said Clause was Thrice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill, by Way of Ryder.

Then the Amendments following were severally proposed to be made to the Bill; vit.

Pr. 7. 1. 10. After " to," to insert " an equal " Share of the Profits of the said " Undertaking, and to."

Pr. 8. 1. lo. To leave out " thereby," And insert " by each such Note/' instead thereof.

Pr. 20. 1. 13. After " being," to insert " and the " other Parties in Difference."

Pr. 32. I.39. To leave out from " Weirs" to " and, " in Pr. 36. 1. 34.

And the said Amendments were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House; and the Bill was amended at the Table accordingly.

Resolved, That the Bill do pals: And that the Title be. An Act for amending the several Acts passed for making, extending, finishing, and completing the -Canal Navigation from Manchester to or near Ashton under Lyne and Oldham, and the several Cuts and other Works authorized to be made and done by the Company of Proprietors of the said Canal Navigation, and for granting to the said Company further and other Powers.

Ordered, That Mr. Stanley do carry the Bill to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence.

Ordered, That the Order of the Day, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for increasing the Rates of Subsistence to be paid to Innkeepers, and others, on Quartering Soldiers, be now read.

And the said Order being read accordingly;

Ordered, That the Report, which was made from the Committee, to whom the several Petitions of the Innkeepers, Victuallers, and Publicans, which have been presented to the House in this Session of Parliament, respecting the Allowances to be made for the Quartering of Horl'e and Foot Soldiers, were referred, be referred to the said Committee.

Then the House resolved itself into the said Cotnmittee.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

A Motion being made. That the ingrossed Bill from the Lords, intituled, An Act for uniting the North Mediety of the Rectory of Leverton, in the County of Lincoln, with the South Mediety of the same Redtory, from and after the next Avoidance of either Benefice, be now read the Third Time;

Mr. Douglas, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of His Majesty's most Gracious Mef-sage of the 2d Day of April last, communicating to this House the Resolutions of the Lords and Commons of Ireland, respecting an Union between the Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland, with their Address to His Majesty thereupon, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read j and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it be the First Article of the Union of the Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland, That the said Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland shall, upon the First Day of January which shall be in the Year of Our Lord One thousand Eight hundred and One, and for ever after, be united into One Kingdom, by the Name of " The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and that the Royal Stile and Titles appertaining to the Imperial Crown of the said United Kingdom and its Dependencies, and also the Ensigns Armorial, Flags and Banners thereof, shall be such as His Majesty, by His Royal Proclamation under the Great Seal of the United Kingdom, shall be pleased to appoint.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee^ That it be the Second Article of Union, That the Succession to the Imperial Crown of the said United Kingdom, and of the Dominions thereunto belonging, shall continue limited and settled in the same Manner as the Succession to the Imperial Crown of the said Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland now (lands limited and settled, according to the existing Laws, and to the Terms of Union between England and Scotland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it be the Third Article of Union, That the said United Kingdom be represented in One and the same Parliament, to be (liled " The Parliament of the United " Kingdom of Great Britain and ."

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it be the Fourth Article of Union, That Four Lords Spiritual of Ireland, by Rotation of Sessions, and Twenty-eight Lords Temporal of Ireland, elected for Life by the Peers of Ireland, shall be the Number to fit 6 A and
