and if no Claim shall be made to the Inheritance of such Peerage, in such Form and Manner as may from Time to Time be prescribed by the House of Lords of the United Kingdom, before the Expiration of the said Period of a Year, then and in that same such Peerage shall be deemed extinct, provided that nothing herein shall exclude any Person from afterwards putting in a Claim to the Peerage so deemed extinct; and if such Claim shall be allowed as valid, by Judgment of the House of Lords of the United Kingdom reported to His Majesty, such Peerage^shall be considered as revived; and, in case any new Creation of a Peerage of that Part of the United Kingdom called Ireland, shall have taken Place in the Interval, in Consequence of the supposed Extinction of such Peerage, then no new Right of Creation shall accrue to His Majesty, His Heirs or Succeil'ors, in Consequence of the next Extinction which shall take Place of any Peerage of that Part of the United Kingdom called Ireland: That all Questions touching the Election of Members to fit on the Part of Ireland in the House of Commons of the United Kingdom, shall be heard and decided in the same Manner as Questions touching such Elections in Great Britain now are, or at any Time hereafter shall by Law be heard and decided; l'ubjefl neven-theless to such particular Regulations, in respect of Ireland, as from local Circumstances the Parliament of the said United Kingdom may from Time to Time deem expedient: That the Qualifications, in respect to Property, of the Members elected on the Part of Ireland to fit in the House of Commons of the United Kingdom, shall be respectively the same as are now provided by Law in the Cafes of Elections for Counties, and Cities, and Boroughs, respectively, in that Part of Great Britain called England, unless any other Provision shall hereafter be made in that Respect by Act of Parliament of the United Kingdom: That, when His Majesty, His Heirs or Successors, shall declare His, her, or their Pleasure for holding the First or any subsequent Parliament of the United Kingdom, a Proclamation shall issue, under the Great Seal of the United Kingdom, to cause the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, who are to serve in the Parliament thereof on the Part of land, to be returned in such Manner as by any Act of this present Session of the Parliament of Ireland shall be provided; and that the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, of Great Britain, shall, together with the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, so returned as aforesaid on the Part of Ireland, constitute the Two Houses of the Parliament of the United Kingdom: That if His Majesty, on or before the First Day of January One thousand Eight hundred and One, on which Day the Union is to take place, shall declare, under the Great Seal of Great Britain, that it is expedient that the Lords and Commons of the present Parliament of Great Britain should be the Members of the respective Houses of the First Parliament of the United Kingdom on the Part of Great Britain, then the said Lords and Commons of the present Parliament of Great Britain shall accordingly be the Members of the respective Houses of the First Parliament of the United Kingdom on the Part of Great Britain, and they, together with the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, so summoned and returned as above on the Part of Ireland, shall be the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, of the First Parliament of the United Kingdom; Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it be the Fifth Article of Union, That the Churches of that Part of Great Britain called England, and of Ireland, shall be united into One Church; and that whenever His Majesty shall summon a Convocation of the Clergy, the Archbishops, Bishops, Priests, and Clergy, of the several Provinces in England and Ireland, shall be respectively summoned to, and fit in, the re-Yo 1 $5'

land-, and that the Doctrine, Worstiip, Discipline, and Government, of the said United Church, shall be preferred as riow by Law established for the Church of England, and shall be deemed and taken to be a fundamental Article of the Union, and that the Doctrine,

Worship; and Discipline, and Government, of the Church of Scotland, shall likewise be preserved as now by Law, and by the Act of Union, established for the Church of Scotland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That it be the Sixth Article Of Union, That His Majesty's Subjects of Great Britain and Ireland shall, from and after the First Day of January One thousand Eight hundred and One, be entitled to the same Privileges, and be on the same Footing as to Encouragements and Bounties on the like Articles, being the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture, of either Kingdom respectively, and generally in respect of Trade and Navigation in all Ports and Places in the United Kingdom and its Dependencies; And that in all Treaties made by His Majesty, His Heirs and Successors, with any Foreign Power;

His Majesty's Subjects of Ireland shall have the same Privileges, and be on the same Footing, as His Majesty's Subjects of Great Britain: That," from the First Day of January One thousand Eight hundred and One, all Prohibitions and Bounties on the Export of Articles the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture, of either Country to the other, shall cease and determine, and that the said Articles shall thenceforth be exported from one Country to the other without Duty or Bounty on such Export: That all Articles, the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture, of either Kingdom (not herein after enumerated as subject to specific Duties) shall from thenceforth be imported into each Country from the other free from Duty, other than such countervailing Duty as shall be annexed to the several Articles contained in the Schedules No. I. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it be the Seventh Article of Union, That the Charge arising from the Payment of the Interest, and the Sinking Fund for the Reduction of the Principal, of the Debt incurred in either Kingdom before the Union, shall continue to be separately defrayed by Great Britain and Ireland respectively, except as herein after provided: That, for the Space of Twenty Years after the Union shall take Place, the Contribution of Great Britain and Ireland respectively towards the Expenditure of the United Kingdom in each Year, shall be defrayed in the Proportion of Fifteen Parts for Great Britain, and Two Parts for Ireland:That, at the Expiration of the said Twenty Years, the future Expenditure of the United Kingdom (other than the Interest and Charges of the Debt to which either Country shall be separately liable) shall be defrayed in such Proportion as the United Parliament shall deem just and reasonable, upon a

subject only to such particular Exemptions or Abatements in Ireland, and that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, as Circumstances may appear from Time to Time to demand; that, from the Period of such Declaration, it shall no longer be necessary to regulate the Contribution of the Two Countries towards the future General Expences, according to any specific Proportion, or according to any of the Rules hereinbefore prescribed: Provided nevertheless, That the Interest: or Charges which may remain on Account of any Part of the separate Debt with which either Country is chargeable, and which shall not be liquidated or consolidated proportionably as above, shall, until extinguished, continue to be defrayed by separate Taxes in each Country: That a Sum, not less than the Sum which has been granted by the Parliament of Ireland, on the Average of the lad Six Years, as Premiums for the internal Encouragement of Agriculture or Manufactures, or for the maintaining Institutions for pious and charitable Purposes, shall be applied, for the Period of Twenty Years after the Union, to such local Purposes in Ireland, in such Manner as the Parliament of the United Kingdom shall direct: That, from and after the First: Day of January One thousand Eight hundred and One, all Public Revenue arising from the Territorial Dependencies of the United Kingdom, shall be applied to the general Expenditure of the Empire, in the Proportions of the respective Contributions of the Two Countries.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it be the Eighth Article of Union, That all Laws in Force at the Time of the Union, and all the Courts of Civil and Ecclesiastical Jurisdiction within the respective-Kingdoms, shall remain as now by Law established within the same; subject only to such Alterations and Regulations from Time to Time as Circumstances may appear to the Parliament of the United Kingdom to require; provided that all Writs of Error and Appeals depending at the Time of the Union, or hereafter to be brought, and which might now be finally decided by the House of Lords of either Kingdom, shall, from and after1 the Union, be finally decided by the House of Lords of the United Kingdom; and provided that, from and after the Union, there shall remain in Ireland an Instance Court of Admiralty for the Determination of Causes Civil and Maritime only, the Appeals from Sentences of the said Court to lie to His Majesty's Delegates in His Court of Chancery in that Part of the United Kingdom called Ireland; and that all Laws at present in Force in either Kingdom, which shall be contrary to any of the Provisions which may be enacted by any Act for carrying this Resolution into Effect, be, from and after the Union, repealed.

A PETITION of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for dividing, allotting, and inclosing, the Open Common Fields, Meadows, Pastures, Commons, ami Waste Lands, within the Parish of Cook ham, in the County of Berks; and Setting forth. That, although the said Commons are Wade, they are far from being, in their present State, unprofitable to the Petitioners, and others, having Rights thereon, as they enable the Farmers to rear a great Stock of Cattle at little Expence, and to preserve, their Sheep in good Health by a Change of Palturage, and the Poor Cottagers arc thereby enabled to keep Cows, Pigs, and ^Poultry, and to supply themselves with Furze for Fuelt'and Fern for Litter, which they have been entitled to from Time immemorial, and by that Means many of them have brought up large Families with very little oc-callonal Assistance frofli the Parish; and that the Petitioners are convinced, that any Division and Inclosureof the said Commons will be productive of great Loss and Injury to the Petitioners, and other Persons interested in, or having Rights on, the said Commons; And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, or Agents, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pass into a Law,

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the said Bill be read & Second Time: And that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, or Agents, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

A Petition of the Merchants, Manufactureers, Mill Owners, and others, concerned in the Wool and Woollen Trade, in the County of Cornwall, was pretented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe with inexpressible Concern, in the Arrangement for an Union with the Siller Kingdom of Ireland, it is proposed to repeal those Laws which prohibit the Exportation of British Wool to that Kingdom, whilst on her Part file continues the protecting Duties for her Woollen Manufactures; and that the Growth of Wool in England is by no Means adequate to supply the Manufacturers with a Quantity equal to the present Demand for the Home and Foreign Markets, and therefore, if any Part of the Raw Wool is permitted to be exported, it will materially and infallibly injure the Petitioners and their Labourers; and that the Petitioners are fearful that, if British Wool be permitted to be exported to Ireland, considerable Quantities will be conveyed to Foreign Parts under the Pretext of conveying it to Ireland, and even after its Arrival there, it will be clandestinely exported agaiu, and thus afford the Foreigner the Means of rivalling the Petitioners in Foreign Markets, without benefiting the new Members of the British Empire: And therefore praying, That, in the Arrangement of the Two Kingdoms for an Union, Britain may not be deprived of that Article which has been the Foundation of its Prosperity and Happiness.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, John Soane, Esquire, an Architect, being examined, laid.

That, pursuant to several Acts of Parliament, sundry Houses, Ground, Hereditaments, and Premises, were purchased by and vested in the Petitioners, and the Edifice of the Bank was very much enlarged and extended, and the Passages leading thereto made more commodious for the Public: That, in Consequence of

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution so amended. That it be the Fifth Article of Union, That the Churches of England and Ireland, as now by Law established, be united into One Protestant Episcopal Church, to be called " The United Church of England and and

that the Doctrine, Worship, Discipline, and Government, of the said United Church, shall be, and shall remain in full Force for ever, as the same are now by Law established for the Church of England, and that the Continuance and Preservation of the said United Church, as the established Church of England and Ireland, shall be deemed and taken to be an elsential and fundamental Part of the Union; and that, in like Manner, the Doctrine, Worship, Discipline, and Government, of the Church of Scotland, shall remain and be

by Law, and Kingdoms of

preserved as the same are now established by the Acts for the Union of the Two England and Scotland.

That it be the Sixth Article of Union, That His Majesty's Subjects of Great Britain and Ireland shall, from and after the First Day of January One thousand Eight hundred and One, be entitled to the same Privileges, and be on the same Footing as to Encouragements and Bounties on the like Articles, being the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture, of either Kingdom respectivelyj and generally in respect of Trade and Navigation in all Ports and Places in the United Kingdom and its Dependencies: And that in all Treaties made by His Majesty, His Heirs and Successors, with any Foreign Power, His Majesty's Subjects of Ireland shall have the same Privileges, and be on the same Footing, as His Majesty's Subjects of Great Britain: That, from the First Day of January One thousand Eight hundred and One, all Prohibitions and Bounties on the Export of Articles the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture, of either Country to the other, shall cease and determine, and that the said Articles shall thenceforth be exported from one Country to the other without Duty or Bounty on such Export: That all Articles, the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture, of either Kingdom (not herein after enumerated as subject to specific Duties) shall from thenceforth be imported into each Country from the other free from Duty, other than such countervailing Duty as shall be annexed to the several Articles contained in the Schedules N° I. A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That an Address be presented to His Majesty, humbly begging Leave to acquaint His Majesty, that, in Conformity to His Majesty's Gracious Message, laying before us the Resolutions of the Lords and Commons of Ireland, we have proceeded to resume the Confederation of the great and important Subject of a'Legislative Union between Great Britain and Ireland: That it is with un-fpcakable Satisfaction we have observed the Conformity of the said Resolutions to those Principles which we humbly submitted to His Majesty in the last Session of Parliament, as calculated to form the Balls of such a Settlement: That, with the few Alterations and Additions which we have found it necessary so suggest, we consider these Resolutions as fit to form Articles of Union between Great Britain and and if those

Alterations and Additions shall be approved by the Two Houses of the Parliament of , we are ready to

confirm and ratify these Articles, in order that the same may be established for ever by the mutual Consent of both Parliaments.

That we offer to His Majesty our humble Congratulations upon the near Prospect of the Accomplishment of a Work, which His Majesty, as the Common Father of His People, has justly declared to be so near His Heart, concurring with His Houses of Parliament in

Ireland, on the full Conviction that, by incorporating the . Legislatures, and consolidating the Resources of the Two Kingdoms, we shall increase the Power and Stability of the British Empire, and, at the same Time, contribute in

the most effectual Manner to the Improvement of the Commerce, the Security of the Religion, and the Preservation of the Liberties, of His Majesty's Subjects in Ireland.

Mi TVxien's A Petition of Thomas Foden, of the City of Pcutton. Chymist, and Cotton Manufacturer, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer (by His Majesty's Command) acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner has, after several Years Application, and great Labour and Study, and at a very considerable Expence, discovered a Chrystaline Size and Paste, made from Mineral Substances, as a Substitute, mixed with a Proportion of Vegetable Substance, for Wheat Flour, in all Purposes of Manufacture, and for which he has obtained His Majesty's Letters Patent; and that the Petitioner has Submitted the said Discovery to the Manufacturers and Printers of the County of Lan- easter, who appointed a Committee of the principal Manufacturers of Cotton Goods to investigate the fame, and to whom the Petitioner disclosed the Ingredients of the said Chrystaline Size and Paste, in Consequence whereof the said Gentlemen prepared the Ingredients for making ' the fame, and found the like Effects produced as was

done by that prepared by the Petitioner, and in their Report the said Manufacturers and Printers declared it as their unanimous Opinion, after a most careful and at- tentive Investigation of the Properties of the said Size and Paste, that, from the Excellence, simple Process in the Preparation, and comparative Cheapness of the Articles, they will be preferred to Flour and Starch; and that the Use of the same will not only lessen the Consumption of Wheat, but will be found infinitely preferable to the common Preparation of Paste, and will be highly beneficial to the Weaver, Printer, and every other Manufacturer, concerned in the Branch; and that, in the various Processes of the Linen Manufactures of this Country, as well as in the Cotton, a very large Quantity of Wheat Flour is made use of, which will be saved by the Use of the Chrystaline Size and Paste: The Petitioner conceives also, that, if his Discovery shall be made as available to the Public as it may be, it will also prevent the very great Consumption of Wheat Flour now used in making Starch, and for other Purposes; and that the Petitioner, anxious to save the great Consumption of Wheat Flour, at all Times, in the various Manufactures before mentioned, particularly at this Period, is willing to relinquish all Right and Title to the Interest he now has in the said Discovery, on receiving such Rc-compenccand Reward for the heavy Expences he has incurred, and the Time and Labour he has bellowed, as

the House shall think just and proper: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant the Petitioner such Recompence and Reward as (b useful and important a Discovery shall appear to merit.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, it appeared by the Will of the late Lord Bigot, (which was produced to Your Committee) That upon the Death of Lord Bigot, the Diamond, mentioned in the Petition; became the Joint Property of Sir Robert Bigot, the Pe-tioner's Father, of Admiral Pigot, and of his Sifter Margaret Fisher, and, on the Death of Sir Robert Bigot± and Admiral Bigot, the said Diamond became the Joint Property of Sir George Bigot, Baronet, Margaret Fisher, and Frances Bigot, the late Admiral's Widow: Then,

Mr. Thomas Jefferys, a Jeweller, having been Thirty-six Years in the Business, being called in, informed Your Committee, That he had examined the said Diamond; and said, that he had never seen such a Diamond, uniting the Four Qualities of Weight, Size, Water, and Brilliancy, and thinks it to be well worth, and cheap; from Twenty-five to Thirty Thousand Pounds: And,

Mr. James Watson, a Jeweller, having been Forty Years in the Business, being then called in and examined, confirmed Mr. Jefferys's Evidence, as to the Value of the said Diamond, and added. That he had never seen such a fine Diamond, and that he made but little Doubt, that it cost from Twenty-five to Thirty Thousand Pounds in India, in its rough State.

Mr. Philip Gilbert, a Jeweller, who has been Sixteen Years in the Business, confirmed the above Evidence; and the said several Witnesses added, That, on Account of the immense Value of the Diamond, it was improbable to expect, that the same would or could have been purchased by any Individual.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to enable Sir George Pigot, Baronet, Margaret Fisher, and Frances Pigot, to dispose of a Diamond by Lottery;

Mr. Shaw Lefevre, according to Order, reported from Reportrefpea-the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was re- «"g Waste ferred to consider of the Report which was made from Lands the Select Committee appointed to consider of the most effectual Means of facilitating, under the Authority of Parliament, the Inclosure and Improvement of the Waste, uninclosed, and Unproductive Lands, Commons, Common Arable Fields, Common Meadows, and Common of Pasture, in this Kingdom, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, in order to promote the Cultivation and Improvement of the Waste, Unincloled, and Unproductive Lands, Commons, Common Arable Fields, Meadows, and Common of Pasture in this Kingdom, it may be expedient to adopt such Regulations as would diminish the Expence of inclosing and improving the same, under the Authority of Parliament.

Resolved;That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, in order to diminish the Expence of Bills of Inclosure, it may be expedient that Regulations should be adopted, by the Two Houses of Parliament, for the Admission of Affidavits, authenticated by the Certificate of One or more Magistrates, as sufficient Evidence of the Notices, the Consents, and the Allegations in the Preamble of such Bills, instead of the Parole Evidence now required, unless where the latter should appear at the Time to be necessary from particular Circumstances.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, for the same Purpose, it may be expedient that a General Law should be passed, comprizing all such Provisions as by Experience have been found necessary in

most

V

4o Geo. III. 7 — 8

most Bills of Inclosure; to which act such Bills in future might refer.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in order to diminish other Expences incidental to Bills of Inclosure, it may be expedient, that Provision should be made in such General Law, for taxing the Charges of the Solicitor, regulating the Conduct of the Commissioners, and preventing any unnecessary Delay in parrying such Bills into Effect.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That in the same of smalllnclosures, not exceeding Three Hundred Acres, it may be expedient to provide, that such Bills should be considered, as to the Payment of Fees, only as Single Bills; and that those for the Inclosure of smaller Tracts of Land, not exceeding One Hundred Acres, should be subject only to the Payment of Half the Fees due on a Single Bill: The Admeasurement in both Cafes to be proved in the same Manner as is proposed by the Second Resolution regarding Notices and Confers.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into further Consideration upon Monday Morning next.

Minutes of Kviilence on Petitions of the Cotton Wc tvers of Che Her, See.

James Hoi croft. Weaver, at , in Lancafiire;

Called in, and Examined.

How long have you been in the Trade?

About 14 Years.

' Can you speak of the Wages paid in 1792?

The general Wages paid for Velvcrets were about 24/. the Web, of Yards: that was the Average.

Was that the general Length?

We made more of that Length than any other: they were on the Average Yards.

What was the Average Lefigth of Pieces and Wages paid in 1793?

I cannot speak to the Wages in 1793, only in this Cafe: I got Work of Mr. Green; the Trade being then bad, he gave 16 s. for what was in general paid 24 for in 1792. I worked that Work until he had reduced it to gs.

Can you speak to that being the general Price paid by others i n the Trade?

I cannot speak as to others.

What was the Length of the Pieces, and Wages paid in 1794?

I cannot speak as to 1794 or 1795. In 1796 I worked at Sprig Muslinets; I received then 36 for about 55 Yards.

Was that the Number of Yards which that Description of Work was made of in former Years?

I cannot say. In 1797 I worked at Quiltings — 2 s. 8 d. per Yard for Sattins, and 2 3 d. I received

without Sattins.

What was the Length of Velvere ts in 1 97, and the Wages paid?

The Length was increased to 50 Yards in general, and the Wages were generally 16 the Web. In 1799 the Lengths were increased to 58 and 60 Yards, and the Wages decreased to iu. I know it by going into different Workshops.

Did you work with your own Looms; or those which were provided for you?

Sometimes, Quiltings I worked with Looms provided — Velvcrets with my own.

When Looms were provided for you, was there any Abatement made in Consequence?

When I (poke of 1 r. 6 d. per Yard, it was what was paid at the Warehouse; and 1 always received a certain Proportion, deducing 6 d. for providing the Loom and Draw-Boy who afiilts the Weaver.

What Effect had the Lengthening the Webs from Yards to 60, between 1792 and 1799, upon the Wages paid?

No more, but less Wages paid, notwithstanding the increased Lengths.

Had it any EfTecft upon the Quality of the Workman-ship?

In strong Goods it is extremely difficult to work the latter End of the Piece of the fame'Goodnels as the Firffc; add to that, it makes it harder, particularly for weak Constitutions.

Did it occasion any additional Labour to the Workmen with respect to the Drefiing?

Not with respect to Drefiing, except as to tho Length.

How much per Week, clear Gain, at the present Rate of Wages, can a good Workman earn on Velveteens and Velvcrets, Wffking 14 Hours a Day?

About 6 s. per Week clear, deducting Two Hours

for Meals.

In ascertaining the clear Gain, what Deductions do you make from the Gross Wages?

In the FirstCafe, if I receive 11 s. for weaving a Vel-veret Piece, I have to pay the Bobbin Winder for winding 18 lbs. of West, at about 1 I d. per lb.; I have to buy Candles to enable me to work the Hours, to find Flour for dressing, to find Looms, and -every Utensil, and what remains is Net Money.

In working Mullins, at the present Rate of Wages, what can you earn?

Some can get more, and some less — but, upon the Average, 1 os. per Week, clear.

How many Yards of Velveret can a good Workman manufacture in a Day?

He mull work very' close to work Six Yards, One Day with another.

Are the Wages paid by the Yard, or by the Piece?

By the Piece.

What Description of Work did you do in 1.798?

Quiltings.

Were the same Wages paid in that Year as in the preceding?

They were reduced at different Periods in that Year; but I cannot speak precisely to the Reduction.

What did you receive in 1798?

I cannot recoiled: Wages fluctuating so much, as not to charge my Memory with the precise Difference.

In the Year 1799 what Work was you employed in?

Quiltings.

What Wages did you receive in that Year?

For the same Work which I received 2 3 d. for, I

had only 1 s. 6d.

Was there, between 1792 and 1799, any Improvement in Machinery,-by which you could do the same Work in less Time?

None.

Do any Disputes happen between the Mailers and Men, respecting the Quality of the Work?

They do frequently; and likewise with respect to any Damps or Stains that may happen to the Work.

Are any Deductions made by the Mailer for these Damages?

He claims, the Right to deduct what he thinks the Amount of the Damages.

How are these Disputes settled?

It very frequently happens, that the Workmen are in such a Situation in respect to their Mailer, that they are obliged to submit to his Decision.

Does it ever happen that less Wages are paid for the Work when done than was contracted for?

It frequently happens, that the Mailer will give out a Web of a certain Length, containing perhaps Four or Five Pieces; he will agree, when you take this Web out, that you shall have a certain Price; he may, perhaps, give it you for the First Piece, and for the Remainder will abate you a certain Proportion.

What

40 Geo. III.

What Remedy have you, in those Cafes, been accustomed to resort to?

The Remedy People apply to in such Cases is to a Magistrate; but they are often in such a Situation, that they dare not have Recourse to this Method, for Fear of being turned out of Employ, which may perhaps be of great Disadvantage to them and their Families.

What creates the Neceflaty of submitting to the De-' cifion of your Matters, when Disputes happen between you and them?

A Person may be employed in working a Kind of Work, when to change to another, neither his Time or his Circumstances would, perhaps, permit; and, in some Cafes, the Manufacturers are in the Habits of lending to their Men a certain Sum of Money to purchase Uten-liis. In such a Ca;e, not having the Money to repay, and the Utensils perhaps thrown on their Hands useless, they chute rather to submit to their Decision, than to run the Ritk of their Displeasure.

When you are employed in new Work, how much Time is sometimes lott in preparing for it?

Some Sorts you may begin in One Day, some Two, and in others, perhaps, a Week, or Ten Days.

Is any Expence occasioned to the Workmen in the Purchase of Materials or Utensils for such new Work?

The Workmen generally pay the whole Expence of such Utensils.

Is it upon an Average of the whole Year that you clear 6 s. per Week?

It is upon the Average generally; and generally Utensils are considered, but not in some particular Cafes. When I say a Person can get 6 s. Week at strong Goods, I mean to make good Loss of Time, Utensils, &c. relating to the Work.

What has been the utmost Expence incurred by the Workmen, in any Inttance within your Knowledge, to begin a new Pattern?

In beginning the Sprig Muslinets, the Expence has been £. io. to the Workmen.

In making your Estimate of the clear Gain, do you

deduct what is paid for these Materials?

When I lay ioj. clear, I allude to the present Prices; and that if £. io. be expended on Utensils for new Work, at the present Prices, the £. io. mutt go

out of the Weekly Earnings.

Upon what Grounds will the Matter give a less Price for the remaining Piece than he does for the First?

If I take a Quilting Warp or Web of Five Pieces, the Matter will agree, when I take this Warp out, that 1 shall receive ij. 6 cl.per Yard; he will pay, perhaps, for the First Piece the Price agreed on; when the Second Piece is taken Home, he will abate the Wages or 3 per Yard, saying that the Markets are so bad that he cannot afford to give more.

Is this a same that happens often?

It is not common with the great Body of Matter Weavers; in particular Cafes, there are Men who will 'take these Advantages.

What Prices have been given for V verets this Year?

They are higher this Year than the last; they are 145. 6 d.for 60 Yards; but in general they are not so long.

When Pieces -are made of an extraordinary Length, are they not frequently cut into Two, and sold as such?

They very often are.

Is the Workman paid, when Pieces are of extraordinary Length, as One, or Two, Pieces?

For One Piece. w. Voe. 55.

487

Do you mean to say, that you would receive no higher ^Iv'l^c,e°5n -Wages for weaving a Piece of 66 Yards, than y ju would Petitions of for weaving a Piece of Yards, in every Respect, of the ,he Cotlon _

fame Quality r chester, &c. —

I should receive more, but that depends upon the continud. Matters; for some are in the Habits of increasing their Pieces, and paying the Workmen no more.

If a Piece of Velveret was to contain 17lbs. of Cotton to the 50 Yards, is not the Price so the Workman, for weaving and spinning, £. 1. 14.;.?

I know of no Calc where that is paid; but whether it may be paid for the superior Sort, I cannot tell.

Withdrew.

Mr. Edward Carli/le, Wholesale Haberdasher, Bow,

Cheapside,

Called in, and Examined.

Do you deal in Manchester Goods?

Yes; all Sorts of small Wares, such as Tapes,

Bobbins, &c.

Do you buy those Goods by the Piece?

By the Dozen and the Gross.

When- you order the Dozen or the Gross, are you aware of the Quantity you buy?

Not positively.

Do you considerthis as a Grievance?

Yes; for Want of a regular Standard.

In complying with the Order ybu give at stated Prices, is any Regard paid by the Manufacturer )'ou deal with, to the Quality of the Article, or to the

Lengths?

I conceive to both; because there are Three or Four different Degrees of Articles.

Would it obviate the Objection, that the Pieces flaould run of specific Length?

I think it would.

What Inconvenience arises to your Trade, if the Prices are different for the different Lengths or Qualities?

Because the Short Lengths may be sold for the same Price as the Long Lengths.

Do the Pieces which you call the " Long Lengths" run of different Lengths?

Yes, they do.

Is it the same with what you call the " Short Lengths ?"

It is.

Does the Manufacturer charge you, or do you charge your Customers, the same Price for the Short Lengths as you do for the Long ones, supposing them of equal Quality?

I have been charged so repeatedly by the Manufacturers; and I have charged so to my Customers.

Is it not universally the Cafe, that you are charged by the Manufacturer the same Prices for the Short Lengths, however they may vary?

No; I conceive he shortens the Length according to the Price that is offered. ft

Withdrew.

James Ho/cro/t,

Again called in, and Examined.

Are not Velverets made of different Qualities?

Yes; the Evidence I before gave had only Relation to common Velverets; there are made Chain-back Velverets, and also Velverets of a superior Quality, but what are paid for them I cannot tell.

Do not those who make their Pieces fongeft, generally pay kfs Wages than those who manufacture the shorter Lengths?

Yes.

Do those who manufacture the short Pieces, generally make and sell the best Quality of Goods?

Yes.

Do they pay the best Prices?

Molt generally they do.

Would the making of Pieces of thorter Lengths than they are at present made, be attended with any, and what, Advantage to the Parties concerned, or to the Manufacture?

In the First Place, the Weaver would make better Goods with more Ease, and the Public would be served with Goods of abetter Quality; and, to use the Words of a Mr: Rycroft, an eminent Manufacturer in , it would be attended with a mutual Advantage to both Parties — with respect to the Weavers, by having a more frequent Return of Money, they would be kept from buying their Provisions, &c. from Shops, and although the Manufacturers had more frequently Money to pay to the Weavers, they would have a more frequent Return of Goods for the Market.

By your being prevented from buying at Shops, do you mean to say that you at present buy at a Disadvantage?

Yes.

Are the Disputes between Masters and Men respecting the Breaches of Contract of the Masters, in paying lets Wages than they had agreed upon, of a Nature to be settled, to the Satisfaction of both Parties, by Magistrates?

No; because they, in general, -are not competent Judges of the Nature of the Dispute, with respect to Damage done to the Work, in which same it must be referred to Manufacturers, or some other Persons who undeistand it.

What renders it unintelligible to the Magistrates?

Because they in general do not understand the Manufacture.

Supposing such Disputes not cognizable before the Magistrates, but in the ordinary Courts of Justice, why not appeal to the latter?

I have already stated, that 6 s. upon some Kinds of Work, and io s.upon others, clear Money, is what the Workman can get by working One Week, so that we have not Money to go to Law with our Masters', when any Dispute ariles.

Are the great Body of Manufacturers delirous of lengthening Pieces or reducing of Wages?

I believe they are not; but that they are compelled to this Practice by those who do it.

Do you know that the Numbers are so considerable who reduce their Wages, and lengthen their Pieces, that it can have any considerable Effect upon the Manufacture in general?

i believe they are, and so great as to affect those who are better disposed.

What induced you to fix upon the Year 1792, as the Standard for regulating the Price of Weaving?

All I understood from that, was to thew to the 1 Committee the Reduction that had taken place from that Period to this.

Do not you know, that in 1792 Wages were raised beyond any former Period, and tar beyond the Average of any Number of preceding Years ? .

I believe there were far greater Wages given before 1792, than during that Year, or fmcc.

9

What occasioned that extraordinary Rife in 1792?

I know of none in 1792.

Do not you know that the Manufacturers of Sail Cloth in Warrington, and of Woollen Goods on the Borders of York/liire, and adjoining to Lancajliire, have

very much declined, in consequence of the Cotton Manufacturers extending into those Situations?

I cannot answer from my own Knowledge.

Has the Population of the Town and Neighbourhood of Bolton increased; and are you not convinced, that if the Wages had been ascertained or confirmed by Law at the extravagant Rate of 1792, or Years preceding, that the Trade of the County would have been destroyed, or removed to some other Situation?

Since I have known the Neighbourhood, which is Five Years only, the Population has decreased, owing to the Army and other Circumstances. I believe, on Account of higher Wages being given for a certain Description of Goods at Mancliester, it has taken Workmen there. I am very well convinced, that to rate Wages at any extravagant Price, must be highly injurious to the Manufacture, and endanger its total Ruin.

Do you not know that the- Wages of Labourers in Husbandry have been advanced within these few Years?

I believe they have.

Have not the Wages of Mechanics of all Descriptions, such as Carpenters, Bricklayers, &c. advanced very much, and are now uncommonly high, far beyond the Wages of 1792, and that in these Trades there is a Scarcity of Workmen?

I cannot speak to that Point.

Would not a new Regulation put the good and bad Workmen upon the same Footing?

I think it would not; because the Wages might be j-cgulated according to the Quality, or by the Number of Shoots in One Inch, which would leave the Masters at Liberty to manufacture Goods according to the Market they fold Goods to; so that if Weavers could not manufacture Goods of superior Quality, they might be employed in the inferior Quality, always paying by the Shoots in One Inch, with an Addition for the Fineness of the Reel.

Is it the Wilh of the Weavers, by any proposed Regulation, that a Manufacturer should be obliged by Law to give equal Wages to a bad Workman and a good one?

It is not.

Would it not, under such a Law, happen that, in many Cafes, the inferior Weavers would be altogether unemployed, as the Manufacturer would be precluded from employing them at a Price adequate to their Labour?

The Answer I have given to a former Question will shew that the Manufacturer will be at Liberty to manufacture what Kind of Goods he thinks proper, provided he pays according to the regulated Price; for 'Instance, if a Manufacturer willies to put 200 Shoots in One Inch, another willies to put 400, each would pay in Proportion to the Quality of the Goods he orders, and all Manufacturers would pay the same Price for the same Quality of Goods, which cannot possibly injure any Manufacturer, but be a Means of uniting them and the Workmen more together.

Can any Laws be devised more forcible for producing Justice to the Weavers, than those at present in Existence?

I believe there may, if a Clause could be inserted in a Bill to be passed into a Law respecting Arbitration;

I think it would answer the Purpose of both Manufacturers and Weavers better than any Law I know on the Subject, because each Party would then be at Liberty

to

40 Geo. III. 8° Mail. 489

to chuse each an Arbitrator, Men who understand the Nature of the Manufacture.

Does it occur to you to be preferable for any other Reason?

According to the Nature of the Clause, each Party would beat Liberty to compel the other to Justice.

Would the Expence of such a Remedy be within the Reach of the Weavers?

1 believe it would.

You have said, that when Goods are of equal Quality, the Weaver is paid in proportion to the Length; how then can you state the Difference of Length to be an Injustice to the Weaver?

In that same it cannot be an Injustice to the Weaver, any further than the Increase of Length makes it more laborious to the Workman.

Have the Houses in ' increased since you have

known it?

They have since 1796, when I first went there.

Is it the Wish of the Weavers to have any Standard Price, or not?

We wish for no particular Wages, but what may be fixed upon mutually between the Manufacturers and Workmen, or by the Quarter Sessions.

Is it not regulated at present by the Manufacturers and Workmen?

No; we wish to be regulated similar to the Silk Manufacturers.

Where did you work previous to 1796?

At Leigh and Louden.

Are the Wages higher at Bolton than at Leigh?

Yes; better Work is done at Bolton.

Do you not know that the Wages of Labourers of all Sorts vary in different Parts of the Counties of Lan-

cashire and Cheshire?

I believe they do.

Are there any Instances of a higher Price being paid for the Weaving of a Second or Third Piece than for the First, and of a higher Price being paid than was agreed upon when the Work was delivered?

I know of none, but I believe there are.

Why did you not?

When your Wages were reduced below what your Master had contracted to pay you, was any, and what, Reason given for the Reduction?

Yes; sometimes they laid it to the War, and Sometimes to the Badness of the Market.

Did you Submit to the Reduction?

Yes, generally.

Is the increasing the Length of Pieces any, and what. Disadvantage to the Workman and Work?

Yes; it is both a Disadvantage to the Men and the Work. In the First Place, a weak Man cannot make so good Cloth at the End of the Piece as he can at the Beginning; and it is often the Cafe, that the Workman wants Money before he has done those long Pieces.

Have the Wages been increased in Proportion to the increased Length of the Work?

No; they have decreased when paid for by the Piece.

We have no Remedy we could make use of, because we are in the Matter's Hands, with regard to the Account of Cotton he had in Book against us. They used to allow us an Ounce in a Pound Weight for Loss, but now only Half an Ounce, which is not a sufficient Allowance.

What Remedy did he resort to and obtain?

He took out Warp for Four Pieces; and took in the Three First without Complaint, and was regularly paid. When he took in the last Piece, they stopt the whole of his Wages for that Piece, on Pretence of the whole of the Work being spoiled. He summoned the Matter to a Justice Meeting, and the Work was produced, and the Justices could not determine it, and it was turned over to a Quarter Sessions. The Man was poor, and not being able to pursue it, he loft his Wages. Another Circumstance, which happened to myfel£ was, I took out a Warp of Fancy Muslin, of Four Pieces, at 15 d. per Yard, and before I had well begun, I was told I must have 13 \d.per Yard. I was obliged to agree, or my Utensils would have been unemployed, which cost me so much; and when I took in the First Piece, he would only pay me 1 s. per Yard, and told me, if I did not like that, I must work the Remainder plain; which would have been a Loss to me of at least 2 r. per Week.

Each Piece 24 Yards.

Two Yards.

Are not Weavers in general very delirous of undertaking Works with new Patterns?

Formerly I was desirous of it; but have experienced such Inconveniencies, that I no longer wish it.

Are not Wages always higher for Works of 4 new Pattern than old?

They are.

Does not the Increase of Wages for new Works in a great Degree, if not wholly, compensate you for the Expences in purchasing Utensils?

In some Degree; but in the last Instance above-mentioned, I mean Lappets, there was no Compensation at all.

In any Instances, is it equal to the Expence?

It is not.

Mr. Bragge reported from the Committee, to whom Report on it was referred to consider of His Majesty's most Gracious Message, which was presented to the House upon ship arnttd the nth Day of February last, by Mr. Chancellor of the ^raMoS -Exchequer, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Message, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the fame, together with an Appendix thereunto, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Report was read; and is as followeth; viz. '

Your Committee have thought it proper, in the First Place, to enquire into the Circumstances which led to the Order in Council, referred to in His Majesty's Message; and with this View proceeded to examine the several Papers presented to the House in consequence of an Address to His Majesty, and by them referred to Your Committee, containing all the Proceedings, relative to this Transaction, which have taken place under the Authority of the Lords of the Privy Council.

It appeared from these, That in pursuance of the Act passed in the last Session of Parliament, by. which His Majesty was " empowered, with the Advice of His Privy " Council, to grant Permission for the Importation of " all Goods coming from the Levant Seas without " Clean Bills of Health, without such Goods having " been opened and aired in the several Lazarets in the " Mediterranean Sea, mentioned in the Act passed in the Twenty-sixth Year of his late Majesty, subject to " such Regulations, with respect to opening and airing " such Goods previous to the landing thereof, and to c< the Performance of Quarantine by the Crews and other " Persons on board the Ships in which such Goods " should be imported, as His Majesty, by and with such " Advice, should by any Order make or direct}" and in consequence of a Memorial of the Levant Company, praying that early Measures might be taken for the above Purpose, the Lords of the Privy Council had appointed a Committee to consider and prepare such Regulations, in order that the same might be laid before His Majesty in Council for His Consideration; which Committee consisted of Four of His Majesty's Physicians in Ordinary, Four other Physicians, Two of whom were Commissioners of Sick and Hurt, and One other of whom had been formerly Physician to the Factory at

Aleppo, the Comptroller of the Navy, the Commissioners of the Customs, and Two Members of the Levant Company; and that an experienced Navy Surgeon had also been sent to reside in the Neighbourhood of

Creek, in order to examine into the Health of the Crews and other Persons on board the Ships that might arrive under such Circumstances.

Your Committee found, that of the Ships referred to in His Majesty's Message, and which were severally named The Aurora, The Mentor, and The Lark, the former arrived in Standgate Creek towards the End of the Two latter about the Middle and End of Oelobct last, all with Cargoes from Mogador, on the Coast of Barbary, and all with Foul Bills of Health. That previous to the Arrival of the last, which had been detained at Lifboni and then dismisshd without being permitted to land any Part of her Cargo, these and other Circumstances

fiances of Alarm as to the Danger of Infection from their Cargoes, which consisted principally of Hi'des and Skins in the Hair, had been communicated to some of His Majesty's Ministers; and that in consequence, not only the usual Quarantine had been strictly observed, but an Examination into all those Circumstances had been made with great Accuracy by the Quarantine Committee appointed as before dated, who in their Report of the 5th of December 1799, submitted the Result to the Lords of the Council; and therein dated it " to be their indispensable Duty to submit to the Wisdom of the " Lords of the Council, the Propriety of taking such " Measures as to their Lordships might seem fit for the " effectual Destruction of the said Ships and Cargoes."

It further appeared, That the Lords of the Council, not being satisfied with the Reasons given for making an immediate Order for the Destruction of the said Ships and the Whole of their Cargoes, referred it again to the Quarantine Committee, " to re-consider the Subject,

" and to date the special Reasons on which they " grounded their Opinion that the said Ships, and the " Whole of their Cargoes, diould be destroyed; and " whether Inch Rcalons applied to all the Articles of K the said Cargoes, or only to a Part of them." — That in Obedience to this Reference, the Quarantine Committee proceeded, in their Report of the 28th of ber, to date their special Reasons which induced them dill to adhere to the Suggedion proposed by them in their former Report; which Reasons were as follow:

* id. The violent and fatal Prevalence of the Plague " at Mogador during the Shipping the Whole or

* Part of the Cargoes of the Vessels in question.

<c 2d. The peculiar Sufceptibility of Infection, and " Liability to retain Infection, attached to the Articks forming a principal Part of the Cargoes " of those Vessels, especially the Goat Sking, which " are entire, u'ith the Hair turned inside: And " the great Difficulty, if not Impracticability, of c such Airing and Expurgation thereof, as would ' " be a sufficient Security against the Danger of " Contagion: Having regard as well to the Nature " and Form of the Article itself, as to the Circumstances of the Time and the Place when the Artides were brought into, lodged in Warehouses at, handled and packed, and carried on board " the Vessels from Mogador; in which Process the " Natives, many of whom were supposed to have " died of the Plague, appear to have been concerned. 3d. The great Proportion of these enumerated and " noxious Articles to those non-enumerated and " less susceptible, in the Cargoes of the Several " Vessels j and the Rilk of Infection which might " arise from opening the Hatchways, and from the " Communication and Intermixture necessary to " Separate and convey away the enumerated and " non-enumerated Parts of their Cargoes.

" 4th. The Non-existence, at present in this Country, of a System of Quarantine, properly digested and arranged to receive and provide for " Vessels and their Cargoes arriving in the Predi-

" cament under which these Vessels Hand. And " in this Remark the Committee do not allude " merely to the Circumstance of their having come " in without Clean Bills of Health, but to that of " the excessive Height with which the Plague " raged, and the vast Mortality which it had occasioned at the Port of Shipping and the adjacent of Places, and the consequent increased Peril of In- " section.

" 5th. That notwithstanding the continued good " Health of the Crews and Persons on board these " Vessels (with the Exception of the for-

" mer Mailer ot The La, who died at Mogador of " a Disorder llrongly lufpe<5led to be the Plague)

<! and the Time elapsed since their Departure from " Mogador, the Committee cannot but entertain

" Apprehensions of the Possibility of lurking and " dormant Infedlion being retained in Articles " thus susceptible, and unapt for the Application " of the ordinary and efficacious Methods of Purification.

6th. That in a Matter of this Moment, involving " Considerations and Circumstances of the greatest " Importance, and where an Errqr in Judgment,

" or an unadvised Exposure to Hazard, might be " pregnant with a Calamity of the raoft dreadful " Nature, the Committee thought jt their bounden " Duty to conduct themselves with the utmost " Circumfpedlion, and to be guided rather by the: " Principle of extreme Caution and Prudence, than " to be satisfied with the common, and possibly in " most Cafes justifiable. Rules of Discretion.

7th. That although the Committee were aware of " the Improvidence and Inexpedience of any Suggestion which might create Expence to the Publie, unless absolutely necessary j and reluctant at " all Events to be compelled to suggest any Measur of an expensive Tendency; yet under the " full Force of these Impressions, they could not " but be of Opinion that the Charge connected " with their Suggestion, however material, might " be overbalanced by other Considerations ilill " higher and more weighty.

And the Committee think it may not here be improper to observe, that superadded to the gcneral Evil which mull ensue, should any Accident to the Public Health unhappily result, the " Object of attracting and securing to this Country an extensive and valuable Branch of Com- " merce, which they understand is in Contemplation, by instituting an improved and enlarged " System of Quarantine in this Kingdom, might, " in the Issue of so calamitous an Event, be maj " terially counteracted and defeated.

; The Committee on this Point beg Permission further to observe, that the Measure, if adopted, " could not, according to their Judgment, lead " to the Inconvenience of furnishing Grounds for " entailing Charges of a similar Kind on the Publie, inasmuch as the Circumstances respecting " the Vessels in question are altogether special; " and as they trust such an Establishment for Quarantine will at no distant Period be framed as " will be adapted to admit and dispose of, upon a " regular safe Plan, Vessels arriving under every " Predicament, sanctioned by the Legislature.

8th. The Committee beg finally to observe, that " in the Proposition submitted, they had in View, " as they thought it behoved them to have, the " Line of Conduct which was pursued heretofore, " upon an Occasion of apprehended Danger of a " like Kind, and where it leemed to them the " Cause of Apprehension was less cogent than in the present Instance. It appears so Your Committee, That the Lords of the Council having taken the above mentioned Reasons, and the Facts on which they were founded, into their Consideration, did, by their Order of the 3d of January last, ch'-ect " That the Quarantine Committee be desired to " report their Opinion, whether any Danger to the " Health of His Majesty's Subjects would arise from " the said Ships being continued in their present Situation under the strictest Quarantine, or placed in any " other which the said Committee may think, more advitable, and not destroyed, as recommended, until " Parliament should meet, which will be on the-21st " Day of this Instant January, in order that, previously " toluch Diltruiftion, it may be submitted to the Legislature to determine, whether any Compensation " should be granted to the Owners of the Ships abovementioned, and of the Cargoes, and if it should be " thought fit to grant any Compensation, in what Manner the Amount of the same should be ascertained."

In answer to which, the Quarantine Committee, in their Report of January 4th, stated, " That they had " fully considered the Subject of the Reference, and " having also taken into Consideration the several Circumstances transmitted to the Commissioners of the " Customs by One of their Officers, relative to the " present crowded State of the Persons on board the " Ships from Mogador; the imminent Danger to be apprehended, in regard to their general Health, from " the Effluvia arising from Skins which are already becoming putrid; and the great Danger of Embezzlement of the Cargoes, which are generally understood " to be intended to be destroyed without any previous " Examination} were humbly of Opinion, that Danger " to the Health of His Majesty's Subjects would arise from these Ships being continued in their present, or " in any other. Situation under any Precautions which " can be devised; and therefore the Committee humbly " submitted, that it would be advisable to direct that " the said Ships, together with their Cargoes, be immediately destroyed."

And the Committee further submitted, " That the " Persons on board the said Ships, with the Exception " of so many only as may be necessary to assist in conducting the Vessels to the Place where they are to be " destroyed, in case such a Measure should finally be " determined upon, should be taken out of the said " Ships, and received on board a proper and convenient " vessel to be hired for that Purpose, and that they " should be subjected to the Performance of Twentyone Days Quarantine on board the said Vessel, and " at the Expiration thereof, provided they continued " free from any Appearance of Infection, that they " should be discharged from any further Restraint on " Account of Quarantine."

Your Committee find. That in consequence of this Representation, it was, by an Order in Council dated January 7th, which recited the above Representation, directed, " That the said Three Ships, with the Cargoes on " board, should be forthwith carried out to Sea, and " there funk in deep Water," according to the Special Directions therein given; " and that the Mailers, Mates, " and Mariners, should be received on board proper and convenient Vessels, to return to Standgate " and there to remain under Quarantine for Fourteen " Days — Which Order was accordingly carried into

Execution, and the several Ships and Cargoes funk, as directed, on the 18th January last.

Your Committee proceeded in the next Place to af-ccrrain, by their own Examination of Witnesses, Letters, and other Documents, all the Circumstances relating to the same referred to their Consideration} the Result of which they now submit to the House.

It appeared that The Aurora, having been engaged as a Transport Ship from London to Gibraltar, was there 4

chartered about the 3d of May 1799, in consequence of Directions lent by Mr. Baldry from Mogador about the 3d of April, on Account of himself and Messrs. Reeve and Green, Merchants in London, to take a Cargp from Mogador to that Port; that Ibe failed accordingly from Gibraltar towards the End of and arrived at Mogador on the 1 ft of June, and began taking in her Cargo on the 27th of the same Month, and having completed it on the 23th of July, failed on the next Day direct for London, and arrived at Standgate Creek on the 27th of August.

That The Mentor having also been engaged as a Transport from London to Gibraltar, was there chartered on the 23th of May 1799, in consequence of Directions from Messrs. Court and Company, Merchants at dor, dated in March, on their own Account, to take a Cargo from Mogador to Hamburgh: That Ihe failed accordingly in Company with The Aurora, and arrived with her at Mogador, where her Destination was, by Agreement between the Parties, altered from Hamburgh to London, and a new Charter Party executed, duly certified by the British Vice Consul, and Bills of Lading made out accordingly: That Ihe began loading her Qargo on the 4th of July, and completed it on the 30th, and failed on the 6th of August last, but was captured by a encli Privateer on the 20th, and retaken by a British Ship of War on the 23th, and sent into Cork, where Ihe arrived on the 30th, and was detained there under Quarantine till the nth of October, when she failed with a fresh Crew (except Three Mariners) and arrived at Standgate Creek on the 17th of that Month.

That The Lark was dispatched by her Owners, the said Mr. Baldry and Messrs. Reeve and Green, as a Transport from London to Lisbon, where Ihe arrived on the 23th of

June, and failed from thence in Ballast on the 10th of July to Mogador, where she arrived on the 13th to take in a Cargo to Lisbon and London, which Ihe accordingly began loading on the 25th of that Month, and completed on the 28th of August, and failed on the 6th of September for Lisbon, where Ihe arrived on the 18th, and landed all her Passengers, but was not permitted to unload any of her Cargo, but was. obliged to depart on the 4th of 0 Bober, and failed with Convoy for London, and arrived in Standgate Creek on the 23d of that Month.

Your Committee find that the Plague first appeared in the Neighbourhood of Fez and Mequinox early in the Year 1799, from whence it spread in all Directions towards the Coast; down which the Infection proceeded in a Southerly Direction, and readied the Town of Saphie, situated near Sixty Miles to the North of Mogador, about the Middle of June; and broke out in the latter Place at least as early as tlac Beginning of: That by the 4th of that Month Six Persons were believed to have died of it there in One Day, and shortly after Twelve or Fifteen: That its Ravages progressively increased from that Time, so that by the 27th it was thought dangerous to venture on Shore j and the European Merchants were about that Time all shut up in their Houses: That on the 6th of August the Mortality had advanced to One Hundred and Twenty per Day, and soon after to One Hundred and Fifty per Day, from whence it decreased to Forty Day on the 6th of September-, by which Time it was computed that 7,300 Persons had perillied there, leaving only about 1,300 Inhabitants alive.

It appears that each of the Cargoes of the Ships in question was in general composed of the same Commodities; viz. Goat Skins and Cow Hides in the Hair, Almonds, Gum, Salt Petrc, Pomegranate Peels, Worm-feed, and as to One of them, Olive Oil and Bees Wax } of which the Two first-mentioned Articles formed nearly Half of the whole Investment.

40 Geo. III. 8° Mail

4 99

It was admitted that these are peculiarly susceptible and tenacious of Infection; and though it appeared most probable that great Part of them had been collected at Mogadorprevious to the breaking out of the

Plague in that Town or Neighbourhood; yet even if it could have been proved that all were of that Description, there would (till have remained great Reasons for Apprehcnsion, from the Mode in which they are conveyed on board the respective Ships; for Your Committee find it to be an admitted Fact, that whatever Care may be taken in packing the Skins and Hides in the Merchants Houses, (which is generally done in Mats, which are supposed to be Id's capable of retaining and conveying Infection,) yet they are always carried by the Natives, or conducted by them, if carried on Mules and Alfes, from the Warehouses to the Sea Side, where the Duties are colluded; for which Purpose it is uiual for the Officers of Government to open an indefinite Number of the Bales at their Pleasure, and to take out and reckon the Skins and Hides, in order to ' prevent Frauds on the Revenue; and that the Whole are also conveyed by the Natives in their own Boats from the Shore to the Ship, and put on board by them.

Considering the known Negligence of the ausin general, as to the Prevention of this fatal Infection, and the Unavoidable Exposure of such an Article to the Reception of it in the Conveyance, as above defended, through the narrow Streets of a small Town, in which so many were daily dying, and carried out for Interment through it, it might seem sufficient to state this Circumstance alone as a Ground for the Precautions that have been thought necessary; for thus much unquestionably applies as well to The Aas to the Two other Ships which failed later; for it was in Proof before Your Committee, that Part of the Skins of which her Cargo was composed, were taken on board during the lait Three Weeks of her Stay, and a large Quantity even within Three Days of her failing.

But besides this. Your Committee found that these Skins are often collected from a Distance not less than 200 or 300 Miles, and therefore if all had been deposited at Mega dor, before the Plague actually appeared

there, it would be impcHible to ascertain whether they might not be infected when iirft purchased in Parts of the Country where it had raged for so long a Period; and Bill further it has been proved to Your Committee by an Eye Witness, that Skins were actually purchased from the Country after the Plague broke out at by One of the first European Merchants there, who shipped Skins on board each of the Ships, and particularly feme on Board The Aurora, within Three Days of her failing.

Whatever Circumstances of Hazard may be supposed to apply to that Ship, of course affect in a greater Degree the Two others, which took in,-and completed, their Cargoes at a later Period. With respect to The Mentor, it was in Proof before Your Committee, that a Parcel of Cow Hides, Part of her Cargo, was actually brought from Sallee, where the Plague broke out about the Middle of May, to Moya dor, while it was raging the re, and which instead of being taken into the Merchant's House to whom it was consigned, was left in the open Air near the Gate of the Towm, and from thence carried in the usual Way on board that Ship.

That with respect to The Lark, though fiie began loading her Cargo on the 25th July, yet the Prevalence of the Plague threw such Impediments in the Way of her completing it, that on the 6th August not more than a Fourth Part of what die actually brought Home was on board, and that it was not without the greatest Exertions of the Master that the Remainder could be shipped. That for this Purpose, the Ship's-Crew were employed in packing the Hides and Skins in the Merchants Houses, which had been for some Time (hut up Vol. 55.

from all Intercourse with the Natives, who nevertheless Report on were necessarily employed, as above dated, to convey. J^^iperting them, and the other Goods, from the Houses to the Ships arrived0 Ship. That Part of the Cargo was composed of Skins frmn Mogador font from Saphie, and collected in Hade, in order to make it up, from Persons in didrelfed Circumstances, wrho consequently would not be extremely cautious as to the Means of procuring the m. That with all these Exertions, it was not possible to get at all the Skins intended for the Cargo, a great Number of which were deposited in a Warehouse so near the Place where the numerous Dead were daily carried out to be buried, and which Interment, from the Hade and Negligence of those employed, was made at so small a Depth in the Earth, that the Effluvia was such as to prevent any Persons from approaching that Warehouse: That on the 24th August, the Mader of the Ship, who had been

employed with the Crew in packing the Skins, was suddenly taken ill, and in Two Days became delirious, and died on the 27th; and although it does not appear that he exhibited any peculiar Symptom of the Plague, and those who attended him in his Frenzy, and were frequently in contact with his naked Body, received no Infedtion, yet an Idea certainly prevailed at the Place, which the Circumstances of his Seizure seem in great Measure to countenance, that he actually died of that Disorder.

With this single Exception, Your Committee find that none of the Crews or Passengers in any of the Ships were affected with any Kind of illness during their Stay at Mogador, or from their Departure to the present Time.

Your Committee having thus examined into all the Circumstances attending the Transaction in question, directed their Attention, lastly, to the Allowance to be made to the Parties for the Lollessustained in consequence of the Destruction of the Ships and Cargoes, in case it should appear to the House, on the Consideration recommended by His Majesty's Message, that they are entitled to any. Your Committee beg Leave to fug-gest to the Wisdom of the House, on this Point, that there exists at present no Restriction, by positive Law, on Ships coming directly from any Place infected with the Plague to Great Britain; and particularly as to Mogador, as well as the Whole of the Coast of Barbary without the Streig/ils(not being included in the Provi-

fions above mentioned, of the 26th Geo. II. c. 18.) that it was never subject to ar.y such Restriction: That with respect to infected Places in the Levant, to which alone such Restriction, when in Force, applied; it seems to have been considered by the Legislature, that Commercial Intercourse might with Safety be permitted with them, if the Goods liable to Infection there taken on board, were opened and aired in certain Lazarets in the Mediterranean, subject to such Quarantine as His Majesty might think necessary on their Arrival here; and that although it has been thought proper by the Legilla-ture to enable His Majesty to licence the Importation of Goods coming from the Levant, without Clean Bills of Health, without having been opened and aired in such Foreign Lazarets as above mentioned; and although Ships arriving from the Port of Mogador and Western Coast of Barbary, might at any Time import Goods without such Licence, yet it has not as yet been found p radii cable to establish such Lazarets in Great Britain as might effectually prevent the Danger of landing Goods imported under such Circumstances: Your Committee however have learnt, with Satisfaction, that Arrangements for attaining that very desirable End are now in forwardness, so as to give Reason to hope, that a Measure, which has so frequently been called for by temporary Circumstances, and which received the express Sandtion of this House as long sincea^the Year 17S3 may at length be carried into Effect, lb as to prevent the Necessity of the Public again incurring an Expence

limilar to that at present in question. It appears further, that the Merchants interested in the several Cargoes thus destroyed, have been engaged in Trade with this Port and Coast for several Years part, where they have established Connections in Bufipefs, and made regular Consignments with aView to regular Returns: That the several Ships were engaged in this Trade before it could be supposed that this dreadful Distemper, which had not been known.in that Country for above Fifty Years part, would have appeared at; and that

though it is most probable, as before dated, that some Parcels of Skins may have been brought in from the Country during the Prevalence of the Plague there, yet the principal Part of the Cargoes were certainly provided before, and expected to be ready when the respective Ships should arrive.

In estimating the Compensation for Losses, Your Committee have thought it proper to follow, as nearly as Circumstances would admit, the Mode adopted in former Instances of a similar Nature, and in particular that of the Ships Bristol-AIerchant and,

destroyed by Order of his Majesty, with their Cargoes, in the Year 1721; and the Allowance for which was previously voted by this House: They found that in no same the Compensation had been carried beyond the Prime Cost Value of the Goods, including Port and other necessary Charges; and that in the one just mentioned, it had extended to the Charge of Freight, together with the extraordinary Expences of the Owners and Mailers, Seamen's Wages, and Provisions, incurred on Account of Detention from the Time of Quarantine being expired till the Destruction, together with their Apparel, Cabin Furniture, and other Necessaries; and together with the Value of the Ships.

They have been accordingly attended by the Agent for all Parties concerned, tjpth in the Ships, Freight, and Cargoes, and have been furnished with the Invoices, Bills of Lading, and Letters of Advice, regarding almost every Article of the several Cargoes; and they have examined some of the Merchants concerned, and other indifferent Witnesses, as to the Value of the several Articles; the Mode of paying the several Duties upon Exportation from Mogador; and the customary incidental Charges made by the Merchants there on their Correspondents here, all which they have found to agree with the several Invoices produced; and therefore they fee no Reason to doubt that such Invoices contain a fair Account of the Prime Cost of the respective Articles, in the Manner in which the several Shippers and Con-lignees usually conduct their Commercial Concerns, and on which they all'o calculate the Insurance to be made. Your Committee find, in all these Invoices, a Charge for Commission at a per Centage on the Value of the Goods; but they have not thought it reasonable to add this to the Allowance to be made, where they are shipped, (as is frequently the Cafe) on the Account and Rilk of the Foreign Merchant; conceiving that in such same it amounts in Truth to a Profit; but they have thought it a proper Charge when made on the signee, as (landing on the same Footing with the other Expences of Exportation, to which he is necessarily liable.

These Invoices being all calculated in Barbary Money, Your Committee have procured all the Information in their Power, as to the fair Rate of Exchange for transferring the same into Sterling Money; which they have done, with the general Acquielcence of the Parties interested, at the Rate of 40 Barbary Ounces to the Pound Sterling; but finding that the Duties collected at the Port are actually paid in Dollars, they

thought it right not to estimate them, as is done in the Invoices, in Barbary Ounces; but to ascertain the Value of the Dollar in Sterling Money; which, in this Cafe, considering the bxpence of exporting Dollars for this Purpose, together with their actual Value at the Time, they have calculated at the Rate of Five Shillings each.

The Practice of Insurance being now become so general as to render the Premium paid an almost constant Mercantile Charge, Your Committee did not conceive the Parties would be fully indemnified unless they should be reimbursed this Expence, as well as the Charges above mentioned incidental to the Shipping of the Goods. They have accordingly examined the Policies actually effected, and the Premiums finally adjusted, with the several Underwriters, and compared them with the respective Interests of the Parties insured, by which Examination they have in some Instances reduced the Allowance for Premiums below the Amount actually settled with the Underwriters.

The Ships themselves, with their Tackle and Apparel, were estimated, previously to their being funk, by an Officer of the Customs, sent down for that Purpose, but who was prevented going on board by the Appre-hension of Infedlion. And Your Committee have also examined the Persons employed by the Underwriters at Lloyd's Coffee House to ascertain the Condition of Merchant Ships, and the Book prepared under their Direction, in which all Particulars, relating to them are accurately stated. From the Result of this Companion, they have stated the Value of The Lark at the Price claimed by the Owners, which is rather below the Estimate of the Custom House Officer. The Aurora was valued by him at £.1,169, on the Presumption of its being Venetian built: But Your Committee being satisfied, not only from the Certificate of Registry, but from the Testimony of Eye Witnesses, that (he was actually British built, have adopted the Estimate formed upon that Supposition by the Persons above referred to as employed by the Underwriters, and have accordingly stated the Value at £. 2,300. That of The Aleut or they have taken from the Estimate formed at Cork, with a View' to Salvage, when carried into that Port on her Re-capture, and where a more accurate Survey could be taken than was afterwards done while under the suspicious Circumstances of Detention here; and as it is understood such Valuations are seldom made upon too large a Scale, it was thought by Your Committee safe to advance the Estimate from £. 1,141. made here, to£. 1,300.

In adjusting the Freight, Your Committee have examined the Bills of Lading of The Aurora and , and calculated it accordingly in Favour of the Owners of the latter, and the Parties who had chartered the former, conceiving it would occasion leis Embarrassment in the Arrangement (if to be allowed at all) that it should be paid in One Sum, rather than allowed to each Individual Consignee of Goods, to be by him afterwards paid to the same Persons. On The Mentor they have estimated only the Sum stipulated by the Charter Party, having received no Claim for the specific Freight reserved on the Bills of Lading, and the principal Part of the Cargo being shipped by the Merchants themselves who chartered the Ship; from whole Consignments, on their owm Account, they have deducted Two Items, agreed to be paid by them to the Owners of the Ship; the one for Demurrage at Alogador ,the other for cancelling a Policy of Insurance on the first intended Voyage to Hamburgh; which not being an actual Charge on the specific Cafgo, has not been taken into Account as an allowable Charge. Conceiving the several Contrafts to be virtually difiblved by the Act of the Crown in detaining the Ships beyond the usual Time of Quarantine, and which ended in their total Destruction, for which a Compensation is estimated, Your Committee have not calculated the Allowance on that Account upon the Footing of Demurrage, as stipulated in the Charter Parties, but have proceeded upon the Principle of the Precedent above referred to, and have estimated the necessary Expences, in Wages of the Crew and Provisions, from the Expiration of the ordinary Quarantine to the Time when the Crew were ultimately released after the Ships were funk.
