Copy of a Letter from Lord Grenville to Mr» Hammond; dated Downing , 24,

1800.

Sir, Downing Street, Sept. 24, 1800.

M. Otto having been empowered by the French Government to negotiate a Convention for an Armistice between this Country and France, with a View to Negotiations for General Peace; and having expressed an earned; Desire to enter into verbal Explanations on this Subject with some Person properly authorized on His Majesty's Partj the King, willing to omit nothing which can contribute to the great Work of restoring solid and permanent Tranquillity to Europe, has been pleased to make Choice of you for the Purpose of meeting M. Otto, and of receiving from him such verbal Communications as he may wish to make in Addition to what has already passed in Writing respecting the different Projets proposed on either-Side for a Naval Armistice.

This Letter will point to you the Reasons which induce His Majesty to consider M. Otto's Second Projet as unsatisfa&ory in all the material Points in which it differs from the Counter Projet prepared here by His Majesty's Command.

You will state to M. Otto His Majesty's Decision in this Respect, and you will enter without Reserve into the Discussion of the Grounds on which it rests. His Majesty has no other Object in View in this Transaction than to contribute to the Restoration of General Peace. He is not unwilling for this Purpose to sacrifice some present Advantage, in the Opinion that by so doing He consults the permanent Interests of His People; but He can neither consent, at the Opening of a Negotiation for Peace, to place Himself in a Condition of Inferiority to His Enemies, such as the Result of the War in which He is engaged by no Means warrants; nor does He think that the Object of Peace itself would be promoted or accelerated by rendering the intermediate Situation of His Enemies, under Colour of an Armistice, such as they might be desirous to prolong, rather than to ter- minate it by any admissible Conditions of Peace.

His Majesty fees, in the last Projet of the French Government, little Prpgress towards an Accommodation} it is indeed Hated in M. Otto's Letter to me of the 2fft Instant, that satisfactory Explanations are there given on the Two most important Points which had been in lifted on by His Majesty.

The Admission of His Majesty's Allies to partake in the same Terms of Armistice in which France claims to 5

include her Allies, is indeed not only an important, but an indispensable Condition of any such Agreement; but there can be no Ground for representing this equal and necessary Arrangement as a Concession on the Part of France, rather than on the Part of His Majesty. And with respect to the other Point stated by M. Otto (that which relates to the French Ships of War) the Offer of France still falls very short both of the King's Demand, and of what would be necessary even to assimilate the Naval Armistice to that of the Continent. The Article in its present Shape is therefore so far from containing any Facility which could soften or remove the other Obstacles in the Way of an amicable Conclusion of this Business, that it must still be regarded in Justice as an unequal and inadmissible Claim on the Part of the King's Enemies.

On other Points of no less Importance, the new Projet adheres to the former Demand, and even in one Instance brings forward a fresh Pretention which had not before been stated.

In examining in Detail the several Articles of the proposed Convention, some verbal Differences between the English Counter Projet and the Second French Projet, are not intended to be here adverted to.

If the more important Points of the Negotiation were satisfactorily adjusted, it would be necessary to make some Remarks on these, and possibly also to propose, for the Sake of Precision, a few verbal Alterations or Additions to the original Articles: But none of these appear likely in that same to create any lerious Difficulty.

It might be sufficient to include under this Keferve the Two Variations made in the Preamble of the Convention.

But it may perhaps be more proper for you to state at this Time the following Observations respecting them; viz.

«. That tire Mention of the respective Allies, in the Form in which those Words are introduced into the French Preamble, seems to imply of Necessity, not only that the Negotiations shall (as is the King's Intention) be carried on with a View to a General Peace alone, so as to include in the final Adjustrnent all the Allies on both Sides, but also that those Allies should immediately be called upon to take Part by their Ministers in the proposed Negotiations: a Question which His Ma- % jesty conceives may more conveniently be referred to future Discussion, instead of being prejudged by the Terms of any separate Agreement for an Armistice between Great Britain and France.

2. The Expressions used in the French Projet respecting the Continental Armistice, appear unbecoming towards the King's Allies, and cannot therefore be agreed to by His Majesty.

3. The Word " Equivalent," as there inserted, seems to assume, as the Basis of the Naval Armistice, that Principle of full Compensation to which the King has already refused His Consent.

It should in like Manner be mentioned by you, that, in the First Article, the Omission of the Words " Forces " of" seems to imply a more complete Suspension of the State of War between the Two Powers, than accords with the Nature of an Armistice, or is confident with the Conditions (particularly those respecting the Transport of Naval and Military Stores) on which His Majesty judges it necessary for him to insist.

In the remaining Part of this Article very material Changes are made in the Conditions offered by His Majesty. These are,

1. The extending the Term of Notice for the Deflation of the Armistice, from Fourteen Days to OncMonth.

2iThe requiring that this Notice of One Month should in all Cases be given only in consequence of Orders from the respective Governments, and by the Commanding Officer of one Country to the Commanding Officer of the other, in the different Parts of the World respectively.

3. The

4i Geo. III.

13° Novem.

819

3. The Total Omission of the Clause by which the Continuance of the Naval Armistice was made to depend on that of the Continent.

It is probable that tire Two first of these Alterations arc principally prqposed in the same View which led to the Omission of this last Clause; and the Effect of the Whole would be, that if the Armistice with shoukl at any Period be terminated by France, His Majesty would still for some considerable Time be restrained from assisting His Ally.

The bare Statement of such a Condition is sufficient to shew that it never can be admitted by His Majesty, who is bound by the Spirit of His Engagements to assist Mis Ally immediately on the Renewal of Hostilities; and to whom no other Inducement has or could be offered for acceding to a Naval Armistice, except that of preventing; the Renewal of Hostilities on the Continent.

The last Clause in the EnglijArticle mull therefore be absolutely infilled on, and no Variation can be ad- mitted in the other Parts of it which shall be inconsistent with the Object of that Stipulation.

The Term of Fourteen Days is in fact longer than that which is provided in either of the Two Conventions of Armistice in Italy and Germans, and appears fully sufficient for all the Purposes which such a Provision is fairly intended to answer; and as His Majesty enters into any Stipulation for Naval Armistice in the foie Hope of a speedy Conclusion of the intended Negotiations, He does not think proper to bind Himself for so long a Period as a Month, should He have the Mortification of finding that His Enemies refuse to adopt those Principles of Negotiation on which alone He judges that permanent Tranquility can be restored to Europe.

The French Government has in all its Communications expressed the same Hope and Delire for the speedy Conclusion of Peace, and has even professed an Anxiety to render this Object more peculiarly interesting to His Majesty. There can therefore be no Reason to wfilh on either Side that the'Perm of Notice should be prolonged so much beyond the Necessity of the Cafe.

The Third Article of the Counter Projet was drawn with a Reference to the corresponding Articles in the Preliminaries of Peace in 1763 and 1783, from which it differs only by the more explicit Statement of that which is understood to have been the established Pra<ftice of the Courts of Admiralty on both Sides, with respect to such Ships of War as should have made any Prizes after having actually received Notice of the Cessation of Hostilities.

The Addition to this Article proposed in the French Projet is objectionable;

First, Because thereTeems to be no Necessity forex-plaining the general Effect of a Stipulation which has in the Practice of the Two last Negotiations for Peace been found sufficiently distinct, and has fully answered the Purpose intended by it.

Secondly, Because the Explanation there given is not a just Conclusion from the Premises. It is indeed true, that by the Effect of this Article Ships, clearing out directly from Great Britain or France might immediately after the Exchange of the Ratifications fail in full.Security, because they might carry out with them Notice of the Armistice; but the same Thing would not be true of Ships in other Parts of the World, as these (under the express Terms of this Article) could not be entitled to Restitution if captured, unless Proof were given that actual Notice of the Armistice had been received by their Captors, or unless the Period assigned by this Article for the Part of the World where the Capture took - place, had expired before the actual Capture.

Thirdly, the Expression of navigating fjeely as before the War, might be construed to extend to the Admission of the Ships of one Country into the Ports of the other respectively; to which, for obvious Reasons, the King would not think proper to agree. And these Words are

Vo L. 55.

besides inconsistent both with the Stipulations on which His Majesty thinks it necessary to infill; respecting the Transport of Troops and of Naval and Military Stores, and even with those which France proposes as to the blockaded Places.

The Fourth Article of the French Projet still maintains the Contradiction of professing to afiimilate the blockaded Places to those of Germany, and of applying to them at the same Time, Conditions which are the very Reverse of those - adopted in the German Armistice.

The Manner in which that Armistice is spoken of in this Article, affords another Instance of Expressions unne-ceffarily and improperly offensive to the King's Allies.

There seems no Reason for altering this Paragraph of the Counter Projet, which is perfectly distinct, and conveys no Implication injurious to either Party.

The King cannot agree that 10,000 Rations per Diem shall be assumed as the Consumption of Malta. If the Fact be so, it will appear to the Commissaries who will be named for that Purpose, in Conformity to those Stipulations of the German Armistice to which France professes the Intention of aflimilating this Article.

But a still more material Objection arises to the Proposal respecting Egypt.

If the Situation of the French Army in that Country were to become Matter of Discussion between the Two Governments, His Majesty and His Allies have a Right, on every Principle of good Faith, as practised between civilized Nations, to require that the French should evacuate Egypt, on the Terms stipulated in the Convention o I El Ari/h-, those Stipulationshaving been ratified both by the Turkish Government and by the French Commanding Officer; and His Majesty having also in-strudled His Admiral commanding in those Seas to accede to them as soon as they were known here. This Demand would be made with the more Reason, because even subsequent to the Re-commencement of Hostilities in Egypt (under Circumstances to which His Majesty forbears to advert) an Official Engagement was entered into by General Kleber in his Letter to the Kaimakan, dated the 10th April 1800, by which that General, then commanding in Chief the French Army in Egypt, and consequently possessing full Powers to bind his Government in this llefpedt, formally undertook that the Convention of El Arish should be executed so soon as the King's Acquiescence in it should be notified to Him.

But when, instead of performing this Engagement, the French Government, under a Pretence of aflimilating Egypt to the blockaded Places of Germany, requires that Six Frigates shall carry thither, without Molestation or Search, and even under the open Protection of a British Officer, whatever Articles the French Garrisons there may be most in need of, it is natural to alk by what Article in the German Armistice Ulm or Ingoljladt are to receive in covered Waggons as many Troops, as much Provisions, and as great a Quantity of every Species of Arms, Ammunition, and Stores, as might be conveyed to Egypt in Six French Frigates ? And this Comparison is still more striking, when it is considered that by the German Armistice the blockaded Places are expressly restrained from receiving, during the Armistice, any Thing which can supply additional Means of Defence: And on the other Hand, that the Proposals for the Evacuation of Egypt originated on the Part of the French themselves, who now desire to avail themselves of the Benefit of an Armistice to strengthen that very Position which by an Agreement made in consequence of their own Request, they have actually engaged to abandon.

This Part of the French Article is therefore wholly inadmissible. It contains a Pretension unjust in itself, injurious to His Majesty's Interest, and repugnant both to the general Principle of the Negotiation, and to that which is specified in the very Beginning of the Article itself: And it implies a Breach of Faith on His Majesty S'

Part towards an Ally to whom He is bound by a solemn Treaty.

Besides all these Considerations, His Majesty has no Power to re ft rain, by such an Engagement as is here propos'd, the Ships of The Ottoman Porte from refilling the Admission of this Supply into Egypt, unlel's His Ally had acceded to the Armistice, which if it be concluded on such Terms as these, there can be no Reason toexpedl.

The Manner in which this particular Subject of Egypt is spoken of, both in the Projet and in M. Otto's Note of the 16th Instant, makes it necessary that you should distinctly declare that the Offer which was contained in the Counter Projet goes in this Respefl to the very utmost Extent that His Majesty's Regard for the Interests of His Subjects can admit of And His Majesty is confident that no Want of Conciliation can justly be imputed to Him, on Account of His having at once brought forward explicitly and without Rel'erve the Whole of those Concessions which it appeared possible for Him to make.

This Observation applies equally to the remaining Articles of the Projet.

In the Fifth Article His Majesty finds Himself obliged to infill that the Freedom of Navigation there stipulated for on the Part of His Enemies, shall not be extended to the Transport of Troops or of Naval and Military Stores. The Justice of this Exception and its Nccellity are too obvious to require any further Explanations in Addition to those contained in the Official Notes; and it follows as a Consequence of this Principle, as well as from the Nature of the Subject itself, that the Restriction as to the failing of Ships of War would be wholly illusory, were it, as now proposed, confined to Ships of the Line only.

It would indeed, neither be indifferent in Practice nor just in Principle, that France should be enabled during the Armistice to change the Stations of all her Frigates; but when it is considered how much it is the Usage of the French Marine to employ those Vessels for the Transport of Troops and Military Stores, the Two Parts of this Article become so blended with each other that they cannot be separated; and His Majesty cannot depart from the latter without equally abandoning the former.

The Naval Supply of the Articles which are here in question, is indeed Hated in one of M. Otto's Notes to be a Point of small Moment to France. If it be so, she can with less Reason insist on a Point which can in this same only be infilled on with a View to affect those general Principles which are connected with all the most important Maritime Interests of Great Britain.

The Sixth Article contains a new Demand on the Part of France, superadded to all the Pretensions advanced in her First Projet. It rests on no just or equitable Principle; for while France would reilrain His Majesty from strengthening by the Addition of more Troops the Forces of His Allies in , fire reserves the Power of augmenting her own Armies there, or of assisting her Allies ell'ewhere, precisely as it may suit her future Plans of Operations.

The French Government now possesses, no

Means to prevent the Transport of His Majesty's Troops by Sea; and it is not reasonable that it should acquire the Right of doing so by the Terms of an Armistice which conveys to His Majesty no fresh Means of impeding the future Operations of His Enemies beyond those which are already in His Power, but which even concedes to them considerable Advantages of which they are not now in Possession.

It remains only to speak of the Alterations made in that Article which regards the Allies on both Sides.

His Majesty's Objections to the Form proposed on the Part of France for this Article were detailed in my Answer to the First Projet.

If France considers the Allies in the Light of inde-

pendent Powers, and is in the future Negotiations to treat on that Footing respecting her own Interests and theirs, it is necessary that this Principle should equally be adhered to in the Preliminary Arrangements which precede the Negotiation. It has not appeared to His Majesty by the Communication of any regular oi Official Act, that the French Government has any Authority to treat in this Respect for Spain or Holland. His Majesty, on His Side, has received no such Authority from His Allies; and it would be inconfiilent with good Faith were He, without such Authority, to engage in their Name for an Armistice with France in any other Form than that which is usual in such Cases; namely, that they shall be at Liberty to accede to the Convention if they think fit. In that Form His Majesty is ready to admit the Article as with Respect to the Allies of France, and in that Form only can He agree to

include His own Allies in this Engagement.

If the Article were concluded in the Terms now proposed by France, His Majesty would be bound by the Obligations of good Faith to observe the Armistice towards Spain and Holland, while on the other Hand he could have no reciprocal Claim on those Powers, grounded either in Justice or in the Law or Pra<slice of Nations. Nor could he require the Restitution even of a Angle Merchant Vessel captured by a Spanish Or Dutch Ship of War.

Those Powers, if regarded by France as Independent, cannot be bound by her Act; and must be admitted as Contracting Parties acceding by a regular Diplomatic TransaClion to the Terms of the Armistice, before they can be considered as under any Obligation to fulfil those Terms.

These Considerations are indeed so obvious, that it is not easy to imagine in what View the French Government has proposed to alter the Article from the Form in which His Majesty had offered to consent to it.

I have now only to add, that should the Armistice be concluded, His Majesty would think it necessary, for the Purpose of accelerating the Negotiation (an Object of which the French Government has declared itself to be also very desirous) to limit a Period for its Continuance beyond which it would not be His Majesty's Intention, nor would it be confident with the essential Interests of His Dominions to extend it.

The Power of doing this will be reserved to either Party by the Terms of the Convention. Nor does this Power result only from the Articles as here proposed: It is equally reserved to both Parties by the Effect of the present French Projet; and there is, therefore, no Ne-ceflity for specifying in the Convention itself either His Majesty's Intention in this Resp^A, or, still less, the precise Period of such Limitation.

But it may appear on I lis Majesty's Part more consistent with that Openness which His Majesty is desirous to observe in this whole Transiuftion, that you should express this Intention to M. Otto in this Stage of the Business, reserving to a subsequent Period the formal Notification to be duly made in His Majesty's Name, agreeably to the Terms of the Convention.

You are at Liberty to communicate to M. Otto in the Course of your Discussions the Whole or any Part of this Letter, and to allow him to take either a Copy or such Extracts from it as he may with.

(Signed) Grenville.

Mr. Hammond.

Having suggested to M. Otto whether it might not tend to facilitate the Difcufllon, that we should read over the Counter Projet transmitted by your Lordship to him on the 7th of this Month, and the Projet delivered by him on the 21st in Answer to it; and that I should state to him, from the Instructions which I had received from your Lordship, the Objections on the Part of His Majesty's Government to the several Articles of that Projet; and M, Otto having acquiesced in this Suggestion, we pursued regularly this Course of proceeding,

As it does not appear necessary that I should enter into any Detail of the Conversation which took place between us on those Parts of the Projet which M. Otto conceived that the French Government would relinquish, it will be sufficient for me to observe on this Part of the Subject,

ill, That M. Otto conceived that the French Government would, in forming a regular Convention for an Armistice, have no Objection to adopting the Preamble in the Counter Projet instead of that which was pro-poled in the French Projet.

Before I conclude this Letter, I cannot avoid mentioning, that in the Course of our Conversation, M. Otto threw out the moll pointed Assertions of the Determination of France, in the Event of the Naval Armistice not being concluded, to purlue the Course of her ViClories in Germany, and in Italy, and of the Facilities that the Conquell of Naples and Sicily (Events which he regarded as speedy and inevitable) would afford to the French Government of obtaining by Force those Objects relative to Egypt and Malta, which it had expected to acquire through the Naval Armistice. Of thele Assertions, though frequently repeated, I judged it proper to take no Notice, but to re-call his Attention to the Subject immediately under Discussion.

I have the Honour to be, &c.

Geo. Hammond.

The Right hon. Lord Grenville.

Upon the Continent, the French and Austrian Armies reciprocally enjoy the same Liberty of taking, within the Line of Demarcation, those Positions which appear moil advantageous to them: By the Maritime Armistice, on the contrary, England preserves alone the Right of disposing of her Squadrons, whilst the French Ships of the Line remain in their Ports, and cannot enter into any hostile Combination against Great Britain

3. The Sixth Article of the new Projpt, respecting the English Troops which may be allowed to land in Italy, has been considered as a new Pretehfion on the Part of France, since file had made no Mention of it in her first Projet; but this Pretehfion (if it cati be called so) is only the natural Consequence of a Concession alike new, made by France, in offering to include in the Armistice the Allies of Great Britain. It would indeed be impossible to allow the King of Naples to enjoy Advantages from this Truce, and to leave him also the Power of re-inforcing and of preparing fresh Means of Attack against the Republic.

Citizen Otto confines Iumself to these Observations; which hp. deems of most Importance. Other Objections which have been made, and which in great Measure relate to the Form of drawing up the proposed Convention, might be easily obviated.

I have received the Letter which you did me the Honour to address to me this Morning, requesting that I would acquaint you in Writing with the Substance of the Communication which 1 have been directed to make to you; the Importance of the Object to which it relates rendering you apprehensive left you should not completely have seized the Meaning of the Communication;

The last Notes which were exchanged, and several important Events, which have completely changed the Balls upon which the proposed Armistice was to have been established, having put an End to the Negotiation on foot, I had the Honour to inform you, that notwith-ftinding the Circumstances which are opposed to the Conclusion of & Maritime Truce, the First Consul is invariably disposed to receive any Overtures relative to a separate Negotiation between France and Great Britain, and that the Mode of such Overture entirely depends upon the Option of His Majesty: That when the King shall think proper to fend, for that Purpose, a Plenipotentiary to Paris, I am authorized not only to consent to it, but to deliver to him the necessary Passport. That if,'on the contrary, His Majesty should prefer that the preliminary Negotiations should be begun at London, special Powers will be sent to me for that Purpose. I have the Honour, &c.

(Signed) Otto.

Sir, Downin 9, 1800.

I have the Honour to acknowledge the Receipt of your Letter of Yesterday's Date; and I am directed in return to acquaint you.

That His Majesty's Government entirely agrees in the Opinion there expressed, that all further Discussion of the Terms of a Naval Armistice would be superflu-ous, as the only Object which it was proposed to His Majesty to secure by such' an Arrangement has in the mean Time been made the Ground of separate Sacrifices required from His Ally.

With respect to the Proposal of opening Negotiations for a separate Peace, His Majesty, retaining always the sincere Desire which He has uniformly expressed so the Restoration of General Tranquility in Europe, must at the same Time renew his former Declarations of an invariable Determination to execute with Punctuality and good Faith His Engagements with His Allies; and must therefore steadily decline to enter into any M afures tending to separate His Interests from those of the Powers who shall continue to make Common Cause with Him in the Prosecution of the War. The Emperor has ordered me, Sir, to convey to the r irft Consul, through your Channel, the Invitation for the immediate Meeting of the respective Plenipotentiaries, who with good Faith and Zeal are occupied in concerting, with as little Delay as possible, the Means of re-establishing General Tranquility, after which suffering Europe, has long sighed in vain. His Majesty flatters himself, that through that Measure his pacific Wilhes will be speedily accomplished with the more Certainty because the King of Great Britain, his Ally, has just caUfed it to be declared to him that He is ready, on His Part, to concur in the same Negotiations, as it appears jby the enclosed Copy of the Official Note delivered here by Lord Minto, His Britannic Majesty's Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary. It only remains therefore to agree upon the Place at which the Plenipotentiaries shall meet, which will doubtless be easily let-tied. In order to facilitate the Intercourse of the Plenipotentiaries with their respective Governments, his Majesty thinks that it would be adviseable to give the Preference to some Place nearly central, such as Luneville,&c. or some other; with respect to which, in order to save Time, the French Government might come to an Understanding directly with the British Government. Translation of a Letter from General Kleber to his Paper relat-Excellency the Cairn akarnof The

dated Cairo, 20 Germinal, 8th Year, lOth April, France, — -1800. *

General Kleber, Commander in Chief of the French Army in Egypt, to his Excellency the Caimakam of The Sublime Porte, Illustrious amongst the Great, the Enlightened, and the Wife; May God grant to him a long Life full of Glory and of Happiness!

Health and Friendship.

Your Excellency has, without Doubt, been informed of the Progress and Result of the Negotiations which I had concluded with his Highness the Supreme Vizir Toujfef Pacha; and according to the Assurances to that Effect, which I have received from Persons of Distinction of your Nation, I have reason to think, that the Treaty of El Arijhhas obtained the Approbation of his Majesty the Emperor Selim the Second.

Several Articles of this Treaty had already been executed, and the French Army in particular was faithfully fulfilling its Engagements.

I was upon the Point of evacuating Cairo, when I received from Lord Keith, Commander in Chief of the English Fleet in the Mediterranean, a Letter, which excited the Surprize, and above all, the Indignation of all the French. I herewith annex a Copy of it. This Paper, which evinces the most perfect Ignorance of my Situation, and the Neglect of every Thing due to Allies, rendered illusory not only the Convention of El Arish, but also of every Kind of Treaty which I

might thenceforward conclude with The Sublime.

With regard to the injurious Conditions contained in that Letter, your Excellency will readily perceive, that the French Army in Fgypt can never be reduced to subscribe to them.

I had communicated these Observations to the Grand Vizir, and I proposed to him to postpone the Evacuation of Cairo until this unexpected Difficulty should be removed. I could not demand a more moderate Pledge, of the Execution of our Conventions; his Excellency refused to consent to this Proposal, and chose rather to expose to the Fate of a Battle, the Possession of a Country which was absolutely allured to him. This Battle took place on the 29th of VentoJe\ and Heaven protecting the Justice of my Cause, conferred Victory on me. Nevertheless, the sincere Desire which I have always had to rc-establish the Ties of Friendship and of Interest, which, during so many Centuries, have united the Two Nations, is not altered by that Event. The Sublime Porte mil still find me disposed to deliver up to him the Possession of Egypt upon the Conditions stipulated at El Arish, with the Exception of some Modifications which the existing Circumstances have rendered necessary. Thus all Motive for a fresh Effusion of Blood would be obviated, and a regular Negotiation (the Effect bf which would no longer be prevented by unforefeeti Orders) would restore to the Ottoman Empire those Provinces of which it would be in vain to attempt to deprive us by Force of Arms. If your Excellency shares these Sentiments of Peace and Concord, you will communicate them to his Majesty the Emperor the Second, and without Doubt, you will obtain Orders to resume, without Delay, those Conferences which would conduct us to the Object which we are equally desirous of attaining. I beg your Excellency to believe in the high Consideration I entertain for you.

(L. S.) (Signed) Kleber.

A Petition of the Ministers, Churchwardens, Over-seers of the Poor, and other - Inhabitant Householders of the Parishes of Saint James and Saint John, Clerken-ivcll, in the County of Middlesex, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the great Anxiety which the Petitioners have felt from the Pressure of the Times, and the Scarcity and unprecedented Price of all the Necessaries of Life, the consequent Distress of the Poor, and Diflatisfaction of all'Ranks of Society, has been considerably diminished by His Majesty's paternal Care, in summoning the House to which the Petitioners may address their Grievances, and apply with Confidence for an Alleviation of them; and that the Petitioners, at so eventful a Period, conceive themselves to be particularly called upon by Public Duty, to express their Sentiments on the Subject under Consideration in the Language of Sincerity and Truth; and that therefore the Petitioners humbly presume, in the Exercise-of that Duty, to Hate the Causes which they believe occasion or contribute to the general Calamity; and, first, they beg leave to declare it is their Opinion, that the principal Cause is attributable to the Effect and Operation of the War in which the Country has been so long engaged, because the great Waste and Spoil it has occasioned have considerably increased the Consumption of Provision, and the heavy Burthens which have from Time to Time been imposed upon the Community to support and carry it on, have so reduced the Circumstances of the middling Classes, as to prevent such of them as are engaged in Trade from making Purchases of the Commodities in which they deal in the accustomed Manner, and that consequently their Inability has given an Opportunity to the more wealthy, with whom they can no longer hold a Competition, to ingross' all Sorts of Provision, as well as other Commodities, and (pur-suing their Avarice) to fell what they so ingross at their own Prices to those very Persons who heretofore were their Competitors, as well as to the immediate Retailers: For, by getting in their particular Districts or Situations any specific Commodity within their Power, they can necessarily increase the Price by withholding the Commodity until the Want of it is so much felt that it must be supplied upon their own Terms; nor is this Evil the word, for, by the same Means, the Ingrosser has the Power of imposing upon the Consumer Articles . of the most inferior and unwholesome Quality (which a more general Distribution of the Commodity would prevent) and thereby adding to the Distress which, to a great Number of Persons, had before been almost infup-portable; and that the Petitioners are of Opinion, that the secondary Causes of this Public Grievance, which arise out of, and are occasioned by, the former, are Monopolizing, Ingrofiing, Forestalling, and Regrating, for as the natural Effects of War must so far operate on the Transactions of Life, by diverting or obstructing the usual Channels of Trade and Commerce as to occasion partial Opulence, those in the middle Stations must be reduced in their Circumstances, and be thereby sub-' jedted to such Terms as the Opulent may chuse to dictate, and ultimately to come united to the lower Orders in one Class of common Poverty; and that the same original Cause, the Petitioners conceive, may have greatly contributed to the Consolidation of Farms, and that this has increased the Evil appears to be manifest, for when the Lands were in the Hands of a greater Number of Farmers, who had not the Power of withholding their Produce as the large Farmers now have, the Markets were more regularly supplied, not only with Cattle and Com, but with Poultry, Eggs, and Vegetables, which served to supply a greater Quantity, and thereby to keep down the Prices of those Articles; and that the Petitioners being resident in a manufacturing Neighbourhood, abounding with Artificers, and the middling and labouring Classes of the Community, have an Opportunity of correctly observing the distressing Effect of the Causes they have deplored, and beg leave humbly to represent that, in their Opinion, unless some effectual Remedy be speedily applied, through the Wisdom and Interference of the House, a great Majority of the Persons comprized in those Classes must certainly be reduced to Beggary and Ruin, considering that their Means are at present in no Way adequate to their Support; and that such of the Petitioners, as are not immediately included in this Description of Persons, will, besides the other Burthens they sustain, be soon materially affected, in consequence of the great additional Assessments which must inevitably be imposed on them, for the Support of the already very numerous and alarming Increase of Poor; and that, for the' Preservation of Order, and the Support of the Government and Constitution of their Country, many of the Petitioners have incurred considerable Expence, and made great Sacrifices, by (landing forward as Volunteers in a Military Association, formed in these Parities, and that they will continue to use their Endeavours for preventing all Disorders and Commotions, by which the Distresses so heavily felt would only be increased. But though the Poor in their Neighbourhood have hitherto conducted themselves with the most exemplary Patience, under the Privations and Sufferings they have long endured, the Petitioners most ardently hope that an immediate Alleviation may be administered, to preclude the Effects of

A Motion was made, and the Question was proposed, That there be laid before this House, an Account of the Total Produce of the Tax upon Income, for the Year ending 4th April 1801, as for as the some can be made up and edimated; distinguishing the Amount of the Assessments made by the Commercial Commissioners.

Mr. Abbot reported from the Select Committee, appointed to enquire what Public General Laws have expired within Twelve Months preceding the Commencement of the present Session of Parliament; and also, what Laws are about to expire within Twelve Months subsequent to the Commencement of the present Session, or in the Course of the next Session, or at the End thereof; and to report the some, front Time to Time, to the House, with their Opinion which of them

are fit to be revived, continued, or made perpetual; and to whom the Report which, upon the 12th Day of May, 1796, was made from the Committee who were appointed to inspect and consider all the Temporary Laws of a Public. Nature expired or expiring, was referred; and who were inftracted to enquire and report to the House what Temporary Laws erf a Public or (general Nature which have been made by the Parliaments of England or Great Britain since the Commencement of the Reign of King William the Third, and prior to the present Session of Parliament, are now in forces — distinguishing the Matter of each Statute — its Date — Title — and Period of Continuance; together with their Observations thereon; That the Committee had made a Progress in the Matters to them referred, and had directed him to make several Reports to the House; and he read the Reports in his Place; and afterwards delivered them in at the Cleric's Table: Where the same were read; and arc as followeth; viz.

Your Committee have, pursuant to the Orders of the House, made a Progress in the Matters to them referred, and agreed upon the following Report:

Your Committee conceive, that the Relult of their Enquiries, upon the several Points which they were directed to examine, will be laid before the House in the moil convenient Order, by reporting — First, A Statement of all the Temporary Laws now in Force, which have been enacted from the Commencement of the Reign of King William the Third, to the Commencement of the present Session of Parliament: And Secondly, by selecting the Lift of those Laws which more immediately require Attention; from which latter Description they mail have to report from Time to Time, during the present Session, such as in their Opinion it may be fit to revive, continue, or make perpetual.

In drawing up the General Statement of such Temporary Laws as are now in Force, Your Committee have enumerated them in Chronological Order. They have endeavoured also to specify coiredtly each of the Original Acts, together with their respective subsidiary Acts, by which they have been either amended or continued: And if in so various and minute a Detail any Omission or Errors should be found, they have Reason to hope, that they are neither very numerous nor important; that they may be gradually supplied or corrected as they are discovered; and that at all Events the Statement now reported, will enable Parliament to proceed hereafter with greater Regularity and Precision in exercising this Species of Legislation.

The Matters themselves, which are comprized in this System of Temporary Laws, will upon Inspection appear to be extremely extensive and important. Many of them have been introduced for regulating the Fundtions of Government, and the Admimllration of Public Affairs, in their ordinary Course, and during Times of Tranauility: Many others have been enacted to guard against occasional Evils, and to provide for extraordinary Emergencies and transient Occurrences, during Times when the Public Tranquility has been disturbed.

It will be seen, that the Provision made for the Support of His Majesty's Household, and of the Honour and Dignity of the Crown, and those also for the Preservation of His Majesty's Person and Government against treasonable and seditious Practices and Attempts, have been placed hitherto only upon the Footing of Temporary Arrangement: That in the Administration of Justice, no permanent Laws have been yet enacted for authorizing the Punishment of Offenders by Trans *

Biftation Abroad, or Confinement in Penitentiary oufes at Home; nor for preserving the Police of the Metropolis: That the Measures adopted for the Prevention and Punishment of Attempts to seduce Persons serving in the Army and Navy, depend at present upon

Your Committee have, pursuant to the Orders of the House, made a further Progress in the Matters to them referred, and agreed upon this further Report:

Your Committee having already, in their First Report, laid before the House a Statement of all the Temporary Laws now in Force, which have been made from the Commencement of the Reign of King William the Third, to the Commencement of the present Session of Parliament proceed now to execute the rest of the Purposes for which they were appointed, by feledling the LIII of thol'e which more immediately require the Attention of Parliament in the present Session.

With this View, they have in the First Place prepared and annexed to this their Second Report, an Enumeration of all the Public General Laws which *

have expired within Twelve Months preceding the Commencement of the present Session. This Lift, by Retro spedt, includes all such as have expired since the nth of November 1799; omitting only the Annual Revenue Acts, and thol'e for regulating the Army, &c. which have been continued or replaced by subsequent Acts now in Force: And in this Lift the House will observe some which have been rendered unnecessary, by the Commercial Regulations established upon the Union between Great Britain and , and others

enacted on account of the high Price of Provisions, which have expired during the late Recess; it will also be remarked, that the Act for more effectually preventing Seditious Meetings and Assemblies has expired with the last Session of Parliament.

In

4 'Navembris: 85 t

41 Geo. HI.

In the Second Place, Your Committee have annexed an Enumeration of ail those Laws which are about to expire within Twelve Months subsequent to the Commencement of the present Session, or in the Course of the next Session, or at the End thereof; in which they have thought proper to include, prospectively, all which may expire upon or before the 31st of 1802. In this Lift, besides the Annual Revenue and Military Laws, there are also some which peculiarly concern the Safety of the State, and are about to expire very shortly unless continued: There are also some occasioned by the high Price of Provisions, and others concerning the Regulation of Trade, Navigation, and the Fisheries, which require very early Consideration; and l'ome very important Questions will present themselves for Difcullion, upon the Expiration of the Laws which concern the Police of the Metropolis, the Regulation of Aliens, and the present Modes of Punishment by Transportation, and Confinement in Penitentiary Houses.

In the Third Place, Your Committee have thought proper to subjoin an Enumeration of some Statutes whereof the Duration is temporary; but uncertain, depending upon contingent Circumstances; such as, the Continuance of Lives, the Laws of other Countries, Treaties with Foreign Powers, Hostilities, &c. conceiving it to be also necessary that some of these Statutes

should be brought under the View of the House, in or , der that it may be enabled more distinctly to foresee, and more readily to provide for any of the Exigencies which may arise upon their Termination; in this latter Lift, however, they have not thought it necessary to include several, which, although of a temporary and Contingent Duration, do not seem to require any special Notice; namely, such as have been made for the funding of particular Loans by Tontine, or the granting of personal Annuities for Public Services, Premiums" for Discoveries in Navigation, &c. &c. The House, however, will observe, that in this Lift there are not fewer than Fifty Laws which are to cease with the War, and that the Terms in which their Limitation is prescribed according to this Event, are nevertheless extremely difo ferent in different Acts.

Your Committee propose to report from Time to Time upon such of the several Laws herein after enumerated as concern Matters of ordinary Regulation in Revenue, Manufactures, and Commerce, and the ordinary Administration of Criminal and Civil Justice, so for as in their Opinion they are fit to be revived, continued, or made perpetual; leaving those' which provide for the Support and Discipline of the Army, and ' others which concern the higher Affairs of State, to the Notice ai)d Observation of the House itself.

A Petit ion of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of theml'elves and other Trustees for executing the Acts hereunder mentioned, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That an Act was passed in the Thirty-first Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, for amending several Roads leading from the Town of Tiverton, in the County of Devon; and that another Act was passed in the Seventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, to continue the said Act, and render the same more effectual, and for repairing and widening the lload from Bridge

Cross, near Bick/ey Bridge, to the Sign of the Swan, in the Town of Si/verten, and also the Road from Bick/ey Wood Cross to Ford Village Water, in the said County; and that the Trustees have proceeded to put the said Acts in Execution, and have made great Progress in amending, widening, and repairing the said several Roads, and for that Purpose have expended several considerable Sums of Money, which were borrowed, and are still owing, on the Credit of the said Acts; and that the said Sums of Money cannot be re-paid, nor the Roads effectually amended, improved, and kept in Repair, without the future Aid of Parliament: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, lor effecting the Purposes aforesaid, in such Manner, and under such Regulations and restrictions, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it Ih^ll appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Richard Ryder, Sir Edmund Cradock Hartopp, &c.: And they are to meet To-mor-

row Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Mr. Bragge reported from the Select Committee, appointed to enquire what Public General Laws have expired within Twelve Months preceding the Commencement of the present Session of Parliament; and also, what Laws are about to expire within Twelve Months subsequent to the Commencement of the present Session, or in the Course of the next Session^ or at the End thereof; and to report the fame, from Time to Time, to the House; with their Opinion which of them are fit to be revived, continued, or made perpetual; and to whom the Report which, upon the 12th Day of May 1796, w'as made from the Committee who were appointed to inspect and consider all the Temporary Laws of a Public Nature expired or expiring, was referred; and who were instrucled to enquire and report to the House what Temporary Laws of a Public or General Nature which have been made by the Parliaments of England or Great Britain since the Commencement of the Reign of King liamthe Third, and prior to the present Session of Parliament, are now in force — distinguishing the Matter of each Statute — its Date — Title — and Period of Continuance; together with their Observations thereon; That the Committee had made a further Progress, and had come to several Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Resolutions of the Committee were read; and are as followeth;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for reducing, until " the First Day of June One thousand Eight hundred, " the Duties upon Spiiits distilled from Melasses or Sugar, or any Mixture therewith; for prohibiting the 8 '

" Distillation of Spirits From Wheat or Wheat Flour;

" and for reducing, until the Twentieth Day of " tember One thousand Eight hundred, and better collecting, the Duties payable on the Importation of " Starch," as relates to the Duties upon Wort or Wash brewed or made from Melasses or Sugar, or any Mixture therewith, or to any Distiller or Distillers, or Maker or Makers of Spirits, which was, by another Act of the last Session of Parliament, revived and continued until the First Day of July 1801, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Refo/ved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That an Act, made in the Thirty-ninth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for enabling " His Majesty to prohibit the Exportation, and permit " the Importation of Corn, and for allowing the Impertation of other Articles of Provision without Payment of Duty, to continue in force until Six Weeks " after the Commencement of the next Session of Parliament," which Act was further continued anci amended by Two Acts of the last Session of Parliament, until Forty Days after the Commencement of the next Session of Parliament, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,-That an Act, made in the' last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act to allow, for Nine Months after " the passing of the Act, the Use of Sugar in the brewing of Beer," which Act wars to continue in force until the ill Day of April 1801, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Refo/ved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act to prohibit, until the First Day of " March One thousand Eight hundred, the making of " Low Wines or Spirits from Wheat, Barley, Malt, or " other Sort of Grain, or from any Meal, Flour, or any " Bran, in that Part of Great Britain called ,"

which was, by another Act of the last Session of Parliament, further continued until the ill Day of February 1801, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Capital' Bur- Petition of gestes, and Inhabitants, of the Town of Stafford, was staffordre of presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That spe£ting the the Paternal Care of our Sovereign having called Parlia- provisions of ment together for the express Purpose of taking into Consideration the Distresses of His People, the Petitioners beg Leave to lay before the House the Share which they bear in the general Calamity; they view with a just Abhorrence every Effort that may be made to wrest the Execution of the Laws from those Hands to which the Government has confided it; and they pledge themselves to refill to the utmost of their Power every Tendency to popular Commotion: But,- whilst they lament the unruly Efforts of a few misguided Individuals, they feel themselves called upon to bear their unequivocal Testimony to the general Loyalty of the People, their Attachment to the Person of our Sovereign, and the Happiness which they enjoy under-our excellent Constitution: The Petitioners might appeal to their peaceable and orderly Demeanour during the last Winter, when their Sufferings were extreme from the Pressure of Want and the Severity of the Season: Not merely the lower Orders of the People, but those above them, contemplated with an anxious Eye the Approach of a Harvest which seemed calculated to diminish, or do away, the Difficulties under which they laboured; but they have found themselves disappointed in every Expectation, and the Comforts which they had anticipated, and actually began to feel, have suddenly and unaccountably ended in a grievous Delusion; a Crop avowedly productive, and Seasons unprecedently favourable, have brought to them no Relief: They are left to lament the Horrors of Death in the Midfir of Plenty, and they deem it worthy the Investigation of Parliament, to- ascertain whether the Machinations of interested Individuals may not have contributed to frustrate the benignant Dispensations of Providence:

An Idea so novel in its Kind, as apparent Plenty and Prices enormously high, calls loudly on those whopoflels the Power so repress an Evil so malignant in its Aspect, and so fatal in its Consequences: Under the Pressure, therefore, of Distresses complicated in their Nature, and alarming in their Magnitude, the Petitioners humbly submit themselves to the Wisdom of Parliament, and they do it under the full Conviction, that the Tranquility and Prosperity of the Country are deeply involved in the Interposition^and immediate Efficacy of their Exertions.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Committee appointed to consider of the present high Price of Provisions.

Mr. Bragge, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of so much of several Acts, made in the . last Session of Parliament, as relates to reducing the Duties upon Wort or Wash brewed or made from Melasses or Sugar, or any Mixture therewith, or to any Distiller or Distillers, or Maker or Makers of Spirits; and to the prohibiting the making of Low Wines or Spirits from Wheat, and certain other Articles, in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for reducing, until " the First Day of June One thousand Eight hundred, " the Duties upon Spirits distilled from Melasses or " Sugar, or any Mixture therewith; for prohibiting " the Distillation of Spirits from Wheat or Wheat " Flour; and for reducing, until the Twentieth Day " of September One thousand Eight hundred, and bet-

tercollecting, the Duties payable on the Importation " of Starch," as relates to the Duties upon Wort or Wash brewed or made from Melasses or Sugar, or any Mixture therewith, or to any Distiller or Distillers,' or Maker or Makers of Spirits, which was, by another Act of the last Session of Parliament, revived and continued, until the 1 ft Day of July 1801, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act to prohibit, until the First Day of " March One thousand Eight hundred, the making of " Low Wines or Spirits from Wheat, Barley, Malt, or " other Sort of Grain, or from any Meal, Flour, or " any Bran, in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland," which was, by another Act of the last Session of Parliament, further continued until the ift Day of February 1801, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Gentlemen, who are appointed to prepare, and bring in, a Bill, pursuant to the Second and Third of the Resolutions, which upon Friday last were reported from the Select Committee appointed to enquire what Public General Laws have expired within Twelve Months preceding the Commencement of the present Session of Parliament; and also, what Laws are about to expire within Twelve Months subsequent to the Commencement of the present Session, or in the Course of the next Session, or at the End thereof; and to report the fame, from Time to Time, to the House, with their Opinion which of them are fit to be revived, continued, or made perpetual; and were then agreed to by the House, That they do make Provision in the said Bill, pursuant to the Resolutions now reported, and agreed to by the House.

Mr. Bragge, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the Supply granted t6 His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read} and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That One Hundred and Twenty Thousand Men be employed for the Sea Service for Three Lunar Months, commencing the i ft Day of January 1801, including Twenty-two Thousand Six Hundred and Ninety-six Marines.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Six Hundred and Sixty-six Thousand Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, for Wages for the said One Hundred and Twenty Thousand Men, for Three Lunar Months, commencing the ift Day of January 1801, at the Rate of One Pound Seventeen Shillings per Man per Month.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Six Hundred and Eighty-four Thousand Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, for Victuals for the said One Hundred and Twenty Thousand Men, for Three Lunar Months, commencing the ift Day of January 1801, at the Rate of One Pound Eighteen Shillings per Man per Month.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One Million and Eighty Thousand Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, for the Wear and Tear of the Ships in which the said One Hundred and Twenty Thousand Men are to serve, for Three Lunar Months, commencing the ift Day of January 1801, at the Rate of Three Pounds per Man per Month.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Ninety Thousand Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, for Ordnance for Sea Service on board the Ships in which the said One Hundred and Twenty Thousand Men are to serve, for Three Lunar Months, commencing the ift Day of January 1801, at the Rate of Five Shillings per Man per Month.

A PETITION of the Lord Provost, Magistrates, and Town Council, of the City of Edinburgh, and of divers of the Clergy and Inhabitants of the said City and Suburbs, was presented to the House, and read, Setting forth. That, owing to the Scarcity and high Price of Provisions at the End of the last, and during the Course of the present Year, it was found necessary to grant Relief to a Number of the poor Inhabitants of the City of Edinburgh, and Suburbs thereof, who, under different Circumstances, would not have been Objects of Public Charity; and that, in Hopes of the Necessitiesof the Poor being in a great Measure relieved by the next Harvest, the Petitioners, the Magistrates of Edinburgh, with the Advice of the principal Inhabitants, thought it more advilable to resort to a voluntary Subscription for the Relief of the Poor than to avail themselves of the Authority of the existing Laws to impose additional and extraordinary Poor Rates, for an Occa-lion which they hoped would prove of very short Duration; and that accordingly the Sum of £.9,700 was raised by voluntary Subscription among the Inhabitants of the said City and Suburbs, by Means of which Relief in Money, Provisions and Coals have been afforded, during the current Year, to above Four Thousand indigent, and in general industrious Families; and that the said Fund is now very nearly exhausted, while, at the same Time, the Petitioners fee with Concern, that, owing to the Operation of the same Causes, the Necessity of continuing Relief to the industrious Poor rfe-Vol. 55.

Mr. William Dundas reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Lord Provost, Magi fixates, and Town Council, of the City of , and of

divers of the Clergy and Inhabitants of the said City and Suburbs, was referred; Tha£ the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and lie read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, a Member present informed Your Committee, That, owing to the Scarcity and High Price of Provisions at the End of the last, and during the Course of the present Year, it was found necessary to grant Relief to a 'Number of the poor Inhabitants of the City of

burgh, and Suburbs thereof, who, under different Circumstances would not have been Objects of Public Charity; and a large Sum of Money was raised by Voluntary Subscription among the Inhabitants of the said City and Suburbs, by Means of which. Relief in Money, Provisions, and Coals, has been afforded during the current Year to a great Number of indigent, and in general industrious Families: That the said Fund is now very nearly exhausted, while, owing to the Operation of the same Causes, the Necessity of continuing Relief to the industrious Poor remains to an equal Extent, and will probably be felt for several Months to come: That as the former Mode of railing Money by voluntary Subscription has been generally complained of as partial and . unequal, it is now become necessary to resort to a general Assessment in this extraordinary Emergency:

And he added. That the great Alteration which has taken place in the Circumstances and Manners of the People, renders several Alterations and Modifications of the existing Laws of Scotland necessary, in order to meet the present Emergency, and carry into Execution the above salutary Purposes.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the better Relief of the Poor in the City of,

and the Suburbs thereof, and certain Districts adjoining the reto: And that Mr. Secretary Dundas and Mr. William Dundas do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

by which the Average Price in London, published in The Gazette, in the Third Week after the Importation of such Indian Com or Maize, shall be less than Fifty-five shillings.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Wilmot and Mr. Popham:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for suspending, until the Twentieth Day of One thousand Eight hundred and One, the Duties on Hops imported, and for charging other Duties in lieu thereof; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to prohibit, until the First Day of January One thousand Eight hundred and Two, the Use of Corn in distilling of Spirits or making of Starch j without any Amendment; And also.

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for naturalizing Joseph Augustus; to which the

Lords desire the Concurrence of this House.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

The House, according to Order, proceeded to take into Consideration the Report which was made from the Committee appointed to consider of the present high Price of Provisions j and to whom so much of His Majesty's most Gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament, as relates thereto, and also the several Petitions presented to the House complaining of the high Price of Provisions, were referred.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Bragge took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Bragge reported from the Committee, That he was directed by the Committee to make several Motions, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be now received.

Mr. Bragge accordingly reported from the said Committee, That he was directed by the Committee to move the House, that an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, representing to His Majesty, that, having taken into Consideration the Difficulties experienced by His Majesty's Subjects in consequence of the present high Price of Corn, and being persuaded that the Prevention of all unnecessary Consumption of the same will furnish one of the surest and most effectual Means of alleviating the present Pressure, and of providing for the necessary Demands of the Year, we do most humbly request His Majesty, that He will be graciously pleased to issue His Royal Proclamation, recommending, in the strongest Manner, to all such Personsas have the Means of procuring other Articles of Food, the greatest Economy and Frugality in the Use of every Species of Grain; and that His Majesty will cause such Proclamation to be circulated through every Part of the Kingdom, in such Manner as shall appear to His Majesty's Wisdom bell calculated to produce, to the greatest Extent, those beneficial Consequences which mull result from carrying into full Effect His Majesty's Injundlions on a Point so important to the Subsistence of His People.

And Mr. Bragge moved the House accordingly.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, representing to His Majesty, that, having taken into Consideration the Difficulties experienced by His Majesty's Subjects in consequence of the present high Price of Corn, and being persuaded that the Prevention of all unnecelliiry Consumption of the same will furnish one of the surest and most effectual Means of alleViating the present Pressure, and of providing for the necessary Demands of the Year, we do most humbly fcc^ucft His Majesty, that He will be graciously pleated to issue His Royal Proclamation, recommending, in the strongest Manner, to all such Persons as have the Means of procuring other Articles of Food, the greatest Economy and Frugality in the Use of every Species of Grain; and that His Majesty will cause such Proclamation to be circulated through every Part of the Kingdom, in such Manner as shall appear to His Majesty's Wisdom best calculated to produce, to the greatest Extent, those beneficial Consequences which mull result from carrying into full Effect His Majesty's Injunctions on a Point so important to the Subsistence of His People.

Ordered, That a Committee be appointed to draw up an Address, to be presented to His Majesty upon the said Resolution:

Arid a Committee w'as appointed of Mr. Ryder, Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Secretary at War, Mr. Attorney General, the Master of the Rolls, Mr.

Bragge, Sir William Scot/, Mr. Rose, Mr. Hiley -

ton, Mr. Sargent, Mr. Long, Mr. Solicitor General, Mr. Canning, Mr. John Smyth, Mr. Adams; or any Five of them: And they are to withdraw, immediately, into the Speaker's Chamber.

Ordered, That the Report which was made from the Committee, appointed to consider of the present high Price of Provisions, be referred to the said Corhmittee.

Mr. Ryder reported from the said Committee, That

the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth j viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We", Your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons, of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, beg Leave to tepresent to Your Majesty, that, having taken into Consideration the Difficulties experienced by Your Majesty's Subjects in Consequence of the present hi'gh Price of Corn, and being persuaded that the Prevention of all unnecessary Consumption of the same will furnish one of the surest and most effectual Means of alleviating the present Pressure, and of providing for the necessary Demands of the Year we do most humbly request Your Majesty, that You will be graciously pleased to issue Your Royal Proclamation, recommending, in the strongest Manner, to all such Persons as have the Means of procuring other Articles of Food, the greatest Economy and Frugality in the Use of every Species of Grain; and that Your Majesty will cause such Proclamation to be circulated through every Part of the Kingdom, in such Manner as shall appear to Your Majesty's Wisdom belt- calculated to produce, to the greatest Extent, those beneficial Consequences which must result from carrying into full Effect Your Majesty's Injunctions, on a Point so important to the Subsistence gf Your People.

The said Address being read a Second Time,' was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That a Message be sent to the Lords, to communicate to their Lordships the said Address; and that their Lordships Concurrence be desired thereto.

That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, humbly to allure Him, that we have taken into our most serious Consideration the Papers relative to the Negotiation for Peace with France, and that the Result of our Refledlions on this important Subject, founded as well on due Examination of the Documents now referred to us, as on Experience of the past Condu<ft of most of H is Majesty's Allies, is an humble, but earnest Desire, that His Majesty will omit no proper Opportunity which may arise, consistently with the good Faith ever preserved on the Part of His Majesty, of entering into a separate Negotiation with the Government of France for a speedy and honourable Peace; and farther to implore His Majesty, not to sanction any new Engagements which shall preclude such a Mode of Negotiation;

That the Petitioners feel it their Duty at this Time to state to the House, that the Condition of the labouring People in that populous Borough'and its Neighbourhood is extremely deplorable, owing to the excessive high Price of Corn, and other Articles of Sustenance; and that they are chiefly Manufacturers of Woollen Goods, or connected therewith, and the Produce of their Labour is almost un-fideable, from the general Inability of the Poor to puchase Clothing; and that the Master Manufacturers (a numerous and most valuable Class of Men) have struggled for focne Time with the greatest Difficulties, in endeavouring to find Employment for their Workmen,

of the next Session, or at the End thereof; and to report the fame, from Time to Time, to the House, with their Opinion which of them are fit to be revived, continued, or made perpetual, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table i Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for reducing,.until the " First Day of June One thousand Eight hundred, the " Duties upon Spirits distilled from Melafl'es or Sugar, " or any Mixture therewith, for prohibiting the Distillation of Spirits from Wheat or Wheat Flour, and " for seducing, until the Twentieth Day of September " One thousand Eight hundred, and better collecting " the Duties payable on the Importation of Starch," as relates to the reducing and better collecting the Duties payable on the Importation of Starch, is expired, and fit to be revived and continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled.

An Act for granting a Liberty to carry Sugars of the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture, of any of His Majesty's Sugar Colonies in , from the said

" Colonies directly to Foreign Parts, in Ships built in " Great Britain, and navigated according to Law," which was to continue in Force for Five Years from the 29th Day of September 1739, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, and which, by several subsequent Acts, made in the Seventeenth, Twenty-fourth, and Thirty-first Years of his said Majesty's Reign, and the Fourth, Twelfth, Eighteenth, Twenty-sixth, and Thirty-third Years of His present Majesty's Reign, was further continued until the 29th Day of September 1799, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, is near expiring, and fit to be continued, subject to the Regulations contained in an Act, made in the Thirty-second Year of His present Majesty's Reign, intituled, "An Act for regulating the Allowance of the Drawback " and Payment of the Bounty on the Exportation of Sugar, and for permitting the Importation of Sugar " and Coffee into the Bahama and Bermuda Islands in " Foreign Ships." 1

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Thirty-ninth Year, of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act to " enable His Majesty, by Order in Council, to permit, " until Six Weeks after the Commencement of the " next Session of Parliament, such Goods, as shall be " specified in such Order, to be imported into this " Kingdom in Neutral Ships," which was, by Two Acts of the last Session of Parliament, continued until the Expiration of Forty Days after the Commencement of the then next Session of Parliament, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Thirty-seventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act authorizing His Majesty, for a limited Time, to make " Regulations respecting the Trade and Commerce to " and from The Cape of Good Hope," which was by Four Acts, of the Thirty-eighth, Thirty-ninth, and Fortieth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, further continued, until the Expiration of Forty Days after the Commencement of the present Session of Parliament, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

A Petition of several Master Taylors, on Behalf of themselves and the rest of the Master Taylors residing within the City of London and Five Miles thereof, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by an Act, made ?n the Eighth Year of the lieign of King George the Third, to amend an Act, made in the Seventh Year of King George the First, for regulating the Journeymen Taylors within the \Vreekly Bills of Mortality, it is enacted, that there should be paid to every Servant or Journeyman, to be employed in pursuance of the said Act, a Sum not exceeding Two Shillings and Seven Pence Halfpenny per Diem (except as therein excepted) and that, by the said Act, it is also enacted, that if any Master Taylor, or other Person using or exercising the Art or Mystery of a Taylor, within the Limits therein mentioned, should give, allow, or pay, or cause, permit, or suffer to be given, allowed, or paid, to any Servant or Journeyman in the said Bu-finess, any more or greater Wages or Allowances, than the Wages and Allowances aforesaid, or such other Wages and Allowances as should thereafter, from Time to Time, be ordered and appointed by virtue of the said Act, should be committed to the House of Correction, there to be kept to hard Labour, or to the Common Gaol, for any Time not exceeding Two Months, nor lei's than Fourteen Days, at the Discretion of the Justices before whom such Person should be convicted; and that, by the said Act, it is also enacted, that it should be lawful for the Mayor, Aldermen, and Recorder of the City of London, for the Time being, at their General Quarter Sessions, or General Sessions of the Peace assembled, from Time to Time, upon Application being made to them for that Purpose, to alter, regulate, and appoint the Wages and Allowances to be paid or made to Journeymen Taylors, and Servants retained or employed in the Art or Mystery of a Taylor, within the City of London, or within Five Miles thereof, and the

Hours of Work j and that an Application was, about Twenty-five Years since, made to the Quarter Sessions in the Manner by the said Act directed, to settle the Wages and Allowances to be paid and given to Journeymen Taylors, and which were accordingly settled at the Rate of Eighteen Shillings and Nine Pence per Week, and that no Alteration, or Order of Sessions, has been made since, in respect of the said Wages and Allowances; and that the Journeymen Taylors have, at several Times, since the Wages were settled as aforesaid, entered into Combinations, and struck for an Increase of Wages, which the Petitioners were under the absolute Necessity to comply with; and that the Wages the Journeymen now receive is Twenty-five Shillings per Week, and which were obtained in the Manner above stated, and without any Order of Sessions; and that the Petitioners, at the several Times when the Journeymea struck for an Increase of Wages as aforesaid, gave it them without knowing or conceiving the y were thereby incur-

Petition from A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Town and Neigh-f tctinv'ouo. bourhood of Bradford, in the County of York, was pre-P fented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the

Situation of the Poor of the said Town and Neighbourhood is most deplorable, from the exorbitant Price of Corn and other Provisions, the Dilbelfes wiicreof arc most alarmingly aggravated by great Numbers of industrious Poor being out of Employment; and that the Evil is daily increasing, and the principal S'upport of the Poor of the said Town and Neighbourhood is Meal made from Oats, a large Quantity whereof is bought up for Horses employed only as Pleasure Horles, and for Ilounds and other Dogs: And therefore propoling to the lerious Consideration of the House, as the most, if not the only, effectual Method to relieve the almost infup-portable Dili relics of the Poor in this Part of the Country, will be to prohibit, for a Time to be limited. Oats and other Grain, except Beans, from being given to Pleasure Horses, Hounds, and other Dogs, inaimuch as the Petitioners are convinced that no Measure short of this will relieve the severe Calamities which the Poor of the said Town and Neighbourhood are now labouring under.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Committee, appointed to consider of the present high Price of Provisions.
